arXiv:2611.18542v1 [stat.ML] 13 Nov 2026

Elliptic Sampling: Optimal interpolant schedules for Gaussians and Beyond

Cole Becker ††thanks: Corresponding author: colbeck@mit.edu.    Taylan Kargin ††thanks: Equal contribution.    Kimia Hassibi22footnotemark: 2    Asuman Ozdaglar    Pablo A. Parrilo Affiliation: Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS)
Massachusetts Institute of Technology
Abstract

Generative modeling based on stochastic interpolants requires specifying two key choices: an interpolant schedule bridging the initial and target distributions, and an efficient discretization of the resulting probability-flow ODE. In this work, we introduce a new framework for joint schedule/discretization design based on the analyticity properties of the (complexified) ODE trajectories, which in turn ensure good numerical behavior. Our formulation can be solved exactly via conformal mapping, yielding a natural family of variance-preserving elliptic schedules, parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions. Pairing an elliptic schedule with a tailored discretization, we obtain Zoloflow, a new sampling algorithm closely connected to Zolotarev’s optimal rational function approximants. Crucially, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow explicitly incorporate the condition number κ\kappa of the target distribution and reduce to the classical trig schedule in the limit κ→1\kappa\rightarrow 1. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow achieves minimax optimality among all oblivious score-span algorithms, attaining total-variation error ε\varepsilon using Θ⁡(log⁡κ​log⁡(d/ε))\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)) (exact) score queries. For the log-concave case, the elliptic schedule allows sampling with at most ε\varepsilon 2-Wasserstein-error by requiring merely O~​(d​polylog​(κ,1/ε))\widetilde{O}(\sqrt{d}\,\mathrm{polylog}(\kappa,1/\varepsilon)) score evaluations. Complementing these theoretical results, we empirically evaluate the elliptic schedule on general (non-log-concave) target distributions, including detailed comparisons with alternative schedule proposals on both synthetic benchmarks and existing image generation datasets.

1  Introduction

Generative modeling seeks to produce novel random samples X∼πX\sim\pi from a complicated target distribution π\pi on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} using a representation learned from a finite training dataset 𝒟train={X(i)}\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\{X^{(i)}\} of iid samples X(i)∼πX^{(i)}\sim\pi. Many modern approaches learn an ordinary or stochastic differential equation (ODE or SDE) which progressively transports a simple initial reference distribution, typically Gaussian, to the target π\pi. Stochastic interpolant (SI) framework (Albergo et al., 2025) unifies these flow-based (ODE) and diffusion-based (SDE) approaches and offers flexibility in shaping the transport dynamics through interpolant schedules.

Although different valid schedules all bridge the same initial and target distributions under exact continuous-time transport and are related through time and space reparameterizations, they can induce trajectories with substantially different regularity properties, including Lipschitz continuity and complex analyticity. These properties, in turn, govern how accurately and efficiently the resulting dynamics, most notably the probability-flow ODE (PF-ODE), can be solved numerically. Sampling performance, therefore, depends not only on the choice of interpolant schedule, but also on the discretization scheme used to integrate the induced dynamics with a finite number of evaluations of the learned score/velocity field, typically represented by a deep neural network. Despite this intrinsic coupling, interpolant schedules and the discretization schemes are usually designed separately and chosen largely heuristically. This raises the following central question:

Given a fixed budget of evaluations of the learned score/velocity field, how should one choose both the interpolant schedule and the numerical procedure used to integrate the resulting PF-ODE?

1.1  Contributions

We address this question by developing a principled theory of joint schedule and discretization design, which seeks the best achievable sampling accuracy over a class of target distributions under a finite budget of score/velocity-field evaluations. Our contributions are as follows:

1. Minimax-optimal Gaussian Sampling with Zoloflow.

We formulate sampling from a Gaussian target with condition number at most κ\kappa as a minimax problem over oblivious score-span algorithms with a fixed budget of exact score evaluations, and show that it reduces to a scalar rational approximation problem solved by Zolotarev’s optimal approximants. The resulting algorithm attains dTVd_{\mathrm{TV}} error ε\varepsilon with Θ⁡(log⁡κ​log⁡(d/ε))\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)) score evaluations, which is minimax optimal. It admits a dynamical realization, Zoloflow, which pairs a variance-preserving schedule parametrized by Jacobi elliptic functions with a modified Euler-type discretization; both depend on κ\kappa and reduce to the trig schedule as κ→1\kappa\to 1.

2. Complex-Analytic Optimality of Elliptic Schedules.

We propose a complementary design criterion: the width of the complex strip around real time to which PF-ODE trajectories extend holomorphically, which governs the convergence of high-order numerical integrators. For Gaussian targets, maximizing this width is solved exactly by conformal mapping and recovers the elliptic schedule of the Zolotarev construction. For strongly log-concave targets, we establish explicit lower bounds on the width attained by the elliptic schedule.

3. Efficient Log-Concave Sampling with Elliptic Schedules.

Combining these width bounds with collocation methods for analytic ODEs, we obtain a sampler for strongly log-concave targets that attains W2W_{2} error ε\varepsilon with O⁡(d​log3.5⁡(κ​d/ε))O(\sqrt{d}\,\log^{3.5}(\kappa d/\varepsilon)) score evaluations. Because it relies on a generic high-order solver rather than the Gaussian-specific Zolotarev structure, this result isolates the benefit of the elliptic schedule itself.

4. Empirical Evaluations of Schedule and Discretization.

On Gaussian targets, we empirically confirm the gains of Zoloflow over existing discretizations predicted by the minimax theory. Beyond Gaussians, we pair the elliptic schedule with state-of-the-art numerical solvers, and compare it against alternative schedules at matched evaluation budgets on synthetic and image-generation benchmarks. Across solvers, the elliptic schedule outperforms alternative schedules, including on non-log-concave targets beyond the scope of our theory.

Throughout the rest of the paper, we assume the score/velocity-field function evaluations are exact. All proofs and additional results are deferred to the Appendix.

1.2  Related Work

Interpolant and noise schedules.

Stochastic interpolants (Albergo et al., 2025) separate the path, set by the schedule (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}), from its numerical integration. Schedules are often chosen by hand, as with the trig schedule (Nichol and Dhariwal, 2021) and the noise levels of EDM (Karras et al., 2022b); the continuous-time variational bound depends on the schedule only through its endpoint signal-to-noise ratios (Kingma et al., 2023), and Dieleman (2024) argues that the schedule entangles several design choices. Principled designs optimize the time grid for a given solver (Sabour et al., 2024), minimize an averaged Lipschitz constant of the drift (Chen et al., 2025), or adapt to high-dimensional mixtures (Aranguri et al., 2025), and Gao et al. (2024) study the regularity of the resulting flows. We instead choose the schedule by the analyticity of the flow in complex time. The elliptic family reduces to the trig schedule at κ=1\kappa=1, contains the closed-form Gaussian schedule of Align Your Steps after rescaling (Section K.3.1), and is asymptotically optimal for the worst-case drift-Lipschitz criterion whose Gaussian minimizer is the schedule of Chen et al. (2025) (Section K.4).

Gaussian sampling and rational approximation.

Sampling from 𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) amounts to computing Λ−1/2z\Lambda^{-1/2}z, for which rational approximations, and Zolotarev’s optimal ones in particular, converge far faster than polynomial ones when the spectrum is wide (Higham, 2008; Hale et al., 2008; Nakatsukasa and Freund, 2016; Gawlik, 2019; Beckermann and Townsend, 2017; Trefethen and Wilber, 2025). The closest work to ours is Liu (2026), which samples Gaussians from smoothed-score queries, our interpolant scores in variance-exploding coordinates (Section K.3). Combining these queries through a sinc-quadrature rational approximation of x−1/2x^{-1/2}, Liu obtains O⁡((log⁡κ+log⁡(d/ε))​log⁡(d/ε))O\bigl((\log\kappa+\log(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon))\log(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)\bigr) queries, improving the κ\sqrt{\kappa} dependence of unsmoothed scores to log⁡κ\log\kappa; the accompanying lower bounds count bits received from a finite-precision oracle rather than exact queries. We improve on this in two ways. Zoloflow realizes the endpoint-normalized Zolotarev approximant, which removes the additive log2⁡(d/ε)\log^{2}(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon) term (Theorem 4.4), and we prove a matching lower bound on the number of exact queries for oblivious score-span algorithms, a class that contains Liu’s sampler and the standard diffusion solvers (Theorem 4.4). Moreover, unlike Liu’s sampler, Zoloflow is a schedule plus a discretization of the probability-flow ODE, so the schedule carries over to non-Gaussian targets.

Fast samplers and discretizations.

Many works accelerate sampling for a fixed schedule by improving the discretization: DDIM (Song et al., 2022), the exponential integrators DEIS (Zhang and Chen, 2023) and DPM-Solver(++) (Lu et al., 2022a; Lu et al., 2022b), and the Heun sampler of EDM (Karras et al., 2022b); Align Your Steps (Sabour et al., 2024) instead tunes the time grid for a fixed solver. We design the schedule and the discretization together. On Gaussian targets all of these solvers are oblivious score-span algorithms (Lemmas 4.1 and E), so our lower bound covers them, and on non-Gaussian targets the elliptic schedule also improves standard solvers such as DPM-Solver++ (Section N.2).

Complexity of diffusion and log-concave sampling.

Diffusion samplers converge in polynomially many steps given accurate scores, for both the reverse SDE (Chen et al., 2023b) and the probability-flow ODE (Chen et al., 2023a), while classical samplers for strongly log-concave targets pay polynomially in the condition number (Chewi, 2026). When an ODE solution is analytic, collocation reaches accuracy ε\varepsilon in polylog⁡(1/ε)\mathrm{polylog}(1/\varepsilon) steps (Lee et al., 2018), which Gatmiry et al. (2026) use to give high-accuracy guarantees for diffusion samplers. The step count depends on how far the solution extends into complex time; we choose the schedule to maximize this region, which gives a query complexity polylogarithmic in both κ\kappa and 1/ε1/\varepsilon for log-concave targets (Section 5).

Schedules as approximation problems.

Choosing a schedule so that a fixed budget of steps is as accurate as possible has close analogues. For gradient descent on a quadratic, stepsizes define a polynomial in the Hessian, and Chebyshev stepsizes (Agarwal et al., 2021) attain the minimax O⁡(κ​log⁡(1/ε))O(\sqrt{\kappa}\log(1/\varepsilon)) rate; the silver stepsize schedule (Altschuler and Parrilo, 2025; Altschuler and Parrilo, 2026) accelerates gradient descent beyond quadratics through the stepsizes alone. Score queries instead produce rational functions of the precision (Lemma 4.1), so Zolotarev’s approximant replaces the Chebyshev polynomial and κ\sqrt{\kappa} becomes log⁡κ\log\kappa. Similarly, double-exponential and sinc quadrature (Takahasi and Mori, 1973; Mori, 2005; Stenger, 2000), like the sampler of Liu (2026), change variables so that the integrand is analytic in a wide strip and then use a uniform grid; the elliptic schedule is the time change that maximizes this strip, and Zoloflow queries on a uniform grid in the new time.

2  Preliminaries

2.1  Stochastic Interpolants

Stochastic interpolants provide a general framework for constructing a continuous path between a simple reference distribution and a target (Albergo et al., 2025), and are defined as the stochastic process

xt=αt​z+βt​x1,t∈[0,1],x_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}x_{1},\qquad t\in[0,1], (1)

where z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) is the reference distribution, and x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi is the target, and (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}) is the interpolant schedule. Stochastic interpolants induce a deterministic probability-flow ODE with drift (velocity field) given by

bt​(x)≜𝔼⁡[x˙t∣xt=x]b_{t}(x)\triangleq\mathbb{E}\!\left[\dot{x}_{t}\mid x_{t}=x\right] (2)

so that, under standard regularity conditions, the solution of

X˙t=bt​(Xt),X0∼𝒩⁡(0,Id),\dot{X}_{t}=b_{t}(X_{t}),\qquad X_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), (3)

has marginal law Xt∼ptX_{t}\sim p_{t} where pt=ℒ⁡(xt)p_{t}=\mathcal{L}(x_{t}) is the law of the interpolant at time tt. For the linear interpolant (1), the velocity field can be expressed using the score function st​(x)≜∇log⁡pt​(x)s_{t}(x)\triangleq\nabla\log p_{t}(x) or the conditional mean of the target sample. Indeed, using Tweedie’s formula βt​𝔼​[x1∣xt=x]=x+αt2​st​(x)\beta_{t}\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x_{t}=x]=x+\alpha_{t}^{2}s_{t}(x),

bt​(x)=α˙tαt​x+βt​(β˙tβt−α˙tαt)​𝔼​[x1∣xt=x]=β˙tβt​x+αt2​(β˙tβt−α˙tαt)​st​(x).b_{t}(x)=\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}x+\beta_{t}\left(\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}-\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x_{t}=x]=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}x+\alpha_{t}^{2}\left(\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}-\frac{\dot{\alpha}_{t}}{\alpha_{t}}\right)s_{t}(x). (4)
Definition 2.1 (VP interpolant schedules).

An interpolant schedule (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) is variance preserving (VP) if αt2+βt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1 on [0,1][0,1], with α\alpha strictly decreasing from 11 to 00 and β\beta strictly increasing from 00 to 11. Equivalently, (αt,βt)=(cos⁡φ⁡(t),sin⁡φ⁡(t))(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(\cos\varphi(t),\sin\varphi(t)) for a unique phase φ=arccos⁡α\varphi=\arccos\alpha in

𝒞≜{φ:[0,1]→[0,π2]strictly increasing:φ(0)=0,φ(1)=π2}.\mathcal{C}\triangleq\bigl\{\varphi:[0,1]\to[0,\tfrac{\pi}{2}]\ \text{strictly increasing}:\ \varphi(0)=0,\ \varphi(1)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\bigr\}.

Denote 𝒮\mathcal{S} as the class of VP schedules. Choosing a schedule in 𝒮\mathcal{S} amounts to choosing a phase in 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For VP schedules, αt​α˙t+βt​β˙t=0\alpha_{t}\dot{\alpha}_{t}+\beta_{t}\dot{\beta}_{t}=0, so (4) simplifies to

bt​(x)=β˙tβt​(x+st​(x)).b_{t}(x)=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\bigl(x+s_{t}(x)\bigr). (5)

2.2  Problem Setup

In this paper we study the following algorithm design problem.

Problem 2.2.

Given a class 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} of sampling algorithms that use at most rr score evaluations and a class 𝖯\mathsf{P} of target distributions, we seek the algorithm whose output law π^alg​(π)\hat{\pi}_{\mathrm{alg}}(\pi) is uniformly closest to the target over the class,

infalg∈𝒜rsupπ∈𝖯dist⁡(π^alg​(π),π),\inf_{\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r}}\ \sup_{\pi\in\mathsf{P}}\ \mathrm{dist}\big(\hat{\pi}_{\mathrm{alg}}(\pi),\pi\big), (6)

for a distance dist\mathrm{dist} between probability measures

Algorithms access the target only through an exact score oracle, which returns st​(x)=∇log⁡pt​(x)s_{t}(x)=\nabla\log p_{t}(x) for a queried pair (t,x)(t,x), and their cost is the number of queries. Score oracles for different schedules are interchangeable: by a change of time and spatial scale, one query for a VP schedule answers one query for any other schedule (Proposition K.1), so the schedule is a genuine design choice.

Definition 2.3 (Algorithm class 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r}: oblivious score-span algorithms).

An algorithm alg∈𝒜r\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r} is a pairing of (i) a stochastic interpolant schedule (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}) with (ii) a discretization of the probability-flow ODE (3) that makes rr evaluations of the exact score st=∇log⁡pts_{t}=\nabla\log p_{t} of the corresponding interpolant. Formally, starting from x0=z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{0}=z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), each iterate lies in the span of the previous iterates and score evaluations,

xj∈span{x0,…,xj−1,st0(x0),…,stj−1(xj−1)},j=1,…,r,x_{j}\in\operatorname{span}\bigl\{x_{0},\dots,x_{j-1},\ s_{t_{0}}(x_{0}),\dots,s_{t_{j-1}}(x_{j-1})\bigr\},\qquad j=1,\dots,r,

that is, for predetermined coefficients ai​j,bi​ja_{ij},b_{ij},

xj=∑i=0j−1ai​jxi+∑i=0j−1bi​jsti(xi),j=1,…,r,x_{j}=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}a_{ij}\,x_{i}+\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}b_{ij}\,s_{t_{i}}(x_{i}),\qquad j=1,\dots,r, (7)

and the output is xralg≜xrx_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}\triangleq x_{r}, with law π^alg​(π)≜ℒ⁡(xralg)\hat{\pi}_{\mathrm{alg}}(\pi)\triangleq\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}). The schedule, which determines the oracle sts_{t}, and the discretization, given by the query times t0,…,tr−1∈(0,1)t_{0},\dots,t_{r-1}\in(0,1) and the coefficients ai​j,bi​ja_{ij},b_{ij}, are the design variables. They are fixed in advance (oblivious): they may depend on κ\kappa, dd, and rr, but not on the particular target π∈𝖯\pi\in\mathsf{P}.

This class contains the standard fixed-step explicit ODE solvers (e.g., Euler, Heun, DDIM, and DPM-Solver++); see the remark at the end of Appendix G for its relation to general linear methods and implicit solvers. For the theoretical results in this paper, we make the following assumption on the target distributions:

Assumption 2.4 (Target Distributions).

𝖯\mathsf{P} is one of two nested classes of centered distributions with condition number at most κ≥1\kappa\geq 1: Gaussians with precision spectrum in [1,κ][1,\kappa], and strongly log-concave distributions with curvature in [1,κ][1,\kappa],

𝖦κ={𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1):Id⪯Λ⪯κ​Id}⊂𝖯κ={π∝e−V​centered:Id⪯∇2V⪯κ​Id}.\mathsf{G}_{\kappa}=\big\{\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}):I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}\big\}\;\subset\;\mathsf{P}_{\kappa}=\big\{\pi\propto e^{-V}\ \text{centered}:I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\kappa I_{d}\big\}.
Remark (Zero mean).

Centering is without loss of generality. If x1x_{1} has mean μ\mu, then xt=x~t+βt​μx_{t}=\tilde{x}_{t}+\beta_{t}\mu, where x~t\tilde{x}_{t} is the interpolant of the centered target, so the centered score is s~t​(y)=st​(y+βt​μ)\tilde{s}_{t}(y)=s_{t}(y+\beta_{t}\mu) and each centered query costs one query of the original score. One can therefore sample the centered target and add μ\mu at the end; μ\mu itself is recovered to any accuracy from a single score query near t=0t=0 (Section I.3).

In Section 4, we characterize the minimax query complexity of Gaussian sampling in total variation, up to universal constants, among oblivious score-span algorithms. Every algorithm in 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} outputs q⁡(Λ)​zq(\Lambda)z, where qq has numerator and denominator degrees at most rr. This connects sampling to relative-error rational approximation of λ−1/2\lambda^{-1/2} on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. Zoloflow implements an endpoint-normalized version of Zolotarev’s optimal scalar approximant. Combining this construction with Gaussian TV bounds yields the matching upper and lower query-complexity bounds in Theorem 4.4. For 𝖯=𝖯κ\mathsf{P}=\mathsf{P}_{\kappa} in Section 5 we show that, combined with collocation methods for analytic ODEs, this elliptic schedule samples with W2W_{2} error ε\varepsilon using O⁡(d​polylog​(κ,d,1/ε))O\big(\sqrt{d}\,\mathrm{polylog}(\kappa,d,1/\varepsilon)\big) score evaluations.

3  The Elliptic Schedule

3.1  Elliptic Stochastic Interpolant

Motivation

As discussed in Definition 2.1, a VP schedule is equivalent to a phase function φ∈𝒞\varphi\in\cal C. Our primary criterion for choosing φ\varphi will concern the analyticity properties it induces in the ODE solution XtX_{t}, when extended to the complex plane.

For a Gaussian target 𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}), the ODE (3) can be solved as Xt=(αt2​Id+βt2​Λ−1)12​X0X_{t}=(\alpha_{t}^{2}I_{d}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Lambda^{-1})^{\frac{1}{2}}X_{0}, and thus the eigenmodes are given by

xλ​(t)=α​(t)2+λ−1​β​(t)2​xλ​(0).x_{\lambda}(t)=\sqrt{\alpha(t)^{2}+\lambda^{-1}\beta(t)^{2}}\,x_{\lambda}(0).

This has branch point singularities whenever the expression inside the square root vanishes, i.e., whenever cos(φ(t))2+λ−1sin(φ(t))2=1−(1−λ−1)sin2φ(t)=0\cos(\varphi(t))^{2}+\lambda^{-1}\sin(\varphi(t))^{2}=1-(1-\lambda^{-1})\sin^{2}\varphi(t)=0. Thus, our design problem is to find φ\varphi such that the roots tt of this equation are as far as possible from the real axis, whenever λ∈[1,κ]\lambda\in[1,\kappa]. This ensures that the ODE solution XtX_{t} is analytic on a wide strip. The optimal such φ\varphi can be nicely characterized as follows:

A proof is provided in Appendix D.

The optimality of the Jacobi amplitude leads directly to the following definition:

Definition 3.2 (Elliptic schedule).

For a given κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, let

m=1−κ−1,K=K⁡(m),K′=K⁡(1−m).m=1-\kappa^{-1},\qquad K=K(m),\qquad K^{\prime}=K(1-m).

The elliptic interpolant schedule is the VP schedule corresponding to the Jacobi amplitude phase φ∗​(t)=am⁡(K​t∣m)\varphi_{*}(t)=\operatorname{am}(Kt\mid m):

αt=cos⁡(am⁡(K​t∣m)),βt=sin⁡(am⁡(K​t∣m))t∈[0,1],\alpha_{t}=\cos(\operatorname{am}(Kt\mid m)),\qquad\beta_{t}=\sin(\operatorname{am}(Kt\mid m))\qquad t\in[0,1], (9)

these functions are well understood and known as the Jacobi elliptic functions cn\cn and sn\sn. We thus write the elliptic schedule as

αt=cn⁡(K​t∣m),βt=sn⁡(K​t∣m),t∈[0,1],\alpha_{t}=\cn(Kt\mid m),\qquad\beta_{t}=\sn(Kt\mid m),\qquad t\in[0,1], (10)

The elliptic schedule is variance-preserving, and satisfies all properties in Definition 2.1. The holomorphic properties of φ∗\varphi_{*} guarantee that αt\alpha_{t} and βt\beta_{t} are also holomorphic on the complex strip Sγ∗S_{\gamma_{*}}. A unique property of the elliptic schedule is the dependence on the condition number κ\kappa (Figure 2). For κ=1\kappa=1, this reduces to the trigonometric schedule from Albergo et al. (2025). Figure 3 places it next to common schedules.

3.2  Elliptic schedule as a two-parameter family

While the construction above uses the normalized precision interval spec​(Λ)⊆[1,κ]\text{spec}(\Lambda)\subseteq[1,\kappa], one may extend the elliptic schedule to an arbitrary spectral interval [λmin,λmax][\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}] by applying the elliptic schedule with κ=λmax/λmin\kappa=\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min} to the rescaled target x~1=λmin​x1\tilde{x}_{1}=\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\,x_{1} and dividing the sampled output by λmin\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}} (Section I.1). The elliptic schedule is thus a two-parameter family, which we can express either in endpoint coordinates (ℓ,L)=(λmin,λmax)(\ell,L)=(\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}) or equivalently by center–width coordinates (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa), related by

(λ¯,κ)≜(ℓ​L,L/ℓ),[ℓ,L]=[λ¯/κ,λ¯​κ].(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)\triangleq\left(\sqrt{\ell L},\,L/\ell\right),\qquad[\ell,L]=[\bar{\lambda}/\sqrt{\kappa},\,\bar{\lambda}\sqrt{\kappa}].

Here λ¯\bar{\lambda} is the geometric center of the [ℓ,L][\ell,L] interval: on the log-precision axis, its midpoint is log⁡λ¯\log\bar{\lambda} and its width is log⁡κ\log\kappa. Centering refers to the location of this interval, rather than to subtracting the target mean. At fixed κ\kappa, varying λ¯\bar{\lambda} adjusts the relative source–target scale; at fixed λ¯\bar{\lambda}, varying κ\kappa changes the interval width. Figure 4 illustrates these coordinates for a matched spectral interval.

For κ=1\kappa=1 the elliptic schedule reduces to the trigonometric schedule, written (ℓ,L)=(λ¯,λ¯)(\ell,L)=(\bar{\lambda},\bar{\lambda}) in endpoint coordinates and (λ¯,κ)=(λ¯,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(\bar{\lambda},1) in center–width coordinates. Unless otherwise specified, we use the center–width hyperparameters (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) to separate scale and width.

All schedules (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) can be centered.

We note that any baseline schedule can accommodate a centering parameter λ¯\bar{\lambda} through the same target rescaling mentioned previously11 1 In terms of the hyperparameters (ℓ,L)(\ell,L), this forces ℓ=L\ell=L.. The idea of rescaling source or target is not new; target rescaling and shifts in log-SNR schedules are established design choices (Chen, 2023; Hoogeboom et al., 2023; Esser et al., 2024). As the elliptic family gains the additional width hyperparameter κ\kappa22 2 The Lipschitz-guided schedule of Chen et al. (2025) also depends on κ\kappa and therefore admits a two-parameter family under target rescaling. and reduces to a trigonometric schedule at κ=1\kappa=1, we thus ask whether elliptic width κ\kappa contributes on top of a centering calibration.

Choosing hyperparameters (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)

For a Gaussian target 𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}), matching the parameters to the spectral bounds, (ℓ,L)=(λmin​(Λ),λmax​(Λ))(\ell,L)=(\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda),\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)), or equivalently in terms of positive definite covariance matrix Σ\Sigma

(λ¯,κ)=(1λmin​(Σ)​λmax​(Σ),λmax​(Σ)λmin​(Σ)).(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\,\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}},\ \frac{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)}\right).

makes our proposed algorithm Zoloflow minimax optimal (Section 4). Our experiments describe how extending this choice as a covariance heuristic for non-Gaussian targets may not be optimal. Thus in general we treat both λ¯\bar{\lambda} and κ\kappa as hyperparameters to tune.

Figure 5 compares unscaled and independently tuned rescaled baselines with the elliptic family on a non-Gaussian frond target. A separate covariance-center ablation (Figures 18 and 19) separates the benefits of centering and width.

4  Gaussian Sampling and Zoloflow

We now study the minimax problem (6) over the Gaussian class 𝖦κ\mathsf{G}_{\kappa} with dist=dTV\mathrm{dist}=d_{\mathrm{TV}}

infalg∈𝒜rsupπ∈𝖦κdTV​(π^alg​(π),π).\inf_{\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r}}\ \sup_{\pi\in\mathsf{G}_{\kappa}}\ d_{\text{TV}}\big(\hat{\pi}_{\mathrm{alg}}(\pi),\pi\big). (11)

We structure this section in the following way. First, on Gaussian targets, we show every algorithm in 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} can be understood as a rational function on its precision eigenvalues λi∈spec​(Λ)\lambda_{i}\in\text{spec}(\Lambda). As Gaussian sampling can be realized by a matrix-vector multiplication Λ−1/2z\Lambda^{-1/2}z the best algorithm will correspond to the best uniform approximation of λ−1/2\lambda^{-1/2} on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. Second, we show that the above uniform approximation is nothing other than a reformulation of an optimal rational approximation problem solved by Zolotarev (1877). Third, we show that the elliptic schedule, paired with a custom finite-difference discretization, attains this optimum up to constant factors. The resulting algorithm, Zoloflow (Section 4.3), therefore matches the minimax lower bound on the number of score queries up to constants (Section 4.4).

4.1  Score-Oracle Algorithms for Gaussian Sampling Are Rational Functions

Before getting into the explicit complexity results for Zoloflow, we describe the core intuition behind our results: that every algorithm alg∈𝒜r\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r} (Definition 2.3) has a rational function representation. We formalize this in the following lemma.

Lemma 4.1 (Algorithms in 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} are rational functions on Gaussians).

Suppose the target distribution π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) is a zero-mean Gaussian, with precision matrix Λ=U​diag​(λ1,…,λd)​UT\Lambda=U\text{diag}(\lambda_{1},\dots,\lambda_{d})U^{T}. For any m,n∈ℕm,n\in\mathbb{N} define

ℛm,n≜{r(x)=P⁡(x)D⁡(x)|P,D∈ℝ[x],degP≤m,degD≤n,D≢0}.\mathcal{R}_{m,n}\triangleq\left\{r(x)=\frac{P(x)}{D(x)}\;\middle|\;P,D\in\mathbb{R}[x],\;\deg P\leq m,\;\deg D\leq n,\;D\not\equiv 0\right\}. (12)

as the class of all rational functions whose numerator is a polynomial degree at most mm and denominator a polynomial with degree at most nn. Then for any algorithm in 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} we can express its final iterate as

xralg=qralg​(Λ)​z=U​diag​(qralg​(λ1),…,qralg​(λd))​UT​zx_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}=q_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}(\Lambda)z=U\text{diag}(q_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}(\lambda_{1}),\dots,q_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}(\lambda_{d}))U^{T}z (13)

where qralg​(λ)∈ℛr,rq_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}(\lambda)\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r} is a rational function that can be obtained from the algorithm coefficients ((αtj),(βtj),(ai​j),(bi​j))((\alpha_{t_{j}}),(\beta_{t_{j}}),(a_{ij}),(b_{ij})). We delay a proof of this lemma to Appendix G.

The key idea is that for Gaussian distributions, every algorithm in 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} (more precisely each interpolant schedule and discretization pair) admits a rational function q⁡(⋅)q(\cdot) which acts on the eigenvalues of the precision matrix Λ\Lambda. The performance of each algorithm is nothing more than a question about the quality of the approximation of λ−1/2\lambda^{-1/2}. In particular

q(Λ)≈Λ−1/2⟹q(Λ)z≈Λ−1/2z=d𝒩(0,Λ−1)q(\Lambda)\approx\Lambda^{-1/2}\implies q(\Lambda)z\approx\Lambda^{-1/2}z\stackrel{{\scriptstyle d}}{{=}}\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) (14)

A good algorithm for gaussians must thus give a good rational approximation to λ−1/2\lambda^{-1/2} uniformly over [1,κ][1,\kappa]

4.2  Zolotarev’s optimal rational approximation

Let ℛp,q\mathcal{R}_{p,q} denote the real rational functions whose numerator and denominator have degrees at most pp and qq, respectively. We would like to approximate the function 1/λ1/\sqrt{\lambda} on the interval [1,κ][1,\kappa], with an element of ℛp,q\mathcal{R}_{p,q}. For κ>1\kappa>1 and r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, define the optimal relative approximation error

Eκ,r≜minq∈ℛr,r⁡maxλ∈[1,κ]​|λ​q​(λ)−1|,E_{\kappa,r}\triangleq\min_{q\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r}}\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q(\lambda)-1\right|, (15)

where the minimization is restricted to functions without poles on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. The unique minimizer, which we denote by qκ,r​(λ)q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda), is a reformulation of the classically known Zolotarev (1877) approximation to the sign​(x)\text{sign}(x) function, and is written in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions. We clarify below.

Sign function.

Zolotarev’s theorem Zolotarev (1877) gives the best type-(2​r+1,2​r)(2r+1,2r) rational approximation Z⁡(x)Z(x) to sign⁡(x)\operatorname{sign}(x) on [−κ,−1]∪[1,κ][-\sqrt{\kappa},-1]\cup[1,\sqrt{\kappa}]. Since sign⁡(x)\operatorname{sign}(x) is odd, so is the optimal approximant, and thus it has the form

Z⁡(x)=C​x​P⁡(x2)Q⁡(x2)=x​qκ,r​(x2),deg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤r.Z(x)=Cx\frac{P(x^{2})}{Q(x^{2})}=xq_{\kappa,r}(x^{2}),\qquad\deg P,\deg Q\leq r.

The substitution λ=x2\lambda=x^{2} gives the exact error identity

max1≤|x|≤κ⁡|Z⁡(x)−sign⁡(x)|=maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​qκ,r​(λ)−1|=Eκ,r.\max_{1\leq|x|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}}|Z(x)-\operatorname{sign}(x)|=\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)-1\right|=E_{\kappa,r}. (16)

Thus absolute-error approximation of the sign function is equivalent to relative-error approximation of the inverse square root, and achieves the same optimal error. Rescaling xx by κ\sqrt{\kappa} gives the usual sign-approximation domain [−1,−1−m]∪[1−m,1][-1,-\sqrt{1-m}]\cup[\sqrt{1-m},1], where m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1}; see Nakatsukasa and Freund (2016, Section 3.1). More generally, on any positive interval [a,b][a,b], the approximant a−1/2qb/a,r(λ/a)a^{-1/2}q_{b/a,r}(\lambda/a) has optimal relative error Eb/a,rE_{b/a,r}. Thus, the ratio κ=b/a\kappa=b/a of the interval endpoints directly controls the optimal approximation error.

4.3  Zoloflow

The elliptic schedule given in Definition 10 can in principle be paired with any numerical method (e.g., Euler, Heun, etc.) to solve the probability flow ODE (3). However, if instead we use a non-standard (but natural) discretization we obtain Zoloflow, a sampling algorithm that is essentially optimal on Gaussians.

Definition 4.2 (Elliptic finite-difference discretization).

Fix a step count rr and an interpolant schedule (α,β)(\alpha,\beta). The elliptic finite-difference update is

xj\displaystyle x_{j} =xj−1+h[βtj+h/22−βtj2h​βtj2](xj−1+stj(xj−1)),j=1,…,r.\displaystyle=x_{j-1}+h\left[\frac{\beta_{t_{j}+h/2}^{2}-\beta_{t_{j}}^{2}}{h\,\beta_{t_{j}}^{2}}\right]\left(x_{j-1}+s_{t_{j}}(x_{j-1})\right),\qquad j=1,\ldots,r. (17)

on the grid h=22​r+1h=\frac{2}{2r+1}, tj∈{12​r+1,32​r+1,…,2​r−12​r+1}.t_{j}\in\left\{\frac{1}{2r+1},\frac{3}{2r+1},\ldots,\frac{2r-1}{2r+1}\right\}.

A derivation of this approach, and a comparison with standard Euler and deterministic DDIM discretizations using the same iterate and time-grid notation are presented in Appendix E.

Definition 4.3 (Zoloflow).

Fix κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 and r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}, a target distribution π\pi with x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi, and set m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1}. Zoloflow is the rr-step algorithm obtained by applying the elliptic finite-difference discretization (Def. 4.2) to the flow ODE (3), using the elliptic schedule (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}) given in Def. 10. We use a step size h=2/(2​r+1)h=2/(2r+1) and time grid tj=(2​j−1)/(2​r+1)t_{j}=(2j-1)/(2r+1), j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,r. A formal description is presented as Algorithm 1 above.

On centered Gaussian targets with exact interpolant scores, Zoloflow exactly realizes the endpoint-normalized Zolotarev approximant:

xr=q^κ,r​(Λ)​z,q^κ,r​(λ)=qκ,r​(λ)qκ,r​(1).x_{r}=\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\Lambda)z,\qquad\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)=\frac{q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)}{q_{\kappa,r}(1)}.

Here qκ,rq_{\kappa,r} is the optimal scalar relative-error approximant to λ−1/2\lambda^{-1/2} on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. Endpoint normalization enforces q^κ,r​(1)=1\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(1)=1, preserving the unit-precision mode exactly, and changes the worst-case relative error to

E^κ,r=2​Eκ,r1−Eκ,r.\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}=\frac{2E_{\kappa,r}}{1-E_{\kappa,r}}.

Thus normalization preserves the asymptotic convergence rate, although q^κ,r\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r} no longer minimizes the scalar relative error. The exact realization is established in Lemma H.1.

Although primarily motivated by Gaussian targets, both the elliptic schedule and Zoloflow can be used to sample from any distribution. As we show in later sections, they will perform quite well from both theoretical (in the Gaussian/log-concave case) and empirical (for general distributions) viewpoints, often outperforming competing techniques.

4.4  Score-Oracle Complexity of Gaussian Sampling

We formally define the minimax query complexity as follows:

robl∗​(d,κ,ε)≜min⁡{r∈ℤ≥1:∃alg∈𝒜r​such thatsupId⪯Λ⪯κ​IddTV​(ℒ⁡(xralg,Λ),𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1))≤ε}.r^{*}_{\mathrm{obl}}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\triangleq\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r}\ \text{such that}\\[2.0pt] \displaystyle\sup_{I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}}d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda}),\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1})\right)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}. (18)

Here each algorithm, including its admissible interpolant schedule, query times, and scalar update coefficients, is chosen independently of Λ\Lambda, the initialization, and the oracle responses.

Theorem 4.4 (Gaussian TV query complexity among oblivious score-span algorithms).

There exist universal constants c,C>0c,C>0 and ε0∈(0,1)\varepsilon_{0}\in(0,1) such that, for every d≥1d\geq 1, κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, and 0<ε≤ε00<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_{0},

c​log⁡κ​log⁡(dε)≤robl∗​(d,κ,ε)≤C​log⁡κ​log⁡(dε).c\log\kappa\,\log\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon}\right)\leq r^{*}_{\mathrm{obl}}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\leq C\log\kappa\,\log\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon}\right).

In other words,

robl∗​(d,κ,ε)=Θ⁡(log⁡κ​log⁡(dε)),r^{*}_{\mathrm{obl}}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)=\Theta\!\left(\log\kappa\,\log\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\varepsilon}\right)\right),

with universal implicit constants throughout this parameter regime. Zoloflow attains the upper bound: with a suitable query budget rr, exact interpolant scores, and initialization x0=z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{0}=z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), its output law π^≜ℒ⁡(xr)\widehat{\pi}\triangleq\mathcal{L}(x_{r}) satisfies dTV​(π^,π)≤εd_{\mathrm{TV}}(\widehat{\pi},\pi)\leq\varepsilon uniformly over centered Gaussian targets π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with Id⪯Λ⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}.

We give a proof in Appendix H.

Figure 6 compares solver–schedule pairs on a Gaussian target 𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with spectrum spec⁡(Λ)⊂[1,κ]\spec(\Lambda)\subset[1,\kappa], where κ=100\kappa=100. For each pair alg\mathrm{alg} it plots the worst-case relative error Eκ,r​(alg)=maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​qralg​(λ)−1|E_{\kappa,r}(\mathrm{alg})=\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}(\lambda)-1| of its rational function (Lemma 4.1), which controls the sampling error, DKL(π^∥π)≲dEκ,r(alg)2D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat{\pi}\,\|\,\pi)\lesssim d\,E_{\kappa,r}(\mathrm{alg})^{2} by (102). No pair can fall below the Zolotarev error Eκ,rE_{\kappa,r} of (15), and Zoloflow attains E^κ,r=2​Eκ,r/(1−Eκ,r)\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}=2E_{\kappa,r}/(1-E_{\kappa,r}) (Section N.1).

5  Log-Concave Sampling

We now consider the class 𝖯κ\mathsf{P}_{\kappa} of centered strongly log-concave targets (Section 2.2) and measure error in the 2-Wasserstein distance, dist=W2\mathrm{dist}=W_{2} in (6). Since the score is nonlinear, the rational-approximation reduction of Section 4.4 no longer applies. We instead build on the complex-analytic criterion of Proposition 3.1: after a mild Gaussian smoothing, the elliptic schedule keeps all PF-ODE trajectories holomorphic and bounded on a strip around ℝ\mathbb{R} whose width degrades only polylogarithmically in κ\kappa and 1/ε1/\varepsilon (Theorem 5.1). Collocation methods for analytic ODEs (Lee et al., 2018) then yield W2W_{2}-error ε\varepsilon with O⁡(d​log3.5⁡(κ​d/ε))O(\sqrt{d}\,\log^{3.5}(\kappa d/\varepsilon)) score evaluations (Theorem 5.2).

5.1  Holomorphic Width under the Elliptic Schedule

Holomorphic width.

For an ODE X˙t=bt​(Xt)\dot{X}_{t}=b_{t}(X_{t}) with X0=zX_{0}=z, a radius B>0B>0, and the strip Sω≜{t∈ℂ:|Im⁡t|<ω}S_{\omega}\triangleq\{t\in\mathbb{C}:|\operatorname{Im}t|<\omega\}, define the holomorphic width

ΩB​(b)≜sup{ω>0:t↦Xt​ extends holomorphically to ​Sω​ for all ​‖z‖≤B}.\Omega_{B}(b)\triangleq\sup\bigl\{\omega>0:\ t\mapsto X_{t}\text{ extends holomorphically to }S_{\omega}\text{ for all }\|z\|\leq B\bigr\}. (19)

If, in addition, all such trajectories are bounded by MM on SωS_{\omega} and btb_{t} is LL-Lipschitz in space, then collocation approximates X1X_{1} to accuracy ζ\zeta uniformly over ‖z‖≤B\|z\|\leq B with

N≲max⁡(1,L,ω−1)​(1+L+log⁡M​max⁡(1,L,ω−1)ζ)2N\lesssim\max(1,L,\omega^{-1})\Bigl(1+L+\log\frac{M\max(1,L,\omega^{-1})}{\zeta}\Bigr)^{2} (20)

drift evaluations (Theorem M.1; Lee et al., 2018, Thm. 2.3). For VP schedules, bt​(x)=β˙tβt​(x+st​(x))b_{t}(x)=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}(x+s_{t}(x)), so each drift evaluation is a single score query.

Smoothing as early stopping.

For Gaussian targets, the elliptic schedule makes every trajectory holomorphic on SωS_{\omega} with ω=K⁡(1−m)/K⁡(m)≈π/log⁡(16​κ)\omega=K(1-m)/K(m)\approx\pi/\log(16\kappa), independently of dd and zz (Proposition 3.1). On 𝖯κ\mathsf{P}_{\kappa}, analyticity can fail at t=1t=1 regardless of the schedule (Proposition L.7), although it holds at every t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) for analytic schedules (Section L.2). We therefore target a smoothed distribution: for σ~∈(0,1)\widetilde{\sigma}\in(0,1), z∼N⁡(0,Id)z\sim N(0,I_{d}), and x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi (Lemma M.4),

π~≜ℒ⁡(σ~​z+1−σ~2​x1)∈𝖯κ~,whereκ~≜κ​(1+σ~2​(κ−1))−1≤κ,\begin{gathered}\widetilde{\pi}\triangleq\mathcal{L}\bigl(\widetilde{\sigma}z+\sqrt{1-\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}}\,x_{1}\bigr)\in\mathsf{P}_{\widetilde{\kappa}},\quad\text{where}\quad\widetilde{\kappa}\triangleq{\kappa}(1+\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}(\kappa-1))^{-1}\leq\kappa,\end{gathered} (21)

with smoothing error W2​(π~,π)≤d/κ​(1+σ~2​(κ−1)−1)W_{2}(\widetilde{\pi},\pi)\leq\sqrt{d/\kappa}\,(\sqrt{1+\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}(\kappa-1)}-1). For a VP schedule (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), the PF-ODE transporting N⁡(0,Id)N(0,I_{d}) to π~\widetilde{\pi} and its score are

X~˙t=b~t​(X~t)≜β˙tβt​(X~t+s~t​(X~t)),wheres~t≜sτ⁡(t),andτ⁡(t)≜β−1​(1−σ~2​βt)∈[0,1),\begin{gathered}\dot{\widetilde{X}}_{t}=\widetilde{b}_{t}(\widetilde{X}_{t})\triangleq\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\bigl(\widetilde{X}_{t}+\widetilde{s}_{t}(\widetilde{X}_{t})\bigr),\quad\text{where}\\ \widetilde{s}_{t}\triangleq s_{\tau(t)},\quad\text{and}\quad\tau(t)\triangleq\beta^{-1}\bigl(\sqrt{1-\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}}\,\beta_{t}\bigr)\in[0,1),\end{gathered} (22)

since the smoothed interpolant satisfies αt​z+βt​x~1=(d)ατ⁡(t)​z+βτ⁡(t)​x1\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}\widetilde{x}_{1}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle(d)}}{{=}}\alpha_{\tau(t)}z+\beta_{\tau(t)}x_{1} with x~1∼π~\widetilde{x}_{1}\sim\widetilde{\pi}. Hence each evaluation of b~t\widetilde{b}_{t} costs one query of the original score, and X~t=Xτ⁡(t)\widetilde{X}_{t}=X_{\tau(t)}, so integrating (22) over [0,1][0,1] amounts to stopping the original PF-ODE early at τ⁡(1)<1\tau(1)<1 (Appendix L). Theorem 5.1 (Holomorphic width under the elliptic schedule).

Let κ,κ^>1\kappa,\widehat{\kappa}>1, σ~∈(0,1)\widetilde{\sigma}\in(0,1), B>0B>0, and D≜d+B2+d​log⁡κD\triangleq\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{B^{2}+d\log\kappa}. ω⋆​(κ,d,B,σ~)≥ωκ^≜min⁡(1,σ~​κ^)K​(m^)​(1+30​1−σ~2​D).\omega_{\star}(\kappa,d,B,\widetilde{\sigma})\ \geq\ \omega_{\widehat{\kappa}}\triangleq\frac{\min\bigl(1,\widetilde{\sigma}\sqrt{\widehat{\kappa}}\bigr)}{K(\widehat{m})\bigl(1+30\sqrt{1-\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}}\,D\bigr)}. (23)

and bounded on this strip as

supt∈Sωκ^‖X~t‖≤B+d+1,\sup_{t\in S_{\omega_{\widehat{\kappa}}}}\|\widetilde{X}_{t}\|\leq B+\sqrt{d}+1,\qquad (24)

Restricting the infimum to Gaussian targets and applying Proposition 3.1 with the additional requirement of the phase function to be analytic then gives

so the elliptic schedule is optimal up to the factor D≍d​log⁡κ+BD\asymp\sqrt{d\log\kappa}+B and logarithmic terms.

5.2  Score-Oracle Complexity of Log-Concave Sampling

With m^=1−σ~2\widehat{m}=1-\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}, the smoothed drift satisfies −K⁡(m^)​Id⪯∇b~t⪯0-K(\widehat{m})I_{d}\preceq\nabla\widetilde{b}_{t}\preceq 0 (Lemma M.5), so L≤K⁡(m^)L\leq K(\widehat{m}) and the flow z↦X~tz\mapsto\widetilde{X}_{t} is non-expansive. Combining this with Theorem 5.1 and (20) gives the following result.

Theorem 5.2 (Score-oracle complexity for log-concave targets).

Let π∈𝖯κ\pi\in\mathsf{P}_{\kappa} with κ>1\kappa>1, let 0<ε≤min⁡(1,ε¯)0<\varepsilon\leq\min(1,\bar{\varepsilon}) with ε¯≜(κ−1)​d/κ\bar{\varepsilon}\triangleq(\kappa-1)\sqrt{d/\kappa}, and set σ~2=κ^−1=ε2​ε¯\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}=\widehat{\kappa}^{-1}=\frac{\varepsilon}{2\bar{\varepsilon}}, B=d+2​log⁡(32/ε2)B=\sqrt{d}+\sqrt{2\log(32/\varepsilon^{2})}, ζ=ε4\zeta=\frac{\varepsilon}{4}. Integrate (22) under the elliptic schedule with parameter m^=1−κ^−1\widehat{m}=1-\widehat{\kappa}^{-1} by collocation with tolerance ζ\zeta, starting from X~0=ΠB​(Z)≜min⁡(1,B/‖Z‖)​Z\widetilde{X}_{0}=\Pi_{B}(Z)\triangleq\min(1,B/\|Z\|)\,Z with Z∼N⁡(0,Id)Z\sim N(0,I_{d}). The output X^\widehat{X} satisfies W2​(ℒ⁡(X^),π)≤εW_{2}(\mathcal{L}(\widehat{X}),\pi)\leq\varepsilon using at most

N≤C​log3⁡(e​κ​(d+1)ε)​d​log⁡(κ+1)+log⁡(e​κ​(d+1)ε)=O⁡(d​log3.5​κ​dε)N\leq C\log^{3}\!\Bigl(\frac{e\kappa(d+1)}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)\sqrt{d\log(\kappa+1)+\log\Bigl(\frac{e\kappa(d+1)}{\varepsilon}\Bigr)}=O\Bigl(\sqrt{d}\,\log^{3.5}\frac{\kappa d}{\varepsilon}\Bigr) (26)

exact score evaluations, where CC is a universal constant.

The error splits into the smoothing bias, the projection of the initialization, and the collocation error, each at most a constant fraction of ε\varepsilon. The inverse width contributes the square-root factor and one logarithm, and the accuracy term contributes the remaining log2\log^{2} (Appendix M). Unlike Zoloflow, this result uses a generic solver and thus isolates the benefit of the elliptic schedule. The d\sqrt{d} factor stems from DD and is absent from the Gaussian width in (25); whether it is intrinsic to 𝖯κ\mathsf{P}_{\kappa} remains open.

6  Experiments

Sections 3 and 4 illustrated the elliptic schedule on a 2D target (Figure 5) and Zoloflow on Gaussian targets (Figure 6); Sections N.3 and N.1 give further synthetic comparisons, and Section N.2 adds log-concave experiments for different center–width hyperparameter choices. Here we test the elliptic schedule on image generation.

Image generation.

We generate images using two pretrained models: SiT-XL/2 (Ma et al., 2024), a 675M-parameter model trained on ImageNet to generate class-conditional images,33 3 https://github.com/willisma/SiT. and Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium (SD 3.5M), a 2.5B-parameter text-to-image model.44 4 https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium. Both models learn the velocity field of the linear interpolant, which we convert to other schedules via Chen et al. (2025, Prop. 3.1). We set the classifier-free guidance (CFG) scales to 1.51.5 for SiT-XL/2 and to 4.54.5 for SD 3.5M. Since the elliptic finite-difference discretization of Zoloflow is specific to Gaussian targets, we use DPM-Solver++(2M) (Lu et al., 2022b), which is described in Section E.2.

Figure 7 shows FID-10K scores sampled from SiT-XL/2 using the elliptic schedule with varied hyperparameters λ¯\bar{\lambda} and κ\kappa (explained in Sections 3.2 and J). As a heuristic, we take ℓ^\hat{\ell} and L^\hat{L} as the 0.50.5th and 99.599.5th percentiles of the eigenvalues of the empirical precision matrix of the training set of SiT-XL/2 (Figure 24), and we set κ^=L^/ℓ^\hat{\kappa}=\hat{L}/\hat{\ell} and λ¯^=ℓ^​L^\hat{\bar{\lambda}}=\sqrt{\hat{\ell}\hat{L}}. This heuristic lands in the low-FID region of the sweep, making it a sensible starting point for further tuning. Figures 25, 26, 27 and 28 suggest that as the number of oracle calls increase, the performance of a schedule is less sensitive to the hyperparameters λ¯\bar{\lambda} and κ\kappa.

Tables 1 and 2 compare the performances of different schedules over different numbers of oracle calls. The choice of schedule matters most at low budgets, where the elliptic schedule outperforms the alternatives. As the budget grows, all schedules converge to the same exact ODE solution and the performance differences vanish. Figure 1 displays some images generated by the best-performing rescaled linear, trigonometric, and elliptic schedules at 4 oracle calls of SD 3.5M. Setup details, the list of schedules, and further results are in Sections N.4 and K.1.

7  Discussion

We designed interpolant schedules and discretizations jointly through two complementary lenses, minimax rational approximation and complex-analytic regularity, which lead to the same elliptic schedule. Several limitations remain. Our theory assumes exact scores, and extending it to approximate scores is left open. For Gaussian targets, Zoloflow attains the minimax query-complexity rate among oblivious score-span algorithms using exact interpolant scores. Its discretization is tailored to Gaussian structure, and we do not identify an optimal discretization for log-concave targets. Our log-concave guarantees are upper bounds without matching lower bounds, so it remains open whether the d\sqrt{d} factor is necessary. Finally, for non-log-concave targets, the schedule parameters require heuristic selection or empirical tuning; the covariance rule supplies a starting point but need not select the best width. A more principled selection may exist.

8  AI Usage

Generative AI was not used for ideation; in particular, the optimal schedule and solver for Gaussian targets were developed without it. We used AI tools to help write proofs and suggest mathematical tools, to search the literature, to generate synthetic target distributions, to write and proofread code (verified by manual review and unit tests), and to edit wording. We reviewed all AI-assisted content and take full responsibility for the paper.

Appendix B Jacobi Elliptic Functions

The Jacobi elliptic functions are elliptic generalizations of the trigonometric and hyperbolic functions. Like all elliptic functions, they are meromorphic and doubly periodic on the complex plane. On the real line, they have a natural interpretation as sines and cosines under a nonlinear reparameterization of angle, given by the Jacobi amplitude (inverse of the elliptic integral of the first kind). The Jacobi elliptic functions appear throughout mathematics and physics, particularly in classical mechanics (e.g., pendulum, rigid body rotations); see e.g. Lawden (2013) and references therein. They have been implemented in almost every computer language – in particular, in Python they can be computed with SciPy via scipy.special.ellipj, which simultaneously provides the functions cn,sn,dn\cn,\sn,\dn and the Jacobi amplitude am\operatorname{am}.

B.1  Basic notions

B.1.1  Elliptic functions in terms of sine and cosine

At their simplest level the Jacobi elliptic functions are an extension of the usual trigonometric functions, using the geometry of the ellipse. They are indexed by a parameter55 5 There are two different conventions for Jacobi elliptic functions, either using the parameter mm or the elliptic modulus k=mk=\sqrt{m}. We use the former notation since it is more common in modern software, and provides slightly cleaner notation. m∈[0,1)m\in[0,1). For 0≤m<10\leq m<1, the incomplete elliptic integral of the first kind is

F⁡(φ∣m)≜∫0φ⁡d​θ1−m​sin2⁡θ,K⁡(m)≜F⁡(π/2∣m).F(\varphi\mid m)\triangleq\int_{0}^{\varphi}\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\theta}{\sqrt{1-m\sin^{2}\theta}},\qquad K(m)\triangleq F(\pi/2\mid m). (27)

The incomplete integral F:φ↦uF:\varphi\mapsto u maps a variable angle φ\varphi on a circle to elliptic time uu. The complete integral K⁡(m)K(m) is the time for a quarter-period; a full period takes 4​K​(m)4K(m). Its complementary quarter-period is K⁡(1−m)K(1-m). When m=0m=0, then K⁡(m)=π/2K(m)=\pi/2, which is exactly the quarter period of trigonometric functions.

For every fixed mm, since FF is strictly increasing for real φ\varphi, its real inverse is well-defined: the Jacobi amplitude.

u=F(φ∣m)⟺φ=am(u∣m).u=F(\varphi\mid m)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\varphi=\operatorname{am}(u\mid m). (28)

Here uu is an elliptic time coordinate, while φ\varphi is an ordinary angular parameter. In particular, the amplitude is an angle, not the ‘yy’-coordinate of a curve. The main three Jacobi elliptic functions are defined as

sn(u∣m)=sinφ,cn(u∣m)=cosφ,dn(u∣m)=1−m​sin2⁡φ.\boxed{\ \sn(u\mid m)=\sin\varphi,\qquad\cn(u\mid m)=\cos\varphi,\qquad\dn(u\mid m)=\sqrt{1-m\sin^{2}\varphi}.\ } (29)

where φ≜am⁡(u∣m)\varphi\triangleq\operatorname{am}(u\mid m).

The square root is positive for real uu. Differentiating the inverse relation gives

⁡d​u⁡d​φ=11−m​sin2⁡φ,⁡d​φ⁡d​u=dn⁡(u∣m)∈[1−m,1].\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\varphi}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-m\sin^{2}\varphi}},\qquad\frac{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}\varphi}{\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d}u}=\dn(u\mid m)\in[\sqrt{1-m},1]. (30)

Thus the elliptic clock uu stretches angular intervals most near φ=π/2(modπ)\varphi=\pi/2\pmod{\pi}. A trajectory moving uniformly in uu advances slowly through those angles. When m=0m=0, there is no stretching: u=φu=\varphi. Importantly, dn\dn is also exactly the angular speed d​φd​u\frac{d\varphi}{du} of the angle as a function of the elliptic clock uu. Below we give some plots of uu and φ\varphi for varying parameters mm. In particular note how for larger mm close to the quarter period, the angle φ\varphi moves much slower relative to the elliptic clock uu. Intuitively, for very flat ellipses, this ensures that movement towards the end of the quarter-period (around the top of the ellipse) is not too fast.

B.1.2  Limiting Cases m→0,m→1m\to 0,\ m\to 1

At the m={0,1}m=\{0,1\} endpoints the Jacobi amplitude function am⁡(u∣m)\operatorname{am}(u\mid m) evaluates to

am⁡(u∣0)=u, and ​am⁡(u∣1)=arcsin⁡(tanh⁡u)\operatorname{am}(u\mid 0)=u,\text{ and }\operatorname{am}(u\mid 1)=\arcsin(\tanh u) (31)

allowing us to reduce the Jacobi functions at these parameter endpoints in the corresponding table.

Here tanh\tanh and sech\operatorname{sech} denote the hyperbolic tangent and hyperbolic secant.

We show the standard Jacobi elliptic functions for varying active parameter mm along the quarter period. As the quarter period has infinite limit limm→1K⁡(m)=∞\lim_{m\to 1}K(m)=\infty, we plot these functions in both the real and normalized elliptic time u, and ​t=u/K⁡(m)u,\text{ and }t=u/K(m), making explicit these endpoint conditions. With the normalized clock parameter t=u/K⁡(m)t=u/K(m), these functions cn⁡(t),sn⁡(t)\cn(t),\ \sn(t) are exactly our proposed elliptic schedules αt,βt\alpha_{t},\ \beta_{t}.

B.1.3  The elliptic family and its algebraic identities

There are other Jacobi elliptic functions, which are ratios or reciprocals of the principal three. For example,

sc=sncn=tan⁡φ,cs=cnsn=cot⁡φ,sd=sndn,cd=cndn,ns=1sn.\jsc=\frac{\sn}{\cn}=\tan\varphi,\quad\jcs=\frac{\cn}{\sn}=\cot\varphi,\quad\operatorname{sd}=\frac{\sn}{\dn},\quad\operatorname{cd}=\frac{\cn}{\dn},\quad\operatorname{ns}=\frac{1}{\sn}. (32)

There are twelve functions in total. The mnemonic is to regard the letters s,c,d,ns,c,d,n as sn,cn,dn,1\sn,\cn,\dn,1 and to interpret two distinct letters as a quotient. Their basic identities are

sn2+cn2=1,dn2+msn2=1,dn2=(1−m)+mcn2.\boxed{\ \sn^{2}+\cn^{2}=1,\qquad\dn^{2}+m\sn^{2}=1,\qquad\dn^{2}=(1-m)+m\cn^{2}.\ } (33)

Arguments (u∣m)(u\mid m) are suppressed here and below. These are meromorphic identities, valid wherever the displayed expressions are finite.

B.2  Elliptic functions as differential equations

It is often common, and perhaps more natural to define the Jacobi elliptic functions through a system of first-order differential equations. Indeed sn,cn,dn\sn,\cn,\dn may be defined as the unique solutions to the following initial value problem.

sn˙\displaystyle\dot{\sn} =cndn,\displaystyle=\cn\,\dn,\quad sn⁡(0)=0\displaystyle\sn(0)=0 (34)
cn˙\displaystyle\dot{\cn} =−sndn,\displaystyle=-\sn\,\dn,\quad cn⁡(0)=1\displaystyle\cn(0)=1
dn˙\displaystyle\dot{\dn} =−msncn,\displaystyle=-m\sn\,\cn,\quad dn⁡(0)=1\displaystyle\dn(0)=1

where the arguments (u∣m)(u\mid m) are suppressed and dots denote uu-derivatives. A nice consequence of this interpretation is one gets for free the algebraic identities (33).

The active parameter in these functions is m=1−κ−1m=1-\kappa^{-1}. Thus the associated ellipse has eccentricity m\sqrt{m} and semiaxis ratio 1−m\sqrt{1-m}. Equivalently, the schedule is a cosine–sine (trig) schedule with a nonlinear angular clock:

φt=am⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m),(αt,βt)=(cos⁡φt,sin⁡φt),φ˙t=K⁡(m)​dn​(K⁡(m)​t∣m).\varphi_{t}=\operatorname{am}(K(m)t\mid m),\qquad(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(\cos\varphi_{t},\sin\varphi_{t}),\qquad\dot{\varphi}_{t}=K(m)\dn(K(m)t\mid m). (39)

Appendix C Gaussian Diagonalization and Eigenmodes

When both the initial and target distributions are centered Gaussians, the analysis of the SDEs and ODEs simplifies significantly, since the dynamics can be decoupled by working on an eigenbasis. We describe the details below.

Definition C.1 (Gaussian eigenmodes).

Let π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}), where Λ≻0\Lambda\succ 0, and fix an orthogonal eigendecomposition

Λ=U​diag⁡(λ1,…,λd)​U⊤,U=[u1,…,ud],U⊤​U=Id.\Lambda=U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d})U^{\top},\qquad U=[u_{1},\ldots,u_{d}],\qquad U^{\top}U=I_{d}.

For each k∈{1,…,d}k\in\{1,\ldots,d\}, the kk-th eigenmode of π\pi is the line span⁡{uk}\operatorname{span}\{u_{k}\}, whose precision is λk\lambda_{k}. Any x∈ℝdx\in\mathbb{R}^{d} can be decomposed into eigenmodes as

x(k)≜uk​uk⊤​x,x=∑k=1dx(k).x^{(k)}\triangleq u_{k}u_{k}^{\top}x,\qquad x=\sum_{k=1}^{d}x^{(k)}.

Given a scalar function ff defined on the spectrum spec⁡(Λ)\operatorname{spec}(\Lambda), there is a natural matrix extension given by f⁡(Λ)≜U​diag⁡(f⁡(λ1),…,f⁡(λd))​U⊤f(\Lambda)\triangleq U\operatorname{diag}\!\bigl(f(\lambda_{1}),\ldots,f(\lambda_{d})\bigr)U^{\top}. As a linear map, f⁡(Λ)f(\Lambda) acts modewise, since

f⁡(Λ)​x=∑k=1df⁡(λk)​x(k).f(\Lambda)x=\sum_{k=1}^{d}f(\lambda_{k})x^{(k)}.

Working along an eigenmode means projecting onto its eigendirection, so that multiplication by f⁡(Λ)f(\Lambda) becomes scalar multiplication by f⁡(λk)f(\lambda_{k}). If the specific mode λk\lambda_{k} is understood from the context, we may write λ=λk\lambda=\lambda_{k}, xλ=x(k)x_{\lambda}=x^{(k)} and λ\lambda-eigenmode for short.

Gaussian scores and drifts.

For a centered Gaussian target π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}), the interpolant (1) has law pt=𝒩⁡(0,Σt)p_{t}=\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma_{t}), where Σt=αt2​Id+βt2​Λ−1\Sigma_{t}=\alpha_{t}^{2}I_{d}+\beta_{t}^{2}\Lambda^{-1}. Its score and probability-flow drift are

st​(x)=−Σt−1​x,bt​(x)=(αt​α˙t​Id+βt​β˙t​Λ−1)​Σt−1​x,s_{t}(x)=-\Sigma_{t}^{-1}x,\qquad b_{t}(x)=\bigl(\alpha_{t}\dot{\alpha}_{t}I_{d}+\beta_{t}\dot{\beta}_{t}\Lambda^{-1}\bigr)\Sigma_{t}^{-1}x, (41)

and since the matrices commute, both maps preserve the eigenmodes. In the notation of Definition C.1,

st​(xλ)=−λλ​αt2+βt2​xλ,bt​(xλ)=gλ​(t)​xλ,s_{t}(x_{\lambda})=-\frac{\lambda}{\lambda\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}\,x_{\lambda},\qquad b_{t}(x_{\lambda})=g_{\lambda}(t)x_{\lambda}, (42)

where the eigenmode velocity coefficient is

gλ​(t)≜λ​αt​α˙t+βt​β˙tλ​αt2+βt2=12​dd​t​log⁡(λ​αt2+βt2).g_{\lambda}(t)\triangleq\frac{\lambda\alpha_{t}\dot{\alpha}_{t}+\beta_{t}\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\lambda\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}=\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}\log\!\left(\lambda\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\right). (43)

Consequently, each component of the probability-flow solution evolves independently according to X˙λ​(t)=gλ​(t)​Xλ​(t)\dot{X}_{\lambda}(t)=g_{\lambda}(t)X_{\lambda}(t). For variance-preserving schedules, these expressions simplify to gλ(t)=−(λ−1)βtβ˙t/(λαt2+βt2)g_{\lambda}(t)=-(\lambda-1)\beta_{t}\dot{\beta}_{t}/(\lambda\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}) and bt​(xλ)=(β˙t/βt)​(xλ+st​(xλ))b_{t}(x_{\lambda})=(\dot{\beta}_{t}/\beta_{t})(x_{\lambda}+s_{t}(x_{\lambda})).

Gaussian sampling and the inverse square root.

A natural approach to sampling from 𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) is to consider Λ−12​z\Lambda^{-\frac{1}{2}}z, where z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) is a standard Gaussian. By the arguments above, this leads to consideration of the scalar function λ↦1/λ\lambda\mapsto 1/\sqrt{\lambda}, where λ\lambda is in spec⁡(Λ)\operatorname{spec}(\Lambda). The inverse square root has a singularity (branch point) at the origin, but it can be well-approximated (e.g., by polynomials or rational functions) on compact intervals on the positive real axis. We are particularly interested in optimal rational approximations (see e.g. Higham (2008)); see Section F.

Appendix D Optimality properties of the elliptic schedule

Here we provide a proof of the optimality of the Jacobi amplitude, stated as Proposition 3.1. The basic idea is to construct a conformal map from the singularity-free region to the strip.

Proof.

We first rewrite the nonvanishing constraint as an avoidance condition in the complex φ\varphi-plane. For λ∈[1,κ]\lambda\in[1,\kappa], 1−(1−λ−1)​sin2⁡φ=01-\bigl(1-\lambda^{-1}\bigr)\sin^{2}\varphi=0 if and only if sin2⁡φ=λ/(λ−1)\sin^{2}\varphi={\lambda}/(\lambda-1). As λ\lambda ranges from 11 to κ\kappa, this ranges over the interval [κ/(κ−1),∞)=[m−1,∞).\left[{\kappa}/(\kappa-1),\infty\right)=[m^{-1},\infty). Thus the third condition is equivalent to sin2⁡φ⁡(t)∉[m−1,∞),∀t∈Sγ\sin^{2}\varphi(t)\notin[m^{-1},\infty),\forall t\in S_{\gamma}. Consider the domain Ωm\Omega_{m} given by the connected component containing [0,π/2][0,\pi/2] of {z∈ℂ:sin2⁡z∉[m−1,∞)}\left\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\sin^{2}z\notin[m^{-1},\infty)\right\}. A standard conformal representation of Ωm\Omega_{m} is given by the incomplete elliptic integral

F⁡(z∣m)=∫0zd​ζ1−m​sin2⁡ζ.F(z\mid m)=\int_{0}^{z}\frac{d\zeta}{\sqrt{1-m\sin^{2}\zeta}}.

Namely, Ψm​(z)≜F⁡(z∣m)/K⁡(m)\Psi_{m}(z)\triangleq{F(z\mid m)}/{K(m)} is a biholomorphism Ψm:Ωm⟶Sγ⋆\Psi_{m}:\Omega_{m}\longrightarrow S_{\gamma_{\star}}, with inverse Ψm−1​(w)=am⁡(K⁡(m)​w∣m)\Psi_{m}^{-1}(w)=\operatorname{am}(K(m)w\mid m). The boundary interpolation conditions are satisfied, since Ψm​(0)=0\Psi_{m}(0)=0 and Ψm​(π/2)=1\Psi_{m}(\pi/2)=1, since F⁡(0∣m)=0F(0\mid m)=0 and F⁡(π/2∣m)=K⁡(m)F(\pi/2\mid m)=K(m).

We now prove optimality, using Schwarz-Pick. Let φ\varphi be any other phase satisfying the three conditions of the proposition on SγS_{\gamma}. Since SγS_{\gamma} is connected, φ⁡(0)=0\varphi(0)=0, its image must lie in the component Ωm\Omega_{m}. Hence h≜Ψm∘φh\triangleq\Psi_{m}\circ\varphi defines a holomorphic map h:Sγ⟶Sγ⋆.h:S_{\gamma}\longrightarrow S_{\gamma_{\star}}. The endpoint constraints give h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 and h⁡(1)=1h(1)=1. We now apply the Schwarz–Pick theorem to the two horizontal strips. Recall that z⟼tanh⁡(π​z4​a)z\longmapsto\tanh\!\left(\frac{\pi z}{4a}\right) maps Sa={z:|Im⁡z|<a}S_{a}=\{z:|\operatorname{Im}z|<a\} biholomorphically onto the unit disk. Consequently, the hyperbolic distance between two points x,y∈ℝx,y\in\mathbb{R} on the center line of SaS_{a} is dSa​(x,y)=π2​a​|x−y|.d_{S_{a}}(x,y)=\frac{\pi}{2a}|x-y|. In particular, dSγ​(0,1)=π/(2​γ)d_{S_{\gamma}}(0,1)={\pi}/{(2\gamma)} and dSγ⋆​(0,1)=π/(2​γ⋆).d_{S_{\gamma_{\star}}}(0,1)={\pi}/{(2\gamma_{\star})}. Since holomorphic maps decrease hyperbolic distance, Schwarz–Pick gives dSγ⋆​(h⁡(0),h⁡(1))≤dSγ​(0,1).d_{S_{\gamma_{\star}}}\bigl(h(0),h(1)\bigr)\leq d_{S_{\gamma}}(0,1). Using h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0 and h⁡(1)=1h(1)=1, we obtain

π2​γ⋆≤π2​γ,\frac{\pi}{2\gamma_{\star}}\leq\frac{\pi}{2\gamma},

and hence

γ≤γ⋆=K⁡(1−m)K⁡(m),\gamma\leq\gamma_{\star}=\frac{K(1-m)}{K(m)},

with equality if and only if φ⁡(t)=am⁡(K⁡(m)​t|m)\varphi(t)=\operatorname{am}(K(m)t|m). Thus no admissible phase can be holomorphic on a wider horizontal strip.

Finally, we verify that the bound is attained. The inverse of the extremal conformal map is φ⋆​(t)=am⁡(K​t∣m).\varphi_{\star}(t)=\operatorname{am}(Kt\mid m). It is holomorphic on Sγ⋆S_{\gamma_{\star}}, satisfies the boundary conditions φ⋆​(0)=0\varphi_{\star}(0)=0, φ⋆​(1)=am⁡(K∣m)=π2\varphi_{\star}(1)=\operatorname{am}(K\mid m)=\frac{\pi}{2}, and 1−(1−λ−1)​sin2⁡φ⋆​(t)1-(1-\lambda^{-1})\sin^{2}\varphi_{\star}(t) does not vanish on the strip Sγ⋆S_{\gamma_{\star}} for all λ∈[1,κ]\lambda\in[1,\kappa]. Therefore the Jacobi amplitude φ⋆\varphi_{\star} is admissible and attains the maximal strip width γ⋆=K⁡(1−m)/K⁡(m)\gamma_{\star}={K(1-m)}/{K(m)}. ∎

Appendix E Probability-Flow Discretizations

E.1  Derivation of elliptic finite-difference discretization

Recall that if (αt,βt)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}) satisfy αt2+βt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1 (a variance preserving schedule), the drift terms in (41) can be simplified as

bt​(x)=β˙tβt​(x+st​(x)).b_{t}(x)=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left(x+s_{t}(x)\right). (44)

Since

β˙tβt=dd​t​(log⁡βt)=12​dd​t​(log⁡βt2)=12​βt2​dd​t​(βt2),\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}=\frac{d}{dt}(\log\beta_{t})=\frac{1}{2}\frac{d}{dt}(\log\beta_{t}^{2})=\frac{1}{2\beta_{t}^{2}}\frac{d}{dt}(\beta_{t}^{2}),

we can rewrite the drift term to obtain

bt​(x)=β˙tβt​(x+st​(x))=12​βt2​dd​t​(βt2)​(x+st​(x))≈12​βt2​(βt+(h/2)2−βt2)(h/2)​(x+st​(x))b_{t}(x)=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left(x+s_{t}(x)\right)=\frac{1}{2\beta_{t}^{2}}\frac{d}{dt}(\beta_{t}^{2})\left(x+s_{t}(x)\right)\approx\frac{1}{2\beta_{t}^{2}}\frac{(\beta_{t+(h/2)}^{2}-\beta_{t}^{2})}{(h/2)}\left(x+s_{t}(x)\right) (45)

where in the last step we used a half-step finite-difference scheme to approximate the derivative. This yields the discretization described in Definition 4.2.

Appendix F Zolotarev rational function approximation results

Let ℛp,q\mathcal{R}_{p,q} denote the real rational functions whose numerator and denominator have degrees at most pp and qq, respectively. We would like to approximate the function 1/λ1/\sqrt{\lambda} on the interval [1,κ][1,\kappa], with an element of ℛp,q\mathcal{R}_{p,q}. For κ>1\kappa>1 and r∈ℕ0r\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, define the optimal relative approximation error

Eκ,r≜minq∈ℛr,r⁡maxλ∈[1,κ]​|λ​q​(λ)−1|,E_{\kappa,r}\triangleq\min_{q\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r}}\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q(\lambda)-1\right|, (56)

where the minimization is restricted to functions without poles on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. The unique minimizer, denoted by qκ,rq_{\kappa,r}, is the Zolotarev inverse-square-root approximant. It is classically known Zolotarev (1877) that there is an explicit expression for qκ,rq_{\kappa,r} in terms of Jacobi elliptic functions. To present this, we first discuss optimal rational approximations to the sign function.

Sign function.

Zolotarev’s theorem gives the best type-(2​r+1,2​r)(2r+1,2r) rational approximation Z⁡(x)Z(x) to sign⁡(x)\operatorname{sign}(x) on [−κ,−1]∪[1,κ][-\sqrt{\kappa},-1]\cup[1,\sqrt{\kappa}]. Since sign⁡(x)\operatorname{sign}(x) is odd, so is the optimal approximant, and thus it has the form

Z⁡(x)=C​x​P⁡(x2)Q⁡(x2)=x​qκ,r​(x2),deg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤r.Z(x)=Cx\frac{P(x^{2})}{Q(x^{2})}=xq_{\kappa,r}(x^{2}),\qquad\deg P,\deg Q\leq r.

The substitution λ=x2\lambda=x^{2} gives the exact error identity

max1≤|x|≤κ⁡|Z⁡(x)−sign⁡(x)|=maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​qκ,r​(λ)−1|=Eκ,r.\max_{1\leq|x|\leq\sqrt{\kappa}}|Z(x)-\operatorname{sign}(x)|=\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)-1\right|=E_{\kappa,r}. (57)

Thus absolute-error approximation of the sign function is equivalent to relative-error approximation of the inverse square root, and achieves the same optimal error. Rescaling xx by κ\sqrt{\kappa} gives the usual sign-approximation domain [−1,−1−m]∪[1−m,1][-1,-\sqrt{1-m}]\cup[\sqrt{1-m},1], where m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1}; see Nakatsukasa and Freund (2016, Section 3.1). More generally, on any positive interval [a,b][a,b], the approximant a−1/2qb/a,r(λ/a)a^{-1/2}q_{b/a,r}(\lambda/a) has optimal relative error Eb/a,rE_{b/a,r}. Thus, the ratio κ=b/a\kappa=b/a of the interval endpoints directly controls the optimal approximation error.

Zolotarev approximant and the elliptic grid.

The Zolotarev optimal approximant qκ,rq_{\kappa,r} can be explicitly described using Jacobi elliptic functions. To this end, define the elliptic parameter

m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1} (58)

and notice that m∈[0,1)m\in[0,1). Let K≜K⁡(m)K\triangleq K(m), where K⁡(⋅)K(\cdot) is the complete elliptic integral of the first kind. Define

ui=i2​r+1,γi=sc2(Kui∣m)=sn2⁡(K​ui∣m)cn2⁡(K​ui∣m),i=1,…,2r.u_{i}=\frac{i}{2r+1},\qquad\gamma_{i}=\jsc^{2}(Ku_{i}\mid m)=\frac{\sn^{2}(Ku_{i}\mid m)}{\cn^{2}(Ku_{i}\mid m)},\qquad i=1,\ldots,2r. (59)

Notice that the uiu_{i} describe a uniform grid on [0,1][0,1] (excluding the endpoints), and the γi\gamma_{i} evaluate an elliptic function on this grid. Background on Jacobi elliptic functions is given in Appendix B.

The Zolotarev approximant is

qκ,r​(λ)=Cκ,r​∏j=1rλ+γ2​jλ+γ2​j−1,qκ,r​(1)+κ​qκ,r​(κ)=2,q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)=C_{\kappa,r}\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{\lambda+\gamma_{2j}}{\lambda+\gamma_{2j-1}},\qquad q_{\kappa,r}(1)+\sqrt{\kappa}\,q_{\kappa,r}(\kappa)=2, (60)

where the endpoint condition uniquely determines Cκ,r>0C_{\kappa,r}>0 (Nakatsukasa and Freund, 2016, Section 3.1). The zero and pole shifts are ξj≜γ2​j\xi_{j}\triangleq\gamma_{2j} and ζj≜γ2​j−1\zeta_{j}\triangleq\gamma_{2j-1}, respectively; the actual zeros and poles are on the negative real axis, given by −ξj-\xi_{j} and −ζj-\zeta_{j}. Thus they are generated by evaluating sc2\jsc^{2} at alternating even and odd points of the same uniform uu-grid. In particular, it is the “elliptic times” K​uiKu_{i}, not the shifts γi\gamma_{i}, that are uniformly spaced.

The relative error equioscillates between ±Eκ,r\pm E_{\kappa,r}, with endpoint values

qκ,r​(1)=1−Eκ,r,κ​qκ,r​(κ)=1+Eκ,r.q_{\kappa,r}(1)=1-E_{\kappa,r},\qquad\sqrt{\kappa}\,q_{\kappa,r}(\kappa)=1+E_{\kappa,r}. (61)
Endpoint normalization.

For our sampling construction, we use a slightly modified approximant that is asymptotically equivalent. It differs only by a constant factor, since we will require the approximation to be exact at λ=1\lambda=1. Concretely, we use

q^κ,r​(λ)≜qκ,r​(λ)qκ,r​(1)=∏j=1r1+γ2​j−11+γ2​j​λ+γ2​jλ+γ2​j−1.\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)\triangleq\frac{q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)}{q_{\kappa,r}(1)}=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{1+\gamma_{2j-1}}{1+\gamma_{2j}}\frac{\lambda+\gamma_{2j}}{\lambda+\gamma_{2j-1}}. (62)

This removes the implicit constant Cκ,rC_{\kappa,r} and enforces q^κ,r​(1)=1\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(1)=1, so the unit-precision eigenmode is preserved exactly. Its relative error is

E^κ,r≜maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​q^κ,r​(λ)−1|=2​Eκ,r1−Eκ,r.\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}\triangleq\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda)-1\right|=\frac{2E_{\kappa,r}}{1-E_{\kappa,r}}. (63)

Indeed, λ​q^κ,r​(λ)\sqrt{\lambda}\,\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda) ranges from 11 to (1+Eκ,r)/(1−Eκ,r)(1+E_{\kappa,r})/(1-E_{\kappa,r}), and when the error is small, E^κ,r≈2​Eκ,r\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}\approx 2E_{\kappa,r}. Although endpoint normalization sacrifices exact minimax optimality in (15), it preserves the asymptotic convergence rate and makes all expressions considerably simpler.

Approximation rates.

Set ρκ≜exp⁡(π​K​(1−m)/K⁡(m))>1\rho_{\kappa}\triangleq\exp\!\left(\pi K(1-m)/K(m)\right)>1. The minimax error Eκ,rE_{\kappa,r} satisfies (Beckermann and Townsend, 2017, Appendix A)

4​ρκ−(2​r+1)(1+ρκ−2​(2​r+1))4≤Eκ,r≤4​ρκ−(2​r+1).\frac{4\rho_{\kappa}^{-(2r+1)}}{(1+\rho_{\kappa}^{-2(2r+1)})^{4}}\leq E_{\kappa,r}\leq 4\rho_{\kappa}^{-(2r+1)}. (64)

Consequently, for fixed κ>1\kappa>1 as r→∞r\to\infty,

Eκ,r∼4​ρκ−(2​r+1),E^κ,r∼8​ρκ−(2​r+1).E_{\kappa,r}\sim 4\rho_{\kappa}^{-(2r+1)},\qquad\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}\sim 8\rho_{\kappa}^{-(2r+1)}. (65)

Moreover, the standard elliptic-integral asymptotics give

log⁡ρκ=π​K​(1−m)K⁡(m)∼π2log⁡(16​κ)(κ→∞).\log\rho_{\kappa}=\frac{\pi K(1-m)}{K(m)}\sim\frac{\pi^{2}}{\log(16\kappa)}\qquad(\kappa\to\infty).

Thus, for κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 and sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, the minimum degree required to achieve either error at most ε\varepsilon is Θ⁡(log⁡κ​log⁡(1/ε))\Theta(\log\kappa\,\log(1/\varepsilon))66 6 Ignoring constant factors, see Appendix.. When κ=1\kappa=1, the approximation interval is a singleton and the constant function 11 achieves zero error. These results and their proofs are given in detail in Section F.1.

Fix κ>1\kappa>1 and an integer r≥0r\geq 0, and let m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1} and δκ≜1−m=κ−1/2\delta_{\kappa}\triangleq\sqrt{1-m}=\kappa^{-1/2}. Define

In particular, allowing denominator degree 2​r+12r+1 rather than 2​r2r does not improve the optimal sign approximation error.

Consequently, restricting to this form does not change either sign minimax error. By oddness,

E2​r+1,2​r+1​(δκ)=E2​r+1,2​r​(δκ)=mindeg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤r⁡maxx∈[δκ,1]​|x​P⁡(x2)Q⁡(x2)−1|,E_{2r+1,2r+1}(\delta_{\kappa})=E_{2r+1,2r}(\delta_{\kappa})=\min_{\deg P,\deg Q\leq r}\max_{x\in[\delta_{\kappa},1]}\left|x\frac{P(x^{2})}{Q(x^{2})}-1\right|,

maxx∈[δκ,1]⁡|x​P⁡(x2)Q⁡(x2)−1|=maxx2δκ2∈[1,1/δκ2]⁡|x​P⁡(x2)Q⁡(x2)−1|=maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​q​(λ)−1|.\max_{x\in[\delta_{\kappa},1]}\left|x\frac{P(x^{2})}{Q(x^{2})}-1\right|=\max_{\frac{x^{2}}{\delta_{\kappa}^{2}}\in[1,1/\delta_{\kappa}^{2}]}\left|x\frac{P(x^{2})}{Q(x^{2})}-1\right|=\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,q(\lambda)-1\right|.

As P,QP,Q range over the admissible polynomials of degree at most rr, the rescaled rational function q⁡(λ)=δκ​P⁡(δκ2​λ)Q⁡(δκ2​λ)q(\lambda)=\delta_{\kappa}\,\frac{P(\delta_{\kappa}^{2}\lambda)}{Q(\delta_{\kappa}^{2}\lambda)} ranges over all admissible functions in ℛr,r\mathcal{R}_{r,r}. Hence

mindeg⁡P,deg⁡Q≤r⁡maxλ∈[1,κ]​|λ​δκ​P⁡(δκ2​λ)Q⁡(δκ2​λ)−1|=minq∈ℛr,r⁡maxλ∈[1,κ]​|λ​q​(λ)−1|,\min_{\deg P,\deg Q\leq r}\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\delta_{\kappa}\frac{P(\delta_{\kappa}^{2}\lambda)}{Q(\delta_{\kappa}^{2}\lambda)}-1\right|=\min_{q\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r}}\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}q(\lambda)-1\right|, (68)

where both minima are over the admissible functions described above. Therefore,

E2​r+1,2​r+1​(δκ)=E2​r+1,2​r​(δκ)=Eκ,r.E_{2r+1,2r+1}(\delta_{\kappa})=E_{2r+1,2r}(\delta_{\kappa})=E_{\kappa,r}.

for all κ>1,r≥0\kappa>1,r\geq 0, with m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1},

Appendix G Score-span Algorithms on Gaussians are Rational Functions

Proof of Lemma 4.1.

=∑i=0j−1U[ai​jId−bi​j(αti2Id+βti2(diag(1/λ1,…,1/λd))−1]UTxi\displaystyle=\sum_{i=0}^{j-1}U\left[a_{ij}I_{d}-b_{ij}\left(\alpha_{t_{i}}^{2}I_{d}+\beta_{t_{i}}^{2}(\text{diag}(1/\lambda_{1},\dots,1/\lambda_{d})\right)^{-1}\right]U^{T}x_{i} (89)
=∑i=1j−1U​diag​(ai​j−bi​j​λ1αti2​λ1+βti2,…,ai​j−bi​j​λdαti2​λd+βti2)​UT​xi\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{j-1}U\text{diag}\left(a_{ij}-\frac{b_{ij}\lambda_{1}}{\alpha_{t_{i}}^{2}\lambda_{1}+\beta_{t_{i}}^{2}},\dots,a_{ij}-\frac{b_{ij}\lambda_{d}}{\alpha_{t_{i}}^{2}\lambda_{d}+\beta_{t_{i}}^{2}}\right)U^{T}x_{i} (90)

so along any λ\lambda-eigenmode xλ,jx_{\lambda,j}

We are now ready to prove the upper bound in Theorem 4.4.

Proof of Theorem 4.4.

Write q^≜q^κ,r\widehat{q}\triangleq\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}. By Lemma H.1,

xr=q^​(Λ)​z,z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id).x_{r}=\widehat{q}(\Lambda)z,\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

Let λ1,…,λd∈[1,κ]\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{d}\in[1,\kappa] be the eigenvalues of Λ\Lambda, and define

ek≜λkq^(λk)−1,k=1,…,d.e_{k}\triangleq\sqrt{\lambda_{k}}\,\widehat{q}(\lambda_{k})-1,\qquad k=1,\ldots,d.

The endpoint-normalization identity gives

DKL(π^∥π)\displaystyle D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat{\pi}\|\pi) =12(tr(Λq^(Λ)2)−d−lndet(Λq^(Λ)2))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\left(\operatorname{tr}\!\left(\Lambda\widehat{q}(\Lambda)^{2}\right)-d-\ln\det\!\left(\Lambda\widehat{q}(\Lambda)^{2}\right)\right)
=12​∑k=1d((1+ek)2−1−2​ln⁡(1+ek))\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{d}\left((1+e_{k})^{2}-1-2\ln(1+e_{k})\right)
=∑k=1d(ek+ek22−ln⁡(1+ek)).\displaystyle=\sum_{k=1}^{d}\left(e_{k}+\frac{e_{k}^{2}}{2}-\ln(1+e_{k})\right). (102)

For every u≥0u\geq 0,

Indeed, the difference between the two sides vanishes at zero and has derivative u2/(1+u)≥0u^{2}/(1+u)\geq 0. Applying this inequality to each eke_{k} gives

From KL divergence to total variation.

dTV​(π^,π)≤12DKL(π^∥π)≤(12​∑k=1dek2)1/2≤d2​E^κ,r.d_{\mathrm{TV}}(\widehat{\pi},\pi)\leq\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\widehat{\pi}\|\pi)}\leq\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{k=1}^{d}e_{k}^{2}\right)^{1/2}\leq\sqrt{\frac{d}{2}}\,\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r}. (104)

r≥ln⁡(16​κ)2​π2​ln⁡(8​2​dε)−12.r\geq\frac{\ln(16\kappa)}{2\pi^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{8\sqrt{2d}}{\varepsilon}\right)-\frac{1}{2}. (106)

For κ≥2\kappa\geq 2 and 0<ε≤1/20<\varepsilon\leq 1/2, this is O⁡(ln⁡κ​ln⁡(d/ε))O(\ln\kappa\,\ln(\sqrt{d}/\varepsilon)), with a universal implicit constant. ∎

Next we restate the lower bound. Recall the minimax query complexity

robl∗​(d,κ,ε)≜min⁡{r∈ℤ≥1:∃alg∈𝒜r​such thatsupId⪯Λ⪯κ​IddTV​(ℒ⁡(xralg,Λ),𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1))≤ε}.r^{*}_{\mathrm{obl}}(d,\kappa,\varepsilon)\triangleq\min\left\{r\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 1}:\begin{array}[]{l}\exists\,\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r}\ \text{such that}\\[2.0pt] \displaystyle\sup_{I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}}d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda}),\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1})\right)\leq\varepsilon\end{array}\right\}. (18)

Here each algorithm, including its admissible interpolant schedule, query times, and scalar update coefficients, is chosen independently of Λ\Lambda, the initialization, and the oracle responses.

Proof of Lower Bound in Theorem 4.4.

Fix d≥1d\geq 1, κ≥2\kappa\geq 2, an integer r≥1r\geq 1, and alg∈𝒜r\mathrm{alg}\in\mathcal{A}_{r}. Write δ≜ε\delta\triangleq\varepsilon.

Rational representation.

By Lemma 4.1, there is a real rational function q≜qralg∈ℛr,rq\triangleq q_{r}^{\mathrm{alg}}\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r} such that

xralg,Λ=q⁡(Λ)​z,z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id).x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda}=q(\Lambda)z,\qquad z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}).

Because the schedule, query times, and scalar coefficients are fixed independently of the target, the same function qq applies to every Id⪯Λ⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}. Moreover, qq has no poles on [1,κ][1,\kappa]: the proof of the rationality lemma gives a denominator ∏i=0r−1(αti2​λ+βti2)\prod_{i=0}^{r-1}(\alpha_{t_{i}}^{2}\lambda+\beta_{t_{i}}^{2}), which is strictly positive for λ>0\lambda>0. In particular, qq is continuous on [1,κ][1,\kappa], and

ℒ⁡(xralg,Λ)=𝒩⁡(0,q​(Λ)2).\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,q(\Lambda)^{2}\right).

supId⪯Λ⪯κ​IddTV​(ℒ⁡(xralg,Λ),𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1))≥1100​min⁡{1,d​Eκ,r}.\sup_{I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}}d_{\mathrm{TV}}\!\left(\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda}),\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1})\right)\geq\frac{1}{100}\min\{1,\sqrt{d}\,E_{\kappa,r}\}. (107)

If q⁡(λ0)=0q(\lambda_{0})=0 for some λ0∈[1,κ]\lambda_{0}\in[1,\kappa], choose Λ=λ0​Id\Lambda=\lambda_{0}I_{d}. The algorithm then outputs zero almost surely, whereas 𝒩⁡(0,λ0−1​Id)\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda_{0}^{-1}I_{d}) assigns zero probability to the origin. Their total variation distance is therefore 11, so (107) holds in this case.

Otherwise, continuity implies that qq has constant sign on [1,κ][1,\kappa]. Thus there is a single σ∈{−1,1}\sigma\in\{-1,1\} such that σ​q​(λ)=|q⁡(λ)|\sigma q(\lambda)=|q(\lambda)| throughout the interval. Since σ​q∈ℛr,r\sigma q\in\mathcal{R}_{r,r} is admissible in the definition of Eκ,rE_{\kappa,r},

maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​|q⁡(λ)|−1|=maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|λ​σ​q​(λ)−1|≥Eκ,r.\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,|q(\lambda)|-1\right|=\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,\sigma q(\lambda)-1\right|\geq E_{\kappa,r}.

ℒ⁡(xralg,Λ∗)=𝒩⁡(0,q​(λ∗)2​Id),𝒩⁡(0,Λ∗−1)=𝒩⁡(0,λ∗−1​Id).\mathcal{L}(x_{r}^{\mathrm{alg},\Lambda_{*}})=\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,q(\lambda_{*})^{2}I_{d}\right),\qquad\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda_{*}^{-1})=\mathcal{N}(0,\lambda_{*}^{-1}I_{d}).

Applying the same-mean Gaussian TV lower bound of Devroye et al. (2023, Theorem 1.1), whose relative covariance eigenvalues here are all λ∗​q​(λ∗)2\lambda_{*}q(\lambda_{*})^{2}, gives

Furthermore,

≥|λ∗​|q⁡(λ∗)|−1|≥Eκ,r.\displaystyle\geq\left|\sqrt{\lambda_{*}}|q(\lambda_{*})|-1\right|\geq E_{\kappa,r}.

From TV accuracy to query complexity.

Suppose now that alg\mathrm{alg} satisfies the uniform accuracy guarantee
