14​exp⁡(−π2​(2​r+1)ln⁡κ)≤Eκ,r≤100​δd.\frac{1}{4}\exp\!\left(-\frac{\pi^{2}(2r+1)}{\ln\kappa}\right)\leq E_{\kappa,r}\leq\frac{100\delta}{\sqrt{d}}.

Taking logarithms gives the non-asymptotic necessary condition

2​r+1≥ln⁡κπ2​ln⁡(d400​δ).2r+1\geq\frac{\ln\kappa}{\pi^{2}}\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{400\delta}\right). (109)

Choose the universal constant δ0≜400−2\delta_{0}\triangleq 400^{-2}. For 0<δ≤δ00<\delta\leq\delta_{0} and d≥1d\geq 1, we have d/δ≥4002\sqrt{d}/\delta\geq 400^{2}, so

ln⁡(d400​δ)=ln⁡(dδ)−ln⁡400≥12​ln⁡(dδ).\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{400\delta}\right)=\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\delta}\right)-\ln 400\geq\frac{1}{2}\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\delta}\right).

Since r≥1r\geq 1 implies 2​r+1≤3​r2r+1\leq 3r, (109) therefore gives

r≥16​π2​ln⁡κ​ln⁡(dδ).r\geq\frac{1}{6\pi^{2}}\,\ln\kappa\,\ln\!\left(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{\delta}\right).

This holds for every algorithm and query budget satisfying the uniform accuracy guarantee. Taking the minimum over such budgets proves the lower bound of 4.4, for example with c=1/(6​π2)c=1/(6\pi^{2}) and δ0=400−2\delta_{0}=400^{-2}.

Finally, Zoloflow belongs to 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r}, and Theorem  4.4 supplies a matching upper bound with a universal constant throughout this parameter regime. This proves the lower bound ∎

Appendix I Rescaling and Centering: Approaches for handling 𝒩⁡(μ,Λ−1)\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Lambda^{-1}), where spec(Λ)⊂[λmin,λmax](\Lambda)\subset[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}] and μ≠0\mu\neq 0

Zoloflow is engineered to be optimal for centered Gaussian targets x1∼𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) that are normalized such that spec⁡(Λ)⊂[1,κ]\operatorname{spec}(\Lambda)\subset[1,\kappa]. In this section, we explore how to modify Zoloflow to achieve the same optimal relative error E^κ,r\hat{E}_{\kappa,r} when we instead have μ≠0\mu\neq 0 and spec​(Λ)⊂[λm​i​n,λm​a​x]\text{spec}(\Lambda)\subset[\lambda_{min},\lambda_{max}] for 0<λmin<λmax0<\lambda_{\min}<\lambda_{\max}. We begin with the following two different techniques to accommodate the arbitrary endpoints.

  1. 1.

    Target rescaling works by (1) building a modified stochastic interpolant by rescaling the target x1x_{1} so that the spectrum is normalized to [1,κ][1,\kappa], (2) running the new interpolant ODE where we know Zoloflow is optimal, and then (3) rescaling the output back to the original spectrum.

  2. 2.

    Gauge rescaling works by rescaling the interpolant schedules themselves by a gauge g⁡(t)g(t), a time-dependent spatial rescaling that is amortized over the interpolant time.

We discuss both of these options in Sections I.1 and I.2 for centered distributions. Then in Section I.3, we argue that generalizing to μ≠0\mu\neq 0 is quite simple.

I.1  Target rescaling

Definition I.1 (Target Rescaled Stochastic Interpolant).

For any VP interpolant pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) consider the rescaled target

x1(λmin)≜λmin​x1,Λ(λmin)≜Λλmin,⟹x1(λmin)∼𝒩⁡(0,(Λ(λmin))−1),Id⪯Λ(λmin)⪯κ​Id.x_{1}^{(\lambda_{\min})}\triangleq\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\,x_{1},\ \Lambda^{(\lambda_{\min})}\triangleq\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda_{\min}},\\ \implies x_{1}^{(\lambda_{\min})}\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(0,(\Lambda^{(\lambda_{\min})})^{-1}\right),\ I_{d}\preceq\Lambda^{(\lambda_{\min})}\preceq\kappa I_{d}. (110)

We define the target rescaled Stochastic Interpolant transporting zz to x1(λmin)x_{1}^{(\lambda_{\min})} as

yt=αt​z+βt​x1(λmin)=αt​z+βt​[λmin1/2​x1].y_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}x_{1}^{(\lambda_{\min})}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}\left[\lambda_{\min}^{1/2}x_{1}\right]. (111)

Throughout this subsection, the scale λmin>0\lambda_{\min}>0 is fixed, and we suppress the dependence of yty_{t}, p~t\widetilde{p}_{t}, and s~t\widetilde{s}_{t} on λmin\lambda_{\min}. Intuitively, this rescaling maps the left endpoint of the target precision spectrum to IdI_{d}, which again reduces the distance our initial Gaussian zz must travel and recovers our original setup. The associated probability flow ODE is given by

y˙t=β˙tβt​(y+s~t​(y)),y0∼𝒩⁡(0,I),s~t≜∇log⁡pyt​(y).\dot{y}_{t}=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left(y+\tilde{s}_{t}(y)\right),\quad y_{0}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I),\quad\tilde{s}_{t}\triangleq\nabla\log p_{y_{t}}(y). (112)
Equivalent schedule interpretation and reuse of the original score.

Target rescaling can equivalently be viewed as retaining the original target x1x_{1} and using coefficients

αt∗≜αt,βt∗≜λmin​βt,yt=xt∗.\alpha_{t}^{*}\triangleq\alpha_{t},\qquad\beta_{t}^{*}\triangleq\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\,\beta_{t},\qquad y_{t}=x_{t}^{*}.

Both interpretations define the same interpolant and hence the same probability-flow ODE. Although the starred coefficients are generally not VP or endpoint-normalized, the general case of Proposition K.1 still applies. Under its assumptions, with σ⁡(t)=αt/βt\sigma(t)=\alpha_{t}/\beta_{t}, the time change and spatial scaling are

τ⁡(t)≜σ−1​(σ⁡(t)λmin),ct=Aλmin​(t)≜αt2+λmin​βt2.\tau(t)\triangleq\sigma^{-1}\!\left(\frac{\sigma(t)}{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}}\right),\qquad c_{t}=A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)\triangleq\sqrt{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\lambda_{\min}\beta_{t}^{2}}.

as (ατ⁡(t),βτ⁡(t))=(αtAλmin​(t),βt​λmin1/2Aλmin​(t))(\alpha_{\tau(t)},\beta_{\tau(t)})=\left(\frac{\alpha_{t}}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)},\frac{\beta_{t}\lambda_{\min}^{1/2}}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}\right) gives ct=βt∗/βτ⁡(t)=Aλmin​(t).c_{t}=\beta_{t}^{*}/\beta_{\tau(t)}=A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t). Consequently, the rescaled score and velocity satisfy

s~t​(y)\displaystyle\widetilde{s}_{t}(y) =1Aλmin​(t)​sτ⁡(t)​(yAλmin​(t)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}s_{\tau(t)}\!\left(\frac{y}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}\right), (113)
b~t​(y)\displaystyle\widetilde{b}_{t}(y) =β˙tβt​(y+s~t​(y))=β˙tβt​[y+1Aλmin​(t)​sτ⁡(t)​(yAλmin​(t))].\displaystyle=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\bigl(y+\widetilde{s}_{t}(y)\bigr)=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left[y+\frac{1}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}s_{\tau(t)}\!\left(\frac{y}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}\right)\right]. (114)

Thus the target rescaled flow can be implemented using the original score oracle.

The following proposition states that Zoloflow on the rescaled interpolant also recovers the optimal Gaussian sampling rate. We articulate this method for any VP pair (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) through the following algorithm

Proposition I.2 (Zoloflow optimality on the target-rescaled interpolant).

Let π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with spec⁡(Λ)⊆[λmin,λmax]\operatorname{spec}(\Lambda)\subseteq[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}], set κ≜λmax/λmin\kappa\triangleq\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}, and take the elliptic schedule (αt,βt)=(cn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m),sn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m))(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(\cn(K(m)t\mid m),\sn(K(m)t\mid m)) with m=1−κ−1m=1-\kappa^{-1}. xr=λmin−1/2q^κ,r(Λλmin)z=Qλmin,κ,r(Λ)z,Qλmin,κ,r(λ)≜λmin−1/2q^κ,r(λ/λmin),x_{r}=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/2}\,\hat{q}_{\kappa,r}\!\left(\frac{\Lambda}{\lambda_{\min}}\right)z=Q_{\lambda_{\min},\kappa,r}(\Lambda)\,z,\qquad Q_{\lambda_{\min},\kappa,r}(\lambda)\triangleq\lambda_{\min}^{-1/2}\,\hat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda/\lambda_{\min}), (115)

and

where, writing (αt,βt)=(cos⁡φ⁡(t),sin⁡φ⁡(t))(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(\cos\varphi(t),\sin\varphi(t)), τ⁡(t)=φ−1​(arctan⁡(λmin​tan⁡φ⁡(t)))\tau(t)=\varphi^{-1}\!\big(\arctan(\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\tan\varphi(t))\big). For the elliptic schedule,

Corollary I.3 (Same complexity as Zoloflow).

and dTV​(π^,π)≤εd_{\mathrm{TV}}(\hat{\pi},\pi)\leq\varepsilon whenever r≥ln⁡(16​κ)2​π2​ln⁡(8​2​dε)−12r\geq\frac{\ln(16\kappa)}{2\pi^{2}}\ln\!\big(\frac{8\sqrt{2d}}{\varepsilon}\big)-\frac{1}{2}. I.2  Gauge rescaling

Fix a VP interpolant schedule (α,β)(\alpha,\beta) and a scale parameter λmin>0\lambda_{\min}>0.

Definition I.4 (Gauge).

A gauge is a strictly positive function g∈C1​([0,1])g\in C^{1}([0,1]) satisfying g0=1g_{0}=1 and g1=λmin−1/2g_{1}=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/2}. The corresponding gauge-rescaled schedule is

αt∗≜gt​αt,βt∗≜λmin​gt​βt,t∈[0,1].\alpha_{t}^{*}\triangleq g_{t}\alpha_{t},\qquad\beta_{t}^{*}\triangleq\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\,g_{t}\beta_{t},\qquad t\in[0,1]. (123)

These endpoint conditions ensure (α0∗,β0∗)=(1,0)(\alpha_{0}^{*},\beta_{0}^{*})=(1,0) and (α1∗,β1∗)=(0,1)(\alpha_{1}^{*},\beta_{1}^{*})=(0,1).

For independent z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) and x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi, the gauge-rescaled interpolant satisfies

xt∗=αt∗​z+βt∗​x1=gt​(αt​z+λmin​βt​x1)⏟yt.x_{t}^{*}=\alpha_{t}^{*}z+\beta_{t}^{*}x_{1}=g_{t}\underbrace{\left(\alpha_{t}z+\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\beta_{t}x_{1}\right)}_{y_{t}}. (124)

Thus it is a time-dependent spatial rescaling of the target interpolant yty_{t}, with x0∗=zx_{0}^{*}=z and x1∗=x1x_{1}^{*}=x_{1}. Every gauge preserves the shifted noise-to-signal ratio αt∗/βt∗=αt/(λmin​βt)\alpha_{t}^{*}/\beta_{t}^{*}=\alpha_{t}/(\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\beta_{t}) for t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1).

Let pt∗p_{t}^{*} denote the density of xt∗x_{t}^{*} and define st∗​(x)≜∇x​log​pt∗​(x)s_{t}^{*}(x)\triangleq\nabla_{x}\log p_{t}^{*}(x). Using αt2+βt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1, the associated probability-flow ODE becomes

X˙t=g˙tgt​Xt+β˙tβt​(Xt+gt2​st∗​(Xt)),t∈(0,1),X0=z.\dot{X}_{t}=\frac{\dot{g}_{t}}{g_{t}}X_{t}+\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left(X_{t}+g_{t}^{2}s_{t}^{*}(X_{t})\right),\qquad t\in(0,1),\qquad X_{0}=z. (125)

Equivalently, one can use K.1 to write the ODE in terms of the original score. We consider two choices of gauge.

I.2.1  VP gauge

The choice

gtVP≜1Aλmin​(t)=1αt2+λmin​βt2g_{t}^{\mathrm{VP}}\triangleq\frac{1}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\lambda_{\min}\beta_{t}^{2}}} (126)

gives the variance-preserving schedule

αt∗=αtAλmin​(t),βt∗=λmin​βtAλmin​(t).\alpha_{t}^{*}=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)},\qquad\beta_{t}^{*}=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}}\beta_{t}}{A_{\lambda_{\min}}(t)}. (127)

The associated probability-flow ODE simplifies to

X˙t=β˙tβt​(αt2+λmin​βt2)​(Xt+st∗​(Xt)),t∈(0,1),X0=z.\dot{X}_{t}=\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}\left(\alpha_{t}^{2}+\lambda_{\min}\beta_{t}^{2}\right)}\left(X_{t}+s_{t}^{*}(X_{t})\right),\qquad t\in(0,1),\qquad X_{0}=z. (128)
Proposition I.5 (Gaussian approximation under the VP gauge).

Let π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with λmin​Id⪯Λ⪯λmax​Id\lambda_{\min}I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\lambda_{\max}I_{d}, set κ≜λmax/λmin\kappa\triangleq\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min}, and let (αt∗,βt∗)(\alpha_{t}^{*},\beta_{t}^{*}) be the VP-gauge schedule (127) of the elliptic base schedule with parameter κ\kappa. Then xr=Qλmin,κ,r​(Λ)​zx_{r}=Q_{\lambda_{\min},\kappa,r}(\Lambda)z, where

Qλmin,κ,r​(λ)≜qκ,r​(λ/λmin)qκ,r​(1/λmin).Q_{\lambda_{\min},\kappa,r}(\lambda)\triangleq\frac{q_{\kappa,r}(\lambda/\lambda_{\min})}{q_{\kappa,r}(1/\lambda_{\min})}. (129)

Here qκ,rq_{\kappa,r} denotes the Zolotarev inverse-square-root approximant (60) on [1,κ][1,\kappa], with relative error Eκ,rE_{\kappa,r}. If 1∈[λmin,λmax]1\in[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}], equivalently 1/λmin∈[1,κ]1/\lambda_{\min}\in[1,\kappa], then

maxλ∈[λmin,λmax]⁡|λ​Qλmin,κ,r​(λ)−1|≤2​Eκ,r1−Eκ,r.\max_{\lambda\in[\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]}\left|\sqrt{\lambda}\,Q_{\lambda_{\min},\kappa,r}(\lambda)-1\right|\leq\frac{2E_{\kappa,r}}{1-E_{\kappa,r}}. (130)
Proof.

Write αi≜α⁡(i/(2​r+1))\alpha_{i}\triangleq\alpha(i/(2r+1)), βi≜β⁡(i/(2​r+1))\beta_{i}\triangleq\beta(i/(2r+1)) and Di​(μ)≜μ​αi2+βi2D_{i}(\mu)\triangleq\mu\alpha_{i}^{2}+\beta_{i}^{2} for i=1,…,2​ri=1,\dots,2r, so that the query time tjt_{j} and the half-step tj+h/2t_{j}+h/2 of the jj-th update correspond to i=2​j−1i=2j-1 and i=2​ji=2j; define αi∗\alpha_{i}^{*}, βi∗\beta_{i}^{*} and Di∗​(λ)≜λ​αi∗2+βi∗2D_{i}^{*}(\lambda)\triangleq\lambda\alpha_{i}^{*2}+\beta_{i}^{*2} in the same way for the VP-gauge schedule.

One step. Fix an eigenvalue λ\lambda of Λ\Lambda and let xλ,jx_{\lambda,j} denote the corresponding component of xjx_{j}. I.2.2  Exponential gauge

The choice gtexp≜λmin−t/2g_{t}^{\mathrm{exp}}\triangleq\lambda_{\min}^{-t/2} gives the generally non-VP schedule

αt∗=λmin−t/2αt,βt∗=λmin(1−t)/2βt.\alpha_{t}^{*}=\lambda_{\min}^{-t/2}\alpha_{t},\qquad\beta_{t}^{*}=\lambda_{\min}^{(1-t)/2}\beta_{t}. (135)

Its probability-flow ODE is

X˙t=−log⁡λmin2​Xt+β˙tβt​(Xt+λmin−t​st∗​(Xt)),t∈(0,1),X0=z.\dot{X}_{t}=-\frac{\log\lambda_{\min}}{2}X_{t}+\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}\left(X_{t}+\lambda_{\min}^{-t}s_{t}^{*}(X_{t})\right),\qquad t\in(0,1),\qquad X_{0}=z. (136)
Generalized Zoloflow.

We use an exponential integrator-like discretization of the exponential-gauge ODE: the score-dependent term is approximated by the elliptic finite-difference rule, while the linear term −12​log⁡(λmin)​Xt-\tfrac{1}{2}\log(\lambda_{\min})X_{t} is integrated exactly. Distributing this linear evolution equally across rr updates gives the factor

exp(−log⁡λmin2​r)=λmin−1/(2r)\exp\!\left(-\frac{\log\lambda_{\min}}{2r}\right)=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/(2r)} (137)

per update.

Definition I.6 (Generalized Zoloflow).

Fix λmin>0\lambda_{\min}>0, κ>1\kappa>1, and an integer r≥1r\geq 1. Let (αt,βt)=(cn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m),sn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m))(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(\cn(K(m)t\mid m),\sn(K(m)t\mid m)), where m≜1−κ−1m\triangleq 1-\kappa^{-1}, and let st∗s_{t}^{*} denote the score under the exponential-gauge schedule. Define

h≜22​r+1,tj≜2​j−12​r+1,ωj≜βtj+h/22−βtj2βtj2,j=1,…,r.h\triangleq\frac{2}{2r+1},\qquad t_{j}\triangleq\frac{2j-1}{2r+1},\qquad\omega_{j}\triangleq\frac{\beta_{t_{j}+h/2}^{2}-\beta_{t_{j}}^{2}}{\beta_{t_{j}}^{2}},\qquad j=1,\ldots,r. (138)

Starting from x0=z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)x_{0}=z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}), Generalized Zoloflow performs the updates

xj=λmin−1/(2r)[xj−1+ωj(xj−1+λmin−tjstj∗(xj−1))],j=1,…,r,x_{j}=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/(2r)}\left[x_{j-1}+\omega_{j}\left(x_{j-1}+\lambda_{\min}^{-t_{j}}s_{t_{j}}^{*}(x_{j-1})\right)\right],\qquad j=1,\ldots,r, (139)

For a centered Gaussian target π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with λmin​Id⪯Λ⪯λmin​κ​Id\lambda_{\min}I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\lambda_{\min}\kappa I_{d}, exact scores satisfy, along a precision eigenmode λ\lambda,

λmin−t​st∗​(xλ)=−λ/λmin(λ/λmin)​αt2+βt2​xλ.\lambda_{\min}^{-t}s_{t}^{*}(x_{\lambda})=-\frac{\lambda/\lambda_{\min}}{(\lambda/\lambda_{\min})\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}}\,x_{\lambda}. (140)

xλ,j=λmin−1/(2r)(λ/λmin)​αtj+h/22+βtj+h/22(λ/λmin)​αtj2+βtj2xλ,j−1.x_{\lambda,j}=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/(2r)}\frac{(\lambda/\lambda_{\min})\alpha_{t_{j}+h/2}^{2}+\beta_{t_{j}+h/2}^{2}}{(\lambda/\lambda_{\min})\alpha_{t_{j}}^{2}+\beta_{t_{j}}^{2}}x_{\lambda,j-1}. (141)

xλ,j=λmin−1/(2r)λ/λmin+ξjλ/λmin+ζj1+ζj1+ξjxλ,j−1.x_{\lambda,j}=\lambda_{\min}^{-1/(2r)}\frac{\lambda/\lambda_{\min}+\xi_{j}}{\lambda/\lambda_{\min}+\zeta_{j}}\frac{1+\zeta_{j}}{1+\xi_{j}}x_{\lambda,j-1}. (143)

I.3  Centering

Assumption 2.4 takes the target to be centered; this is without loss of generality. Let x~1∼π\tilde{x}_{1}\sim\pi be centered, and suppose the data instead have mean μ\mu, i.e. x1=x~1+μx_{1}=\tilde{x}_{1}+\mu. Write

x~t=αt​z+βt​x~1,\displaystyle\tilde{x}_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}\tilde{x}_{1},\quad (centered) (145)
xt=αt​z+βt​x1,\displaystyle x_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}x_{1},\quad (not centered) (146)

for the two interpolants, with respective s~t=∇log⁡p~t\tilde{s}_{t}=\nabla\log\tilde{p}_{t} and st=∇log⁡pts_{t}=\nabla\log p_{t}. Then x~t=xt−βt​μ\tilde{x}_{t}=x_{t}-\beta_{t}\mu. Additionally we can write the velocities b~t​(x~)=𝔼⁡[x~˙t∣x~t=x~]\tilde{b}_{t}(\tilde{x})=\mathbb{E}[\dot{\tilde{x}}_{t}\mid\tilde{x}_{t}=\tilde{x}], and bt​(x)=𝔼⁡[x˙t∣xt=x]b_{t}(x)=\mathbb{E}[\dot{x}_{t}\mid x_{t}=x].

Lemma I.7 (Centered score).

For all t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1) and y∈ℝdy\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

s~t​(y)=st​(y+βt​μ).\tilde{s}_{t}(y)=s_{t}(y+\beta_{t}\mu). (147)

Additionally, one can also write the corresponding velocity fields in terms of one another

b~t​(y)=bt​(y+βt​μ)−β˙t​μ.\tilde{b}_{t}(y)=b_{t}(y+\beta_{t}\mu)-\dot{\beta}_{t}\mu. (148)
Proof.

Since xtx_{t} is a deterministic translate of x~t\tilde{x}_{t}, pt​(x)=p~t​(x−βt​μ)p_{t}(x)=\tilde{p}_{t}(x-\beta_{t}\mu). Take ∇log\nabla\log of both sides and substitute x=y+βt​μx=y+\beta_{t}\mu. The velocity expression follows the same logic. ∎

Each evaluation of s~t\tilde{s}_{t} therefore costs exactly one evaluation of sts_{t}; note that the offset is βt​μ\beta_{t}\mu, not μ\mu. Given the oracle sts_{t}, one samples the law of x1x_{1} in two steps.

  1. 1.

    Estimate the mean. By Tweedie’s formula,

    μ^t​(x)≜x+αt2​st​(x)βt=𝔼⁡[x1∣xt=x].\hat{\mu}_{t}(x)\triangleq\frac{x+\alpha_{t}^{2}s_{t}(x)}{\beta_{t}}=\mathbb{E}[x_{1}\mid x_{t}=x]. (149)

    As t→0t\to 0 the likelihood of xtx_{t} given x1x_{1} flattens, so the posterior mean tends to the prior mean: μ^t​(x)→μ\hat{\mu}_{t}(x)\to\mu for every fixed xx for targets with finite moments (e.g., translates of targets in 𝖯κ\mathsf{P}_{\kappa}). A single score query thus recovers μ\mu to any desired accuracy.

  2. 2.

    Sample the centered target, then translate. Run any sampler for π\pi with the centered oracle s~t(⋅)=st(⋅+βtμ^)\tilde{s}_{t}(\cdot)=s_{t}(\cdot+\beta_{t}\hat{\mu}), producing x~^1\hat{\tilde{x}}_{1}, and output x^1=x~^1+μ^\hat{x}_{1}=\hat{\tilde{x}}_{1}+\hat{\mu}.

Appendix J Parameter-selection heuristic for general distributions

As described in Section 3.2, implementing the elliptic schedule requires choosing two parameters:

  1. 1.

    a center λ¯>0\bar{\lambda}>0, the scale set by target rescaling (Appendix I), which any schedule admits;

  2. 2.

    a width κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, the condition number of Eq. 10 (then set m=1−κ−1m=1-\kappa^{-1}), which is specific to the elliptic family.

The paper mostly works with (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa). Here we use the equivalent spectral endpoint parameterization (ℓ,L)=(λ¯/κ,λ¯​κ)(\ell,L)=(\bar{\lambda}/\sqrt{\kappa},\,\bar{\lambda}\sqrt{\kappa}), because the heuristic sets the endpoints directly. For Gaussians, optimal parameter choices for (ℓ,L)(\ell,L) depend on curvature endpoints −∇2​log​π-\nabla^{2}\log\pi or equivalently the smallest and largest eigenvalues of the precision matrix (λmin​(Λ),λmax​(Λ)),(\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda),\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)), where

λmin​Id⪯−∇2​log​π​(x)=Λ⪯λmax​Id.\lambda_{\min}I_{d}\preceq-\nabla^{2}\log\pi(x)=\Lambda\preceq\lambda_{\max}I_{d}. (150)

However, this equivalence decouples for general π\pi, and so it’s not obvious how to pick these parameters. For a general distribution π\pi with precision matrix Λπ=Σπ−1\Lambda_{\pi}=\Sigma^{-1}_{\pi} the two immediate extensions of these choices are

  1. 1.

    Curvature endpoints:

    (ℓ,L)=(λmin​(−∇2​log​π),λmax​(−∇2​log​π))(\ell,L)=\left(\lambda_{\min}(-\nabla^{2}\log\pi),\lambda_{\max}(-\nabla^{2}\log\pi)\right) (151)
  2. 2.

    Precision matrix endpoints

    (ℓ,L)=(λmin​(Λ),λmax​(Λ))(\ell,L)=\left(\lambda_{\min}(\Lambda),\lambda_{\max}(\Lambda)\right) (152)

The immediate issue with the curvature endpoints is generally ℓ<0\ell<0 can occur which is prohibited. Nevertheless even in the log-concave setting we provide evidence that this choice is too conservative in N.2. We propose the precision matrix endpoints as our heuristic:

The heuristic.

Let x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi have mean μ\mu and covariance Σ=𝔼⁡[(x1−μ)​(x1−μ)⊤]\Sigma=\mathbb{E}[(x_{1}-\mu)(x_{1}-\mu)^{\top}]. We use the endpoints of the inverse covariance spectrum to define a reference setting for the target-rescaled elliptic schedule (Section I.1):

ℓ=λmin​(Σ−1)=1λmax​(Σ),L=λmax​(Σ−1)=1λmin​(Σ),κ=Lℓ.\ell\;=\;\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma^{-1})\;=\;\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)},\qquad L\;=\;\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{-1})\;=\;\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)},\qquad\kappa\;=\;\frac{L}{\ell}. (153)

In center–width form, (λ¯,κ)=(1/λmin​(Σ)​λmax​(Σ),λmax​(Σ)/λmin​(Σ))(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=\bigl(1/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)},\,\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\bigr), as stated in Section 3.2. The heuristic has three properties that motivate it:

  1. 1.

    It is exact in the Gaussian case. If x1∼𝒩⁡(m,Λ−1)x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(m,\Lambda^{-1}) then Σ−1=Λ\Sigma^{-1}=\Lambda, so (153) returns the endpoints of the precision spectrum, which is the optimal choice of Section 4.

  2. 2.

    It matches isotropic covariance by rescaling. If Σ=σ2​I\Sigma=\sigma^{2}I, then ℓ=L=σ−2\ell=L=\sigma^{-2} and the schedule is trig rescaled to the data variance, coinciding with the closed-form isotropic Gaussian schedule of Sabour et al. (2024). The heuristic assigns width one in this case; this need not be the best width for a non-Gaussian target with isotropic covariance.

  3. 3.

    It is bounded by the curvature. For strongly log-concave π\pi, we have

    λmin≤λmin​(Σ−1)≤λmax​(Σ−1)≤λmax,\lambda_{\min}\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma^{-1})\leq\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma^{-1})\leq\lambda_{\max}, (154)

    so the interval (153) always lies inside [λmin,λmax][\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}] and is never wider than the curvature recipe.

For general non-Gaussian targets, these properties motivate an initial parameter choice for a given solver and query budget. The covariance center and width can then be adjusted separately. In the covariance-center frond ablation (Figures 18 and 19), we retain the covariance center for all rescaled schedules and sweep the elliptic width: the covariance width κ≈36.1\kappa\approx 36.1 gives NLL 26.3926.39, while the best tested width κ=104\kappa=10^{4} gives 7.067.06. This experiment demonstrates the usefulness of covariance-based centering and the additional benefit of varying width.

In practice, we may not have access to the exact covariance Σ\Sigma, so we recommend computing the sample covariance Σ^\hat{\Sigma} and taking the 0.5th and 99.5th quantiles of the spectrum of λmin(0.5)​(Σ^)\lambda_{\min}^{(0.5)}(\hat{\Sigma}) and λmax(99.5)​(Σ^)\lambda_{\max}^{(99.5)}(\hat{\Sigma})

(ℓ,L)=(1λmax(99.5),1λmin(0.5))(\ell,L)=\left(\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max}^{(99.5)}},\frac{1}{\lambda_{\min}^{(0.5)}}\right) (155)

and using this ℓ\ell and LL for target rescaled Elliptic schedule. Alternatively, it can serve to guide a more in-depth hyperparameter sweep.

Appendix K Interpolant schedules

K.1  Interpolant schedule catalog

We collect the schedules used in the paper. Their dependence on target scale and spectral width is discussed in Section 3.2; the following subsections explain their conversions and the elliptic schedule’s Lipschitz properties.

  • •

    Linear Schedule:

    αl​i​n​(t)=1−t,βl​i​n​(t)=t.\alpha^{lin}(t)={1-t},\quad\beta^{lin}(t)=t. (156)
  • •

    Square Root Schedule:

    αs​q​r​t​(t)=1−t,βs​q​r​t​(t)=t.\alpha^{sqrt}(t)=\sqrt{1-t},\quad\beta^{sqrt}(t)=\sqrt{t}. (157)
  • •

    Trigonometric Schedule:

    αt​r​i​g​(t)=cos⁡(12​π​t),βt​r​i​g​(t)=sin⁡(12​π​t).\alpha^{trig}(t)=\cos\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi t\right),\quad\beta^{trig}(t)=\sin\left(\frac{1}{2}\pi t\right). (158)
  • •

    Elliptic Schedule: For a given κ≥1\kappa\geq 1, with m=1−κ−1m=1-\kappa^{-1} and K=K⁡(m)K=K(m),

    αe​l​l​(t)=cn⁡(K​t|m),βe​l​l​(t)=sn⁡(K​t|m).\alpha^{ell}(t)=\cn(Kt\ |\ m),\quad\beta^{ell}(t)=\sn(Kt\ |\ m). (159)
  • •

    Lipschitz-Guided Schedule: For a given κ>1\kappa>1,

    αl​i​p​(t)=κ1−t−1κ−1,βl​i​p​(t)=κ−κ1−tκ−1.\alpha^{lip}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa^{1-t}-1}{\kappa-1}},\quad\beta^{lip}(t)=\sqrt{\frac{\kappa-\kappa^{1-t}}{\kappa-1}}. (160)

    This schedule was introduced in Chen et al. (2025).

  • •

    EDM Schedule (VP-normalized): For given σmax>σmin>0\sigma_{\max}>\sigma_{\min}>0 and ρ>0\rho>0, let

    σρ​(t)=((1−t)​σmax1/ρ+t​σmin1/ρ)ρ.\sigma_{\rho}(t)=\left((1-t)\sigma_{\max}^{1/\rho}+t\sigma_{\min}^{1/\rho}\right)^{\rho}. (161)

    The VP normalization of the EDM noise schedule (Karras et al., 2022a) is

    αe​d​m​(t)=σρ​(t)1+σρ​(t)2,βe​d​m​(t)=11+σρ​(t)2.\alpha^{edm}(t)=\frac{\sigma_{\rho}(t)}{\sqrt{1+\sigma_{\rho}(t)^{2}}},\quad\beta^{edm}(t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\sigma_{\rho}(t)^{2}}}. (162)

    Thus (αe​d​m​(t))2+(βe​d​m​(t))2=1(\alpha^{edm}(t))^{2}+(\beta^{edm}(t))^{2}=1, and the signal-to-noise ratio is SNR⁡(t)=(βe​d​m​(t)/αe​d​m​(t))2=σρ​(t)−2\operatorname{SNR}(t)=\allowbreak(\beta^{edm}(t)/\alpha^{edm}(t))^{2}=\allowbreak\sigma_{\rho}(t)^{-2}. With finite positive noise endpoints, this traces a truncated VP path: its endpoint SNRs are σmax−2\sigma_{\max}^{-2} and σmin−2\sigma_{\min}^{-2}.

st∗​(x)\displaystyle s_{t}^{*}(x) =1ct​sτ⁡(t)​(x/ct),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{c_{t}}s_{\tau(t)}(x/c_{t}), (165)
bt∗​(x)\displaystyle b_{t}^{*}(x) =c˙tct​x+ct​τ˙​(t)​bτ⁡(t)​(x/ct).\displaystyle=\frac{\dot{c}_{t}}{c_{t}}x+c_{t}\dot{\tau}(t)b_{\tau(t)}(x/c_{t}). (166)

Consequently, any solution X˙u=bu​(Xu)\dot{X}_{u}=b_{u}(X_{u}) on (0,1)(0,1) yields a solution Xt∗≜ct​Xτ⁡(t)X_{t}^{*}\triangleq c_{t}X_{\tau(t)} of X˙t∗=bt∗​(Xt∗)\dot{X}_{t}^{*}=b_{t}^{*}(X_{t}^{*}). Finally, if both coefficient pairs are variance-preserving, then ct=1c_{t}=1, so

st∗​(x)=sτ⁡(t)​(x),bt∗​(x)=τ˙​(t)​bτ⁡(t)​(x).s_{t}^{*}(x)=s_{\tau(t)}(x),\qquad b_{t}^{*}(x)=\dot{\tau}(t)b_{\tau(t)}(x). (167)

Proposition K.1 shows that, under its assumptions, two linear stochastic interpolants with the same target x1∼πx_{1}\sim\pi and Gaussian reference z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) are related by a change of time and a rescaling of space. The time change τ\tau is chosen so that the two schedules have the same noise-to-signal ratio α/β\alpha/\beta at corresponding times, and the scores and velocity fields then transform accordingly. When both schedules are variance-preserving, the spatial rescaling is trivial (ct=1c_{t}=1) and only the time change remains.

K.3  Bijection between VP interpolant schedules and noise schedules

VP interpolant schedules, noise schedules, and SNR schedules are in one-to-one correspondence. For positive coefficients on t∈(0,1)t\in(0,1), the forward map is

σt=αtβt,SNR⁡(t)=βt2αt2=σt−2.\sigma_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\beta_{t}},\qquad\operatorname{SNR}(t)=\frac{\beta_{t}^{2}}{\alpha_{t}^{2}}=\sigma_{t}^{-2}.

Conversely, specifying either the noise level σt\sigma_{t} or the SNR uniquely determines the VP coefficients:

(αt,βt)=(σt,1)1+σt2=(1,SNR⁡(t))1+SNR⁡(t).(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=\frac{(\sigma_{t},1)}{\sqrt{1+\sigma_{t}^{2}}}=\frac{\bigl(1,\sqrt{\operatorname{SNR}(t)}\bigr)}{\sqrt{1+\operatorname{SNR}(t)}}. (168)

Thus a noise schedule specifies the time-varying SNR; its squared noise level σt2\sigma_{t}^{2} is the inverse SNR. Every positive interpolant schedule defines an SNR, and the VP constraint selects a unique interpolant schedule for each SNR. Without that constraint, a common rescaling of αt\alpha_{t} and βt\beta_{t} leaves the SNR unchanged.

In our noise-to-data orientation, full VP schedules correspond to strictly decreasing noise clocks with σt→∞\sigma_{t}\to\infty as t↓0t\downarrow 0 and σt→0\sigma_{t}\to 0 as t↑1t\uparrow 1; equivalently, SNR increases from 00 to ∞\infty. The VP coefficients extend to the endpoints by these limits. Finite positive noise endpoints instead describe a truncated VP path.

Why the correspondence holds.

Let xt=αt​z+βt​x1x_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}x_{1} follow a VP interpolant. Dividing by the data coefficient gives the corresponding VE-corrupted variable:

yt≜xtβt=x1+σt​z,σt=αtβt.y_{t}\triangleq\frac{x_{t}}{\beta_{t}}=x_{1}+\sigma_{t}z,\qquad\sigma_{t}=\frac{\alpha_{t}}{\beta_{t}}. (169)

Conversely, normalizing the coefficients (σt,1)(\sigma_{t},1) of x1+σt​zx_{1}+\sigma_{t}z to have squared sum one gives (168). These operations are inverses, establishing the bijection. The VP and VE states are related by xt=βt​ytx_{t}=\beta_{t}y_{t}, so their probability-flow ODEs transform accordingly: if X˙t=bt​(Xt)\dot{X}_{t}=b_{t}(X_{t}), then Yt=Xt/βtY_{t}=X_{t}/\beta_{t} satisfies

Y˙t=1βt​bt​(βt​Yt)−β˙tβt​Yt.\dot{Y}_{t}=\frac{1}{\beta_{t}}b_{t}(\beta_{t}Y_{t})-\frac{\dot{\beta}_{t}}{\beta_{t}}Y_{t}. (170)

An increasing VE grid σmin=σ0<⋯<σn=σmax\sigma_{\min}=\sigma_{0}<\cdots<\sigma_{n}=\sigma_{\max} therefore corresponds to the reverse-ordered interpolant times ti=σ−1​(σi)t_{i}=\sigma^{-1}(\sigma_{i}). The clock fixes the correspondence between query times; the numerical update rule is an additional choice. The following AYS example makes this conversion explicit.

K.3.1  Gaussian AYS as a special case of the elliptic schedule

For isotropic Gaussian targets, the closed-form AYS noise grid is recovered by the VP form of the target-rescaled elliptic schedule at κ=1\kappa=1. This correspondence concerns the analytic Gaussian example in Sabour et al. (2024, Theorem 3.1), which motivates their later KL-divergence upper bound (KLUB) framework; the identification is with this analytic result, not with schedules obtained by numerical KLUB optimization. We show the correspondence by expressing the Gaussian AYS schedule as a VP interpolant and identifying its coefficients with those of the rescaled trigonometric schedule.

AYS in VP form.

For x1∼𝒩⁡(0,c2​Id)x_{1}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,c^{2}I_{d}) with c>0c>0, this analytic schedule spaces the angle arctan⁡(σ/c)\arctan(\sigma/c) uniformly:

σi⋆=ctan[(1−in)arctan(σminc)+inarctan(σmaxc)],i=0,…,n.\sigma_{i}^{\star}=c\tan\!\left[\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right)\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sigma_{\min}}{c}\right)+\frac{i}{n}\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sigma_{\max}}{c}\right)\right],\qquad i=0,\ldots,n. (171)

A continuous clock generating this grid in our noise-to-data orientation is, with θ⁡(u)=π​u/2\theta(u)=\pi u/2,

σAYS​(u)=c​cot⁡θ⁡(u),arctan⁡(σAYS​(u)c)=π2​(1−u),u∈(0,1).\sigma^{\mathrm{AYS}}(u)=c\cot\theta(u),\qquad\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sigma^{\mathrm{AYS}}(u)}{c}\right)=\frac{\pi}{2}(1-u),\qquad u\in(0,1). (172)

Explicitly, define the interpolant-time grid by

ui≜1−2πarctan(σi⋆c)=(1−in)u0+inun,i=0,…,n.u_{i}\triangleq 1-\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\!\left(\frac{\sigma_{i}^{\star}}{c}\right)=\left(1-\frac{i}{n}\right)u_{0}+\frac{i}{n}u_{n},\qquad i=0,\ldots,n.

Then σAYS​(ui)=σi⋆\sigma^{\mathrm{AYS}}(u_{i})=\sigma_{i}^{\star} exactly. For 0<σmin<σmax<∞0<\sigma_{\min}<\sigma_{\max}<\infty, the times are equally spaced on [un,u0]⊂(0,1)[u_{n},u_{0}]\subset(0,1), with u0>⋯>unu_{0}>\cdots>u_{n}. Sampling traverses i=n,n−1,…,0i=n,n-1,\ldots,0, so uu increases as noise decreases. The grid is uniform in uu; the noise levels themselves are generally nonuniform.

The conversion (168) gives the VP coefficients

(αuAYS,βuAYS)=(c​cos⁡θ⁡(u),sin⁡θ⁡(u))c2​cos2⁡θ⁡(u)+sin2⁡θ⁡(u),(\alpha_{u}^{\mathrm{AYS}},\beta_{u}^{\mathrm{AYS}})=\frac{(c\cos\theta(u),\sin\theta(u))}{\sqrt{c^{2}\cos^{2}\theta(u)+\sin^{2}\theta(u)}}, (173)

which define the interpolant xuAYS=αuAYS​z+βuAYS​x1x_{u}^{\mathrm{AYS}}=\alpha_{u}^{\mathrm{AYS}}z+\beta_{u}^{\mathrm{AYS}}x_{1}, with z∼𝒩⁡(0,Id)z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}) independent of x1x_{1}.

Identification with elliptic at κ=1\kappa=1.

At κ=1\kappa=1, the elliptic coefficients are (cos⁡θ⁡(u),sin⁡θ⁡(u))(\cos\theta(u),\sin\theta(u)). Rescaling the target to x1/cx_{1}/c (Section I.1) makes the coefficients relative to the original target x1x_{1} equal to (cos⁡θ⁡(u),c−1​sin⁡θ⁡(u))(\cos\theta(u),c^{-1}\sin\theta(u)). Their VP normalization is exactly (173). The uniform grid {ui}i=0n\{u_{i}\}_{i=0}^{n} therefore realizes the Gaussian AYS schedule in this rescaled elliptic time. This identifies the schedule and query grid. The cited AYS optimality result concerns Euler/DDIM; Zoloflow uses the elliptic finite-difference update.

K.4  Asymptotic drift-Lipschitz optimality of the elliptic schedule

The Lipschitz-guided schedule of Chen et al. (2025) controls the spatial sensitivity of the velocity field. On the Gaussian class with precision spectra in [1,κ][1,\kappa], it attains the optimal worst-case drift-Lipschitz bound. The elliptic schedule, although chosen for analyticity, approaches the same optimum as κ→∞\kappa\to\infty, both for the worst-case Lipschitz constant and for their averaged squared criterion. We make this connection precise below.

K.4.1  The drift-Lipschitz criterion and its optimal value

Consider π=𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)\pi=\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1}) with Id⪯Λ⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}, where κ>1\kappa>1. We optimize over the class 𝒮~\widetilde{\mathcal{S}} of monotone VP schedules with α0=β1=1\alpha_{0}=\beta_{1}=1, α1=β0=0\alpha_{1}=\beta_{0}=0, positive coefficients on (0,1)(0,1), and

α,β∈C⁡([0,1])∩C1​((0,1)),α2,β2∈C1​([0,1]).\alpha,\beta\in C([0,1])\cap C^{1}((0,1)),\qquad\alpha^{2},\beta^{2}\in C^{1}([0,1]). (174)

This permits the square-root endpoint behavior of the Lipschitz-guided schedule. For a precision eigenvalue λ∈[1,κ]\lambda\in[1,\kappa], the normalized probability-flow solution and its drift multiplier are

xλ​(t)=αt2+βt2/λ,gλ​(t)=dd​t​log⁡xλ​(t),x˙λ​(t)=gλ​(t)​xλ​(t).x_{\lambda}(t)=\sqrt{\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}/\lambda},\qquad g_{\lambda}(t)=\frac{d}{dt}\log x_{\lambda}(t),\qquad\dot{x}_{\lambda}(t)=g_{\lambda}(t)x_{\lambda}(t). (175)

Since the Gaussian velocity field is linear, its spatial Lipschitz constant is maxλ∈spec⁡(Λ)⁡|gλ​(t)|\max_{\lambda\in\operatorname{spec}(\Lambda)}|g_{\lambda}(t)|. Define the worst-case criterion

Lb​[α,β]≜supt∈(0,1)maxλ∈[1,κ]⁡|gλ​(t)|.L^{b}[\alpha,\beta]\triangleq\sup_{t\in(0,1)}\max_{\lambda\in[1,\kappa]}|g_{\lambda}(t)|. (176)

Writing qt=βt2q_{t}=\beta_{t}^{2}, the VP constraint gives

|gλ​(t)|=(1−λ−1)​q˙t2​(1−(1−λ−1)​qt).|g_{\lambda}(t)|=\frac{(1-\lambda^{-1})\dot{q}_{t}}{2\bigl(1-(1-\lambda^{-1})q_{t}\bigr)}.

Because q˙t≥0\dot{q}_{t}\geq 0, this expression increases with λ\lambda, so the worst case is λ=κ\lambda=\kappa. The endpoints xκ​(0)=1x_{\kappa}(0)=1 and xκ(1)=κ−1/2x_{\kappa}(1)=\kappa^{-1/2} therefore imply

Lb​[α,β]=supt|gκ​(t)|≥∫01|gκ​(t)|​𝑑t=12​log⁡κ≜dκ.L^{b}[\alpha,\beta]=\sup_{t}|g_{\kappa}(t)|\geq\int_{0}^{1}|g_{\kappa}(t)|\,dt=\tfrac{1}{2}\log\kappa\triangleq d_{\kappa}. (177)

The bound is attained by xκ(t)=κ−t/2x_{\kappa}(t)=\kappa^{-t/2}, for which gκ​(t)=−dκg_{\kappa}(t)=-d_{\kappa} is constant. Thus the optimal value is dκd_{\kappa}.

K.4.2  The Lipschitz-guided optimizer and its connection to prior work

Solving αt2+βt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1 and αt2+βt2/κ=κ−t\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}/\kappa=\kappa^{-t} gives exactly the Lipschitz-guided schedule in (160). Equality in (177) forces this constant logarithmic speed, so the optimizer is unique for κ>1\kappa>1. It coincides with the Gaussian optimizer of Chen et al. (2025, Proposition 3.9 and Equation (3.11)), taking their smallest covariance eigenvalue to be κ−1\kappa^{-1}.

Their criterion is the averaged squared spatial Lipschitz constant,

A2​[α,β;π]≜∫01𝔼X∼pt​[‖∇xbt​(X)‖op2]​𝑑t.A_{2}[\alpha,\beta;\pi]\triangleq\int_{0}^{1}\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p_{t}}\bigl[\|\nabla_{x}b_{t}(X)\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}\bigr]dt. (178)

For Gaussian targets the Jacobian is independent of XX. Taking the worst case over Id⪯Λ⪯κ​IdI_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d} and applying Cauchy–Schwarz yields

A2wc​[α,β]≜supId⪯Λ⪯κ​IdA2​[α,β;𝒩⁡(0,Λ−1)]=∫01|gκ​(t)|2​𝑑t≥dκ2.A_{2}^{\mathrm{wc}}[\alpha,\beta]\triangleq\sup_{I_{d}\preceq\Lambda\preceq\kappa I_{d}}A_{2}[\alpha,\beta;\mathcal{N}(0,\Lambda^{-1})]=\int_{0}^{1}|g_{\kappa}(t)|^{2}dt\geq d_{\kappa}^{2}. (179)

The Lipschitz-guided schedule attains equality. It therefore minimizes both LbL^{b} and A2wcA_{2}^{\mathrm{wc}}.

K.4.3  The elliptic schedule approaches the same optimum

For the elliptic schedule, with m=1−κ−1m=1-\kappa^{-1}, the worst-mode solution is xκell​(t)=dn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m)x_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{ell}}(t)=\dn(K(m)t\mid m). Hence

gκell​(t)=−K⁡(m)​m​sn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m)​cn​(K⁡(m)​t∣m)dn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m).g_{\kappa}^{\mathrm{ell}}(t)=-K(m)m\frac{\sn(K(m)t\mid m)\cn(K(m)t\mid m)}{\dn(K(m)t\mid m)}. (180)

Maximizing its magnitude, attained when sn2⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m)=1/(1+1−m)\sn^{2}(K(m)t\mid m)=1/(1+\sqrt{1-m}), gives

Lellb=(1−κ−1/2)K(m),Loptb=dκ=12logκ.L_{\mathrm{ell}}^{b}=(1-\kappa^{-1/2})K(m),\qquad L_{\mathrm{opt}}^{b}=d_{\kappa}=\tfrac{1}{2}\log\kappa. (181)

Since K⁡(m)∼12​log⁡(16​κ)K(m)\sim\tfrac{1}{2}\log(16\kappa) as κ→∞\kappa\to\infty,

LellbLoptb=2(1−κ−1/2)K(m)log⁡κ⟶1.\frac{L_{\mathrm{ell}}^{b}}{L_{\mathrm{opt}}^{b}}=\frac{2(1-\kappa^{-1/2})K(m)}{\log\kappa}\longrightarrow 1. (182)

The averaged squared criterion has the same conclusion, because

1≤A2wc​[αell,βell]dκ2≤(Lellbdκ)2⟶1.1\leq\frac{A_{2}^{\mathrm{wc}}[\alpha^{\mathrm{ell}},\beta^{\mathrm{ell}}]}{d_{\kappa}^{2}}\leq\left(\frac{L_{\mathrm{ell}}^{b}}{d_{\kappa}}\right)^{2}\longrightarrow 1. (183)

Thus elliptic asymptotically achieves both Gaussian Lipschitz benchmarks attained exactly by the Lipschitz-guided schedule. These are regularity guarantees for the continuous flow; sampling error also depends on the discretization.

At κ=1\kappa=1, every VP schedule has zero drift for the standard Gaussian target. The elliptic family tends to the trigonometric schedule, while the Lipschitz-guided family tends to the square-root schedule; neither is uniquely selected by the degenerate Lipschitz criterion.

∎

Corollary L.2 (A common canonical holomorphic domain).

Under the assumptions of Lemma L.1, the local extensions agree on overlaps and define a holomorphic trajectory on

𝒟B≜⋃u∘∈(−1,1){u∈ℂ:|u−u∘|<1−u∘230​D}.\mathcal{D}_{B}\triangleq\bigcup_{u_{\circ}\in(-1,1)}\left\{u\in\mathbb{C}:|u-u_{\circ}|<\frac{1-u_{\circ}^{2}}{30D}\right\}. (261)

Moreover, if 𝔼⁡[x1]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{1}]=0, then supu∈𝒟B,‖z‖≤B‖Xu⋆,z‖≤B+d+1\sup_{u\in\mathcal{D}_{B},\,\|z\|\leq B}\|X_{u}^{\star,z}\|\leq B+\sqrt{d}+1.

Proof.

Each disk has radius smaller than the distance of its real center to {−1,1}\{-1,1\}. Two overlapping disks with real centers have a connected intersection meeting (−1,1)(-1,1) in a nonempty real interval. Their local extensions agree with the same real trajectory there, so the identity theorem makes them agree throughout the intersection. They therefore glue to one holomorphic function. The magnitude bound follows from the bound on each disk. ∎

L.2.1  Real Canonical Trajectories and Posterior Estimates

Lemma L.3 (Existence, non-expansiveness, and real trajectory bounds).

The following holds for the canonical ODE (186),

  • i.

    Existence-uniqueness: For every initialization z∈ℝdz\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, a unique solution u↦Xu⋆,zu\mapsto X_{u}^{\star,z} exists for u∈(−1,1)u\in(-1,1).

  • ii.

    Non-expansiveness: For every u∈(−1,1)u\in(-1,1), the flow map z↦Xu⋆,zz\mapsto X_{u}^{\star,z} is nonexpansive, and Xu⋆,zX_{u}^{\star,z} has density pu⋆p_{u}^{\star} whenever z∼N⁡(0,Id)z\sim N(0,I_{d}).

  • iii.

    Boundedness: For centered targets, i.e., 𝔼⁡[x1]=0\mathbb{E}[x_{1}]=0, the trajectories are bounded as

    ‖Xu⋆,z‖≤‖z‖2+d≤‖z‖+d.\|X_{u}^{\star,z}\|\leq\sqrt{\|z\|^{2}+d}\leq\|z\|+\sqrt{d}. (262)
Proof.

The posterior identity in Lemma M.9 and its upper covariance bound give

∇xX^1⋆​(x,s)=s1−s2​Cov⁡(X1∣xs⋆=x),0⪯Cov⁡(X1∣xs⋆=x)⪯(1−s2)​Id.\nabla_{x}\widehat{X}_{1}^{\star}(x,s)=\frac{s}{1-s^{2}}\operatorname{Cov}(X_{1}\mid x_{s}^{\star}=x),\qquad 0\preceq\operatorname{Cov}(X_{1}\mid x_{s}^{\star}=x)\preceq(1-s^{2})I_{d}. (263)

Therefore

∇xbs⋆​(x)=s1−s2​(Cov⁡(X1∣xs⋆=x)1−s2−Id).\nabla_{x}b_{s}^{\star}(x)=\frac{s}{1-s^{2}}\left(\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X_{1}\mid x_{s}^{\star}=x)}{1-s^{2}}-I_{d}\right). (264)

The drift is globally Lipschitz in xx, uniformly on each compact subinterval of (−1,1)(-1,1), and continuous in ss there. At s=0s=0, it equals 𝔼​X1\mathbb{E}X_{1}. Standard real ODE existence and uniqueness, together with this linear-growth bound, yield a unique trajectory throughout (−1,1)(-1,1). Differentiating the stochastic interpolant shows that its conditional velocity is exactly bs⋆b_{s}^{\star}, so its densities satisfy the corresponding continuity equation. Uniqueness for a globally Lipschitz velocity field on each compact time interval then gives ℒ⁡(Xs⋆​(Z))=ps⋆\mathcal{L}(X_{s}^{\star}(Z))=p_{s}^{\star}.

For s≥0s\geq 0, (264) is negative semidefinite. Hence the squared distance between two trajectories cannot increase as ss increases from zero. For negative times, symmetry of the Gaussian reference and uniqueness give

X^1⋆​(x,−s)=X^1⋆​(−x,s),X−s⋆​(z)=−Xs⋆​(−z),0≤s<1,\widehat{X}_{1}^{\star}(x,-s)=\widehat{X}_{1}^{\star}(-x,s),\qquad X_{-s}^{\star}(z)=-X_{s}^{\star}(-z),\qquad 0\leq s<1, (265)

which proves nonexpansiveness there as well. If the target is centered, then 𝔼​Xs⋆​(Z)=0\mathbb{E}X_{s}^{\star}(Z)=0, and

‖Xs⋆​(z)‖=‖𝔼⁡[Xs⋆​(z)−Xs⋆​(Z)]‖≤𝔼​‖z−Z‖≤‖z‖2+d.\|X_{s}^{\star}(z)\|=\left\|\mathbb{E}[X_{s}^{\star}(z)-X_{s}^{\star}(Z)]\right\|\leq\mathbb{E}\|z-Z\|\leq\sqrt{\|z\|^{2}+d}. (266)

∎

L.2.2  Complex Tilting and Local Complex ODE Existence

Lemma L.5 (Complex-valued tilting).

Let X∼p⁡(x)∝exp⁡(−V⁡(x))X\sim{p}({x})\propto\exp(-{V}({x})) be such that ∇2V⪰Id\nabla^{2}{V}\succeq I_{d} and ∇V​(0)=0\nabla V(0)=0, i.e., the mode is at 00. Then, for complex valued χ∈ℂd\chi\in\mathbb{C}^{d} and η∈ℂ\eta\in\mathbb{C} satisfying

‖χ‖<12and|η|<116​d,\|\chi\|<\frac{1}{2}\quad\text{and}\quad|\eta|<\frac{1}{16\sqrt{d}}, (285)

we have that

𝔼⁡[eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]≠0and‖𝔼⁡[X​eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]𝔼⁡[eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]‖≤2​d.\mathbb{E}\left[e^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]\neq 0\quad\text{and}\quad\left\|\frac{\mathbb{E}\left[Xe^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]}{\mathbb{E}\left[e^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]}\right\|\leq 2\sqrt{d}. (286)
Proof.

Let us split the exponent into its real and imaginary parts x⊤​χ+η​‖x‖2=R⁡(x∣χ,η)+i​Θ​(x∣χ,η)x^{\top}\chi+\eta\|x\|^{2}=R(x\mid\chi,\eta)+i\Theta(x\mid\chi,\eta) where

R⁡(x∣χ,η)=x⊤​ℜ⁡(χ)+ℜ⁡(η)​‖x‖2andΘ⁡(x∣χ,η)=x⊤​Im⁡(χ)+Im⁡(η)​‖x‖2.R(x\mid\chi,\eta)=x^{\top}\Re(\chi)+\Re(\eta)\|x\|^{2}\quad\text{and}\quad\Theta(x\mid\chi,\eta)=x^{\top}\operatorname{Im}(\chi)+\operatorname{Im}(\eta)\|x\|^{2}. (287)

After exponentiation, the real part can be absorbed into the distribution p⁡(x)p(x) yielding a tilted distribution

p~​(x∣χ,η)≜1Z⁡(χ,η)​eR⁡(x∣χ,η)​p​(x),Z⁡(χ,η)≜𝔼p​[eR⁡(X∣χ,η)]>0.\widetilde{p}(x\mid\chi,\eta)\triangleq\frac{1}{Z(\chi,\eta)}e^{R(x\mid\chi,\eta)}p(x),\quad Z(\chi,\eta)\triangleq\mathbb{E}_{p}[e^{R(X\mid\chi,\eta)}]>0. (288)

Note that the curvature of this tilted distribution is bounded below by

−∇x2​log⁡p~​(x∣χ,η)⪰(1−2​ℜ⁡(η))​Id⪰(1−2​|η|)​Id⪰78​Id.-\nabla_{x}^{2}\log\widetilde{p}(x\mid\chi,\eta)\succeq(1-2\Re(\eta))I_{d}\succeq(1-2|\eta|)I_{d}\succeq\frac{7}{8}I_{d}. (289)

Thus, the tilted distribution remains strongly log-concave.

The expressions in 286 can be written as expectations under the tilted distribution X~∼p~(⋅∣χ,η)\widetilde{X}\sim\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta) as

𝔼p[eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]=Z(χ,η)𝔼p~(⋅∣χ,η)[ei​Θ​(X~∣χ,η)],\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[e^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]=Z(\chi,\eta)\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta)}\left[e^{i\Theta(\widetilde{X}\mid\chi,\eta)}\right], (290)
𝔼p​[X​eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]𝔼p​[eX⊤​χ+η​‖X‖2]=𝔼p~(⋅∣χ,η)[X~ei​Θ​(X~∣χ,η)]𝔼p~(⋅∣χ,η)[ei​Θ​(X~∣χ,η)].\displaystyle\frac{\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[Xe^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{p}\left[e^{X^{\top}\chi+\eta\|X\|^{2}}\right]}=\frac{\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta)}\left[\widetilde{X}e^{i\Theta(\widetilde{X}\mid\chi,\eta)}\right]}{\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta)}\left[e^{i\Theta(\widetilde{X}\mid\chi,\eta)}\right]}. (291)

Since Z⁡(χ,η)>0Z(\chi,\eta)>0, we only need to show that the magnitude of the purely complex-phase integral 𝔼p~(⋅∣χ,η)[ei​Θ​(X~∣χ,η)]\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta)}\left[e^{i\Theta(\widetilde{X}\mid\chi,\eta)}\right] is bounded below by a non-zero constant and control the magnitude of the numerator 𝔼p~(⋅∣χ,η)[X~ei​Θ​(X~∣χ,η)]\mathbb{E}_{\widetilde{p}(\cdot\mid\chi,\eta)}\left[\widetilde{X}e^{i\Theta(\widetilde{X}\mid\chi,\eta)}\right] from above.

Lemma L.6 (Local Bounds on Jacobi Elliptic Functions).

Let m,m~∈(0,1)m,\widetilde{m}\in(0,1) and define r≜min⁡(1,1−m~1−m)r\triangleq\min\left(1,\sqrt{\frac{1-\widetilde{m}}{1-m}}\right). For any real u∘∈ℝu_{\circ}\in\mathbb{R} and u∈ℂu\in\mathbb{C} such that |u−u∘|<r|u-u_{\circ}|<r, the following holds:

max⁡(|sn⁡(u∣m)|,|cn⁡(u∣m)|1−m~​sn2​(u∘∣m),r​|dn⁡(u∣m)|1−m~​sn2​(u∘∣m))≤11−r−1​|u−u∘|.\max\left(|\sn(u\mid m)|,\frac{|\cn(u\mid m)|}{\sqrt{1-\widetilde{m}\sn^{2}(u_{\circ}\mid m)}},\,\frac{r|\dn(u\mid m)|}{\sqrt{1-\widetilde{m}\sn^{2}(u_{\circ}\mid m)}}\right)\leq\frac{1}{1-r^{-1}|u-u_{\circ}|}. (302)

L.3  Why smoothing is needed

The preceding guarantees use a positive smoothing level to keep the canonical time away from its terminal values. The following example shows that this restriction reflects a real obstruction: curvature bounds alone do not ensure terminal analyticity, even with Gaussian initialization and a freely chosen VP clock.

Proposition L.7 (Almost-sure terminal nonanalyticity).

For every κ>1\kappa>1 and d≥1d\geq 1, there is a centered density πd∝e−Vd\pi_{d}\propto e^{-V_{d}} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, with Vd∈C2V_{d}\in C^{2} and

Id⪯∇2Vd​(x)⪯κ​Id(x∈ℝd),I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}V_{d}(x)\preceq\kappa I_{d}\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}^{d}), (318)

having the following property. Consider any fixed deterministic continuous VP schedule (α,β)(\alpha,\beta), continuously differentiable on (0,1)(0,1), with

(α0,β0)=(1,0),(α1,β1)=(0,1),αt,βt>0(0<t<1).(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})=(1,0),\qquad(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})=(0,1),\qquad\alpha_{t},\beta_{t}>0\quad(0<t<1). (319)

The schedule is chosen independently of the sampled initialization. For its probability-flow ODE, write Xt​(z)X_{t}(z) for the trajectory initialized at X0​(z)=zX_{0}(z)=z, understood by continuous extension at 00. Then

ℙZ∼N⁡(0,Id)​(t↦Xt​(Z)​ is not real analytic at ​t=1)=1.\mathbb{P}_{Z\sim N(0,I_{d})}\bigl(t\mapsto X_{t}(Z)\text{ is not real analytic at }t=1\bigr)=1. (320)

In fact, for each such schedule, at most 7d7^{d} initializations can have a trajectory analytic at t=1t=1. The target is independent of the schedule. Here analyticity at 11 means agreement, for real t<1t<1 sufficiently close to 11, with a real-analytic function on a neighborhood of 11.

Proof.

We first construct a one-dimensional target and analyze its quantiles. Let

λ=κ+12,P(x)=(1−x2)4,ψ(x)=P(x)𝟏{|x|≤1},\lambda=\frac{\kappa+1}{2},\qquad P(x)=(1-x^{2})^{4},\qquad\psi(x)=P(x)\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|\leq 1\}}, (321)

and define

p(x)=λ2​πe−λx2/2+ηψ′(x),η>0.p(x)=\sqrt{\frac{\lambda}{2\pi}}e^{-\lambda x^{2}/2}+\eta\psi^{\prime}(x),\qquad\eta>0. (322)

The function ψ\psi is C3C^{3}, and ψ′\psi^{\prime} is supported on [−1,1][-1,1] and has integral zero. On this compact interval, pp converges in C2C^{2} to the strictly positive Gaussian density as η↓0\eta\downarrow 0. Thus, for sufficiently small fixed η>0\eta>0, pp is a strictly positive probability density, V=−log⁡p∈C2V=-\log p\in C^{2}, and

1<m≜λ+12≤V′′​(x)≤κ(x∈ℝ).1<m\triangleq\frac{\lambda+1}{2}\leq V^{\prime\prime}(x)\leq\kappa\qquad(x\in\mathbb{R}). (323)

Outside [−1,1][-1,1], V′′=λV^{\prime\prime}=\lambda exactly. If W∼pW\sim p, its mean is

μ=𝔼W=−η∫−11(1−x2)4dx=−256315η.\mu=\mathbb{E}W=-\eta\int_{-1}^{1}(1-x^{2})^{4}\,dx=-\frac{256}{315}\eta. (324)

Our centered scalar target is the law of W−μW-\mu; translation preserves the curvature bounds.

Canonical quantile curves.

Write Φ\Phi for the standard normal CDF and FF for the CDF of WW:

F⁡(x)=Φ⁡(λ​x)+η​ψ​(x).F(x)=\Phi(\sqrt{\lambda}x)+\eta\psi(x). (325)

For q>0q>0, let FqF_{q} be the CDF of W+q​GW+\sqrt{q}\,G, where G∼N⁡(0,1)G\sim N(0,1) is independent of WW, and put

Hq​f​(x)≜𝔼​f​(x+q​G).H_{q}f(x)\triangleq\mathbb{E}f(x+\sqrt{q}\,G). (326)

Then

Fq​(x)=Φ⁡(xq+1/λ)+η​Hq​ψ​(x).F_{q}(x)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{q+1/\lambda}}\right)+\eta H_{q}\psi(x). (327)

For a terminal point y∈ℝy\in\mathbb{R}, define

Uy​(q)=Fq−1​(F⁡(y)),Cy​(q)=Uy​(q)−μ1+q.U_{y}(q)=F_{q}^{-1}(F(y)),\qquad C_{y}(q)=\frac{U_{y}(q)-\mu}{\sqrt{1+q}}. (328)

These curves extend continuously to q=0q=0, with Uy​(0)=yU_{y}(0)=y. For a VP schedule, set q⁡(t)=αt2/βt2q(t)=\alpha_{t}^{2}/\beta_{t}^{2} on (0,1)(0,1). Its centered interpolant has the law of (W+q⁡(t)​G−μ)/1+q⁡(t)(W+\sqrt{q(t)}G-\mu)/\sqrt{1+q(t)}. Consequently its scalar PF-ODE trajectory initialized at zz is

Xt​(z)=Cy​(q⁡(t)),y=F−1​(Φ⁡(z)).X_{t}(z)=C_{y}(q(t)),\qquad y=F^{-1}(\Phi(z)). (329)

Indeed, the scalar continuity equation implies that the marginal CDF is constant along a PF-ODE trajectory, and its initial quantile is Φ⁡(z)\Phi(z). Positivity of the densities makes the quantile representation unique. Notice that q⁡(t)>0q(t)>0 and q⁡(t)→0q(t)\to 0 as t↑1t\uparrow 1; no analyticity of qq is assumed.

An analytic reference and its nonzero remainder.

Fix y≠±1y\neq\pm 1 and let dy=dist⁡(y,{−1,1})>0d_{y}=\operatorname{dist}(y,\{-1,1\})>0. We construct a function AyA_{y}, real analytic near q=0q=0, such that

Cy​(q)=Ay​(q)+ry​(q),ry​(q)≠0,limq↓0q​log⁡|ry​(q)|=−dy22.C_{y}(q)=A_{y}(q)+r_{y}(q),\qquad r_{y}(q)\neq 0,\qquad\lim_{q\downarrow 0}q\log|r_{y}(q)|=-\frac{d_{y}^{2}}{2}. (330)

If |y|>1|y|>1, set ay​(q)=y​1+λ​qa_{y}(q)=y\sqrt{1+\lambda q}. Since F⁡(y)=Φ⁡(λ​y)F(y)=\Phi(\sqrt{\lambda}y), (327) gives

Fq​(ay​(q))−F⁡(y)=η​Hq​ψ​(ay​(q))>0.F_{q}(a_{y}(q))-F(y)=\eta H_{q}\psi(a_{y}(q))>0. (331)

If |y|<1|y|<1, introduce instead

B⁡(q,x)=Φ⁡(xq+1/λ)+η​Hq​P​(x).B(q,x)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\sqrt{q+1/\lambda}}\right)+\eta H_{q}P(x). (332)

This is real analytic near (0,y)(0,y): in particular,

Hq​P​(x)=∑j=04qj2j​j!​P(2​j)​(x)H_{q}P(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{4}\frac{q^{j}}{2^{j}j!}P^{(2j)}(x) (333)

is a polynomial. Since B⁡(0,y)=F⁡(y)B(0,y)=F(y) and ∂xB⁡(0,y)=p⁡(y)>0\partial_{x}B(0,y)=p(y)>0, the analytic implicit-function theorem gives an analytic ay​(q)a_{y}(q) satisfying ay​(0)=ya_{y}(0)=y and B⁡(q,ay​(q))=F⁡(y)B(q,a_{y}(q))=F(y). Because PP is nonnegative on the entire real line,

Fq(ay(q))−F(y)=−ηHq(P𝟏{|x|>1})(ay(q))<0.F_{q}(a_{y}(q))-F(y)=-\eta H_{q}\!\left(P\mathbf{1}_{\{|x|>1\}}\right)(a_{y}(q))<0. (334)

The inequalities in both cases are strict for every sufficiently small q>0q>0, since Gaussian kernels are strictly positive.

In either case the positive tail integral Jy​(q)J_{y}(q) on the corresponding right-hand side satisfies

limq↓0q​log⁡Jy​(q)=−dy22.\lim_{q\downarrow 0}q\log J_{y}(q)=-\frac{d_{y}^{2}}{2}. (335)

For completeness, these are integrals of the form

12​π​q​∫Ew⁡(x)​exp⁡(−(x−ay​(q))22​q)​𝑑x,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi q}}\int_{E}w(x)\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-a_{y}(q))^{2}}{2q}\right)\,dx, (336)

where E=(−1,1)E=(-1,1) and w=ψw=\psi in the exterior case, or E=(−∞,−1)∪(1,∞)E=(-\infty,-1)\cup(1,\infty) and w=Pw=P in the interior case. The weight is positive on EE, grows at most polynomially, and dist⁡(ay​(q),E)→dy\operatorname{dist}(a_{y}(q),E)\to d_{y}. For an upper bound, for any θ∈(0,1)\theta\in(0,1) split the Gaussian exponent into factors with coefficients 1−θ1-\theta and θ\theta. The first is bounded by exp(−(1−θ)dist(ay(q),E)2/(2q))\exp(-(1-\theta)\operatorname{dist}(a_{y}(q),E)^{2}/(2q)); the integral of the second against w/2​π​qw/\sqrt{2\pi q} is bounded uniformly for small qq, because ay​(q)a_{y}(q) stays bounded. For a lower bound, integrate over a fixed small closed interval in EE on which w>0w>0 and whose points have distance at most dy+ϵd_{y}+\epsilon from yy. Letting first q↓0q\downarrow 0, then θ,ϵ↓0\theta,\epsilon\downarrow 0, proves (335).

Set Ay​(q)=(ay​(q)−μ)/1+qA_{y}(q)=(a_{y}(q)-\mu)/\sqrt{1+q}. The mean value theorem applied to FqF_{q} between ay​(q)a_{y}(q) and Uy​(q)U_{y}(q) now proves (330). Indeed, both points tend to yy, and Gaussian convolution of pp converges locally uniformly to pp. The intervening density therefore tends to p⁡(y)>0p(y)>0, so division by that density does not change the logarithmic rate. The factor (1+q)−1/2(1+q)^{-1/2} also does not change it. Thus ryr_{y} is nonzero and ry​(q)=o⁡(qN)r_{y}(q)=o(q^{N}) for every N>0N>0.

Only one reference curve has zero endpoint derivative.

Differentiating the defining reference equation at q=0q=0 gives ay′(0)=−p′(y)/(2p(y))a_{y}^{\prime}(0)=-p^{\prime}(y)/(2p(y)), in both cases. Therefore

Ay′​(0)=−12​(p′​(y)p⁡(y)+y−μ)=12​(V′​(y)−y+μ).A_{y}^{\prime}(0)=-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{p^{\prime}(y)}{p(y)}+y-\mu\right)=\frac{1}{2}\bigl(V^{\prime}(y)-y+\mu\bigr). (337)

The last expression, defined also at y=±1y=\pm 1, has derivative (V′′​(y)−1)/2≥(m−1)/2>0(V^{\prime\prime}(y)-1)/2\geq(m-1)/2>0 and tends to opposite infinities at the two ends of the real line. Hence it vanishes at exactly one point, denoted ycy_{c}.

An arbitrary time change cannot regularize two different tail rates.

Fix a schedule. Suppose that Cy1​(q​(t))C_{y_{1}}(q(t)) and Cy2​(q​(t))C_{y_{2}}(q(t)) are both analytic at t=1t=1, with yi∉{−1,1,yc}y_{i}\notin\{-1,1,y_{c}\}. We show that dy1=dy2d_{y_{1}}=d_{y_{2}}. Abbreviate Ai=AyiA_{i}=A_{y_{i}} and ri=ryir_{i}=r_{y_{i}}. Since A1′​(0)≠0A_{1}^{\prime}(0)\neq 0, its local inverse is analytic. Thus

v⁡(t)=A1−1​(Cy1​(q⁡(t)))v(t)=A_{1}^{-1}\bigl(C_{y_{1}}(q(t))\bigr) (338)

is analytic near 11, satisfies v⁡(1)=0v(1)=0, and has the expansion

v⁡(t)=q⁡(t)+r1​(q​(t))A1′​(q⁡(t))+O⁡(r1​(q⁡(t))2).v(t)=q(t)+\frac{r_{1}(q(t))}{A_{1}^{\prime}(q(t))}+O(r_{1}(q(t))^{2}). (339)

In particular v⁡(t)/q⁡(t)→1v(t)/q(t)\to 1, so vv is not identically zero. Its finite order of vanishing implies

q⁡(t)≍(1−t)nq(t)\asymp(1-t)^{n} (340)

for some integer n≥1n\geq 1 as t↑1t\uparrow 1.

The function

D⁡(t)=Cy2​(q⁡(t))−A2​(v⁡(t))D(t)=C_{y_{2}}(q(t))-A_{2}(v(t)) (341)

is analytic near 11. With q=q⁡(t)q=q(t), Taylor expansion gives

D⁡(t)=r2​(q)−A2′​(q)A1′​(q)​r1​(q)+O⁡(r1​(q)2).D(t)=r_{2}(q)-\frac{A_{2}^{\prime}(q)}{A_{1}^{\prime}(q)}r_{1}(q)+O(r_{1}(q)^{2}). (342)

If dy1≠dy2d_{y_{1}}\neq d_{y_{2}}, (330) implies that one of |r1|,|r2||r_{1}|,|r_{2}| dominates the other exponentially. The ratio of derivatives tends to a nonzero constant, so D⁡(t)D(t) is nonzero for all t<1t<1 sufficiently close to 11. On the other hand, both remainders are smaller than every power of qq, and q⁡(t)≍(1−t)nq(t)\asymp(1-t)^{n}. Thus D⁡(t)D(t) is smaller than every power of 1−t1-t. An analytic function with that property vanishes identically near 11, a contradiction. Therefore dy1=dy2d_{y_{1}}=d_{y_{2}}.

For each r>0r>0, the set {y:dist⁡(y,{−1,1})=r}\{y:\operatorname{dist}(y,\{-1,1\})=r\} contains at most four points. Hence the terminal points with analytic trajectories lie in {−1,1,yc}\{-1,1,y_{c}\} together with at most four other points. There are at most seven such terminal points and, because z↦F−1​(Φ​(z))z\mapsto F^{-1}(\Phi(z)) is a bijection, at most seven initializations. Every finite set has zero standard Gaussian probability.

Extension to dimension dd.

Take πd\pi_{d} to be the product of dd copies of the centered scalar target. Its potential has diagonal Hessian with entries satisfying (323), and its PF-ODE acts coordinatewise. For each schedule, a vector trajectory is analytic only if all its scalar coordinates are analytic. Thus there are at most 7d7^{d} such initializations, proving the claim. ∎

Remark (Quantifiers and analytic schedules).

The target above is fixed independently of both the schedule and any failure probability δ>0\delta>0. For each schedule, let ℰα,β\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,\beta} be its finite set of possibly analytic initializations. Taking 𝒵δ=ℝd∖ℰα,β\mathcal{Z}_{\delta}=\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\mathcal{E}_{\alpha,\beta} gives Gaussian probability one, hence greater than 1−δ1-\delta for every δ>0\delta>0.

The exceptional set may depend on the schedule. If α2\alpha^{2} and β2\beta^{2} are analytic near t=1t=1, a common full-measure set works for all these schedules:

𝒵=ℝd∖{−λ,λ}d.\mathcal{Z}=\mathbb{R}^{d}\setminus\{-\sqrt{\lambda},\sqrt{\lambda}\}^{d}. (343)

Indeed, q⁡(t)q(t) is then analytic and has a finite-order zero at 11. For every y≠±1y\neq\pm 1, Ay​(q​(t))A_{y}(q(t)) is analytic, while ry​(q​(t))r_{y}(q(t)) is nonzero and smaller than every power of 1−t1-t, so Cy​(q​(t))C_{y}(q(t)) is not analytic. The two excluded scalar terminal points correspond to z=±λz=\pm\sqrt{\lambda}, since F⁡(±1)=Φ⁡(±λ)F(\pm 1)=\Phi(\pm\sqrt{\lambda}).

The condition of positive noise immediately before 11 is essential: a schedule that reaches (α,β)=(0,1)(\alpha,\beta)=(0,1) early and remains there has constant, hence analytic, terminal trajectories.

Appendix M Score-Oracle Complexity for Log-Concave Targets

M.1  Proof of Theorem 5.2: The Score-Oracle Complexity Bound

We prove Theorem 5.2 for κ>1\kappa>1 in the admissible accuracy regime 0<ε≤min⁡(1,ε¯)0<\varepsilon\leq\min(1,\bar{\varepsilon}), where

ε¯=(κ−1)​dκ.\bar{\varepsilon}=(\kappa-1)\sqrt{\frac{d}{\kappa}}. (344)

The algorithm is the finite-query collocation method in Algorithm 3, applied to the smoothed probability-flow ODE with a projected Gaussian initialization. The supporting smoothing, drift, integration, and initialization estimates are proved below. When κ=1\kappa=1, the standing assumptions force π=N⁡(0,Id)\pi=N(0,I_{d}), so returning the Gaussian initialization already gives an exact sample without any score queries.

Use the theorem parameters:

The restriction on ε≤ε¯\varepsilon\leq\overline{\varepsilon} ensures 0<σ~2≤1/20<\widetilde{\sigma}^{2}\leq 1/2, κ^≥2\widehat{\kappa}\geq 2, and a real positive radius B>0B>0.

Applying Theorem M.1 on the initialization set {z:‖z‖≤B}\{z:\|z\|\leq B\} gives a numerical endpoint X^1z\widehat{X}_{1}^{z} satisfying

sup‖z‖≤B‖X^1z−X~1z‖≤ζ.\sup_{\|z\|\leq B}\|\widehat{X}_{1}^{z}-\widetilde{X}_{1}^{z}\|\leq\zeta. (348)

All segment counts, polynomial degrees, and Picard iteration counts are fixed by the displayed bounds and are uniform over the target class and the initialization ball.

By Lemma M.4 and the inequality 1+u−1≤u/2\sqrt{1+u}-1\leq u/2 for u≥0u\geq 0,

For the original VP schedule, let sts_{t} denote the interpolant score with target π\pi. The score of the smoothed interpolant is s~t=sτ⁡(t)\widetilde{s}_{t}=s_{\tau(t)}, where

M.1.1  Finite-query Integration of Analytic Trajectories

We give a finite-query realization of the collocation bound used above. The construction follows the collocation and Picard-iteration framework of Lee et al. (2018, Theorem 2.3). The proof below supplies the derivative approximation, integrated interpolation estimate, and error propagation needed for the present hypotheses. It uses only drift evaluations at real states and real times.

Theorem M.1 (ODEs with Analytic and Bounded Trajectories).

d​Xtzd​t=bt​(Xtz),X0z=z∈𝒵,t∈[0,1],\frac{dX_{t}^{z}}{dt}=b_{t}(X_{t}^{z}),\quad X_{0}^{z}=z\in\mathcal{Z},\quad t\in[0,1], (357)

where the initialization belongs to a set 𝒵⊂ℝd\mathcal{Z}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}. Suppose the following assumptions hold:

using at most

N⁡(ρ,M,L,ζ)≤C​R​[1+L+log⁡(max⁡(1,M​Rζ))]2,N(\rho,M,L,\zeta)\leq CR\left[1+L+\log\left(\max\left(1,\frac{MR}{\zeta}\right)\right)\right]^{2}, (359)

≤2​ej+4​h​η+ej+M​h/ρ≤3​M+M/2+M/4<4​M.\displaystyle\leq 2e_{j}+4h\eta+e_{j}+Mh/\rho\leq 3M+M/2+M/4<4M. (368)

The JJ Picard iterations therefore satisfy

‖y(J)−uvj‖∞,Ij≤2−J​4​M≤δ,ej+1≤ch​ej+2​ch​h​η+δ.\|y^{(J)}-u_{v_{j}}\|_{\infty,I_{j}}\leq 2^{-J}4M\leq\delta,\qquad e_{j+1}\leq c_{h}e_{j}+2c_{h}h\eta+\delta. (369)

We verify the temporary assumption by induction, starting from e0=0e_{0}=0. If the preceding recurrences have been justified and ej≤ζe_{j}\leq\zeta, the calculation above establishes the recurrence for segment jj. Since −log⁡(1−h​L)≤2​h​L-\log(1-hL)\leq 2hL, we have chQ≤e2​Lc_{h}^{Q}\leq e^{2L}. Unrolling only these already justified recurrences then gives

ej+1≤chj+1​(2​ch​(j+1)​h​η+(j+1)​δ)≤e2​L​(4​η+Q​δ)=3​ζ4<ζ.e_{j+1}\leq c_{h}^{j+1}\bigl(2c_{h}(j+1)h\eta+(j+1)\delta\bigr)\leq e^{2L}(4\eta+Q\delta)=\frac{3\zeta}{4}<\zeta. (370)

This closes the induction and proves eQ≤ζe_{Q}\leq\zeta without assuming an a priori bound on numerical iterates.

Cost.

Each of the QQ segments uses JJ iterations of nn drift evaluations. The final endpoint uses the same queried values as the final stage update, so there is no additional endpoint query and the count is exactly Q​n​JQnJ. Since R≥1R\geq 1 and 0<ζ<M0<\zeta<M, the parameter choices imply

Q≤5​R,n,J≤C⁡(1+L+log⁡M​Rζ).Q\leq 5R,\qquad n,J\leq C\left(1+L+\log\frac{MR}{\zeta}\right). (371)

Their product proves (359). All query states are real and all query times j​h+h​cijh+hc_{i} belong to (0,1)(0,1). ∎

Remark (Arithmetic cost).

The direct dense stage updates require O⁡(d​Q​J​n2)O(dQJn^{2}) arithmetic operations in addition to the drift evaluations and the precomputation of quadrature data. The theorem is an exact real-oracle query bound. A finite-precision implementation would require additional control of quadrature-coefficient, arithmetic, and oracle errors.

Lemma M.2 (Integrated Gauss–Legendre interpolation).

Let ci,wi,ℓic_{i},w_{i},\ell_{i} be the nn Gauss–Legendre nodes, weights, and Lagrange basis on [0,1][0,1]. For arbitrary a1,…,an∈ℝda_{1},\ldots,a_{n}\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

sup0≤θ≤1‖∫0θ∑i=1nℓi​(u)​ai​𝑑u‖≤max1≤i≤n⁡‖ai‖.\sup_{0\leq\theta\leq 1}\left\|\int_{0}^{\theta}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\ell_{i}(u)a_{i}\,du\right\|\leq\max_{1\leq i\leq n}\|a_{i}\|. (372)

On an interval of length hh, the corresponding bound is multiplied by hh.

Proof.

Set P⁡(u)=∑iℓi​(u)​aiP(u)=\sum_{i}\ell_{i}(u)a_{i}. The scalar function ‖P⁡(u)‖2\|P(u)\|^{2} is a polynomial of degree at most 2​n−22n-2, so Gaussian quadrature exactness and positivity of the weights imply

∫01‖P⁡(u)‖2​𝑑u=∑i=1nwi​‖ai‖2≤maxi⁡‖ai‖2.\int_{0}^{1}\|P(u)\|^{2}\,du=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}\|a_{i}\|^{2}\leq\max_{i}\|a_{i}\|^{2}. (373)

For every θ∈[0,1]\theta\in[0,1], the integral triangle inequality followed by Cauchy–Schwarz gives

‖∫0θP⁡(u)​𝑑u‖≤θ​(∫0θ‖P⁡(u)‖2​𝑑u)1/2≤maxi⁡‖ai‖.\left\|\int_{0}^{\theta}P(u)\,du\right\|\leq\sqrt{\theta}\left(\int_{0}^{\theta}\|P(u)\|^{2}\,du\right)^{1/2}\leq\max_{i}\|a_{i}\|. (374)

This proves (372); an affine change of variables gives the factor hh on a segment of length hh. ∎

Given (x0,τ0)∈ℂd×ℂ(x_{0},\tau_{0})\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\times\mathbb{C}, let Ω≜{(x,τ)∈ℂd×ℂ∣∥x−x0∥<δ,|τ−τ0|<ε}\Omega\triangleq\{(x,\tau)\in\mathbb{C}^{d}\times\mathbb{C}\mid\|x-x_{0}\|<\delta,\,|\tau-\tau_{0}|<\varepsilon\} be an open rectangle and suppose F:Ω→ℂF:\Omega\to\mathbb{C} is analytic and bounded with

For p⁡(x)∝exp⁡(−V⁡(x))p(x)\propto\exp(-V(x)) with V∈𝒞2V\in\mathcal{C}^{2} and ∇2V​(x)≻0\nabla^{2}V(x)\succ 0 and any f∈𝒞1f\in\mathcal{C}^{1}, we have that

Let UU have density proportional to e−We^{-W}, with W∈C2​(ℝd)W\in C^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) and λmin​Id⪯∇2W⪯λmax​Id\lambda_{\min}I_{d}\preceq\nabla^{2}W\preceq\lambda_{\max}I_{d} for 0<λmin≤λmax<∞0<\lambda_{\min}\leq\lambda_{\max}<\infty. D​μ​(x)\displaystyle D\mu(x) =aσ2​C​(x),\displaystyle=\frac{a}{\sigma^{2}}C(x), (403)

Lemma M.10 (Stein’s Identity).

Let X∼p⁡(x)X\sim p(x) be a random variable with 𝒞1​(𝒳)\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathcal{X}) probability density over a domain 𝒳⊆ℝd\mathcal{X}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a smooth function f∈𝒞1​(𝒳)f\in\mathcal{C}^{1}(\mathcal{X}), it holds that

𝔼p[∇f(X)]=−𝔼p[f(X)∇logp(X)]whenever∫𝒳∇⋅(f(x)p(x))dx=0.\mathbb{E}_{p}[\nabla f(X)]=-\mathbb{E}_{p}[f(X)\,\nabla\log p(X)]\quad\text{whenever}\quad\int_{\mathcal{X}}\nabla\cdot(f(x)p(x))dx=0. (415)

Appendix N Experiments

N.1  Gaussian experiments

Summary.

On a Gaussian target, every solver we test acts on each precision mode λ\lambda as a rational function M⁡(λ)M(\lambda) (Appendix G), so we compute its worst-case relative error over the spectrum, E=maxλ⁡|λ​M​(λ)−1|E=\max_{\lambda}\bigl|\sqrt{\lambda}\,M(\lambda)-1\bigr|, exactly. EE controls the KL divergence, DKL≲d​E2D_{\mathrm{KL}}\lesssim d\,E^{2} (Appendix H). Two findings:

  • •

    Zoloflow wins by orders of magnitude. The elliptic schedule with the elliptic finite-difference (FD) rule (Definition 4.3) reaches round-off with 1212 score evaluations at κ=100\kappa=100, where every pair with a standard solver is still above 10−210^{-2}, and the FD rule with the rescaled trigonometric schedule needs 2424 (Section N.1.1).

  • •

    Both parameters must match the spectrum. On an unnormalized spectrum (Appendix I), widening the schedule without rescaling, or rescaling without widening, stays orders of magnitude above the optimum (Section N.1.2).

N.1.1  Solvers and schedules on a normalized spectrum

Figures 13 and 14 plot EE on the normalized spectrum [1,κ][1,\kappa] for five standard solvers and the elliptic FD rule (panels), each with six schedule settings (colors), including Trig and Linear before and after center rescaling. Compare the black dashed line, the elliptic FD rule with the Elliptic schedule, with every colored line. The dashed line is the endpoint-normalized Zolotarev error E^κ,r\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r} (63) and falls geometrically in rr. At κ=100\kappa=100 (Figure 13) it reaches round-off at r=12r=12, where the best line with a standard solver is at 1.3×10−21.3\times 10^{-2}; the FD rule with rescaled trig (orange, last panel), which matches the center of the spectrum but not its width, is at 1.6×10−71.6\times 10^{-7} there and reaches round-off only at r=24r=24. At the same budget, FD with rescaled Linear (VP form) has error 1.6×10−41.6\times 10^{-4}. With Euler and Heun, rescaled trig is below the Elliptic schedule (by about 3×3\times and 1.7×1.7\times at r=12r=12): for these low-order solvers the best width is near 11, as in the log-concave sweeps. At r=16r=16 (Figure 14) Zoloflow stays below 2.4×10−82.4\times 10^{-8} up to κ=106\kappa=10^{6}, where the best standard-solver error is 0.150.15 and FD with rescaled Linear has error 0.0760.076. Neither half works alone: with a standard solver, the Elliptic schedule (blue, first five panels) stays above 10−410^{-4} for every r≤40r\leq 40, and the FD rule with Trig (pink, last panel) is still at 10−210^{-2} at r=12r=12.

N.1.2  Both center and width must match the spectrum

Figure 15 takes a Gaussian whose spectrum [λmin,λmax]=[0.01,1][\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]=[0.01,1] is not normalized. It runs Generalized Zoloflow (Definition I.6), the exponential-gauge rescaling of Section I.2.2, with r=12r=12 at every center and width (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) on a grid, that is, with the endpoints (ℓ,L)=(λ¯/κ,λ¯​κ)(\ell,L)=(\bar{\lambda}/\sqrt{\kappa},\bar{\lambda}\sqrt{\kappa}) in place of (λmin,λmax)(\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}). By (144), M(λ)=ℓ−1/2q^κ,r(λ/ℓ)M(\lambda)=\ell^{-1/2}\,\widehat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda/\ell) per mode, so the spectrum’s own center and width, (λ¯,κ)=(λmin​λmax,λmax/λmin)=(0.1,100)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}\lambda_{\max}},\lambda_{\max}/\lambda_{\min})=(0.1,100), give E=E^100,12E=\widehat{E}_{100,12}.

Each curve fixes κ\kappa, and its star marks the curve’s minimum over λ¯\bar{\lambda}, placed in the middle of its flat segment where there is one. Every curve is centered on the spectral center λ¯=0.1\bar{\lambda}=0.1, and only the κ=100\kappa=100 curve reaches E^100,12\widehat{E}_{100,12} there (blue circle). Without widening (κ=1\kappa=1, rescaled trig), the best center is λ¯=0.1\bar{\lambda}=0.1 (orange square, E=1.6×10−7E=1.6\times 10^{-7}), about seven orders of magnitude above the matched setting (2.4×10−142.4\times 10^{-14}). Without centering (λ¯=1\bar{\lambda}=1), even the widest schedule on the grid, κ=104\kappa=10^{4}, only reaches E=9.1×10−9E=9.1\times 10^{-9} (pink triangle); Trig itself, (λ¯,κ)=(1,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(1,1), has E=1.3×10−2E=1.3\times 10^{-2}. The flat segments are exact: once [ℓ,L][\ell,L] contains the spectrum, E=E^κ,rE=\widehat{E}_{\kappa,r} for every such center, so a schedule wider than the spectrum pays for its own, larger κ\kappa.

N.1.3  Setup

Solvers and schedules.

Euler, Heun, RK4, DDIM and DPM-Solver++(2M) (Appendix E), and the elliptic FD rule of Definition 4.3 on its shared grid (46). Both figures include Elliptic (159) with (λ¯,κ)=(κ,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(\sqrt{\kappa},\kappa) (endpoints [1,κ][1,\kappa]), Trig with (λ¯,κ)=(1,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(1,1), rescaled Trig with (λ¯,κ)=(κ,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(\sqrt{\kappa},1), Linear and rescaled Linear with λ¯=1\bar{\lambda}=1 and λ¯=κ\bar{\lambda}=\sqrt{\kappa}, and Lipschitz-guided (160) (Chen et al., 2025). Linear uses the normalized VP coefficients (αt,βt)=(1−t,t)/(1−t)2+t2(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(1-t,t)/\sqrt{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}}, which preserve the linear interpolant’s signal-to-noise ratio. Each rescaled Trig or Linear run integrates on the target rescaled by ℓ=κ\ell=\sqrt{\kappa} and divides the output by ℓ\sqrt{\ell} (Section I.1). For FD, this specifies the implementation: the discrete update is not generally invariant under a time-dependent spatial rescaling.

Initialization and budget.

Every solver but FD starts from x⁡(0)=zx(0)=z at t=0t=0 and steps on a uniform grid to t=1t=1. The budget rr counts score evaluations; evaluations that do not depend on the target are not counted: the denoiser at t=0t=0, and the drift at t=0t=0 and t=1t=1 for Elliptic, Trig and Linear (VP form), where dd​t​βt2=0\tfrac{d}{dt}\beta_{t}^{2}=0. A budget that gives no whole number of steps is not valid for that pair.

Computing EE.

Each solver is run per mode on a fine log-spaced λ\lambda grid with local refinement; values below 10−1410^{-14} are round-off.

N.2  Log-concave experiments

Summary.

The Gaussian theory sets the elliptic schedule parameters from the endpoints of the precision spectrum. For the log-concave targets in this subsection, we evaluate the covariance rule, taking (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) as the center and width of the spectrum of Σ−1\Sigma^{-1} (Elliptic (ours), Appendix J), rather than of the curvature bounds λmin​I⪯∇2V⪯λmax​I\lambda_{\min}I\preceq\nabla^{2}V\preceq\lambda_{\max}I (Elliptic, curvature endpoints). These experiments test whether scale differences across directions, measured by Σ\Sigma, predict useful widening better than curvature variation within a direction. We use log-concave product targets with exact scores, with KL computed by quadrature, so every difference is discretization error. On two-dimensional targets that separate the two effects (Figure 16), the covariance rule is the only rule that is never far from the best. In d=32d=32 (Figure 17) it lies within a factor 1.51.5–3.53.5 of the best (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) on a full grid for DPM-Solver++(2M), where rescaled trig is 1010–2121 times worse. Schedules, targets and the metric are defined at the end (Sections N.2.3, N.2.4 and N.2.5).

N.2.1  Two-dimensional targets: which rule to use

Figure 16 plots KL against the budget rr on four two-dimensional targets (rows, Table 4) for four solvers (columns). Compare the purple line (Elliptic, ours) with orange (rescaled trig) and blue (curvature endpoints). The rows cover three regimes:

  • •

    A, B: scales differ across directions. Purple lies below orange, by a median factor of 22 to 44, for every solver except Euler. Blue is close to purple for DDIM and DPM-Solver++(2M) and worse for Heun and Euler.

  • •

    E1: Σ=I\Sigma=I, curvature varies only within a direction. Purple coincides with orange and pink, while blue widens the schedule to κ=100\kappa=100 and lies far above (a median factor of 7171).

  • •

    G: Gaussian. Purple coincides with blue, the Gaussian optimum, and lies far below orange (a median factor of 1919).

Purple is never far from the best line in any regime. The exception is Euler, for which a near-trig schedule is better.

N.2.2  Validation in d=32d=32: distance to the best (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)

Figure 17 evaluates DPM-Solver++(2M) with r=8r=8 at every (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) on a grid, on the 32-dimensional targets H1 and H2. Each curve is a slice of the KL/d/d landscape and its star marks the slice’s minimum, so the lowest stars locate the best settings. The question is where the purple cross (Elliptic, ours) sits relative to them. It lies within a factor of 1.51.5 (H1) and 3.53.5 (H2) of the best grid setting, while rescaled trig (orange), Trig (pink) and Lipschitz-guided (dashed line) are 77 to 131131 times above it. The curvature endpoints (blue) are near-optimal on H1 but 77 times above on H2, whose coordinates are flat. For Euler and Heun (not shown) the best setting has κ≤6\kappa\leq 6 and rescaled trig is the better choice.

N.2.3  Schedules under comparison

All schedules are variance preserving, αt2+βt2=1\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}=1, with (α0,β0)=(1,0)(\alpha_{0},\beta_{0})=(1,0) and (α1,β1)=(0,1)(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})=(0,1). The elliptic schedule with condition number κ≥1\kappa\geq 1 is

αt=cn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m),βt=sn⁡(K⁡(m)​t∣m),m=1−κ−1,\alpha_{t}=\operatorname{cn}\!\big(K(m)\,t\mid m\big),\qquad\beta_{t}=\operatorname{sn}\!\big(K(m)\,t\mid m\big),\qquad m=1-\kappa^{-1}, (424)

which reduces to (cos⁡π​t2,sin⁡π​t2)(\cos\tfrac{\pi t}{2},\sin\tfrac{\pi t}{2}) at κ=1\kappa=1.

A schedule setting is a center and width (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa), equivalently the endpoints (ℓ,L)=(λ¯/κ,λ¯​κ)(\ell,L)=(\bar{\lambda}/\sqrt{\kappa},\bar{\lambda}\sqrt{\kappa}). It is realized by target rescaling (Section I.1): the elliptic schedule (424) with width κ\kappa is run on the rescaled target ℓ​x1\sqrt{\ell}\,x_{1}, and the output is divided by ℓ\sqrt{\ell}. We compare four settings of this family:

schedule setting (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)
Trigonometric (1,1)(1,1)
Rescaled trig (c,1)(c,1), c=d/𝔼​‖x1‖2c=d/\mathbb{E}\|x_{1}\|^{2}
Elliptic (ours) center and width of spec⁡(Σ−1)\operatorname{spec}(\Sigma^{-1}), Appendix J
Elliptic, curvature endpoints center and width of [λmin,λmax][\lambda_{\min},\lambda_{\max}]

Rescaled trig coincides with the closed-form schedule of Align Your Steps for isotropic Gaussian data with the target’s average variance (Sabour et al., 2024, Theorem 3.1). The sweep also shows the Lipschitz-guided schedule (160) of Chen et al. (2025) at the same (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) as Elliptic (ours).

The target is a product of dd independent, symmetric, two-component mixtures,

p1​(y)=∏i=1dpi​(yi),pi=12​𝒩​(μi,σi2)+12​𝒩​(−μi,σi2),0≤μi<σi.p_{1}(y)=\prod_{i=1}^{d}p_{i}(y_{i}),\qquad p_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(-\mu_{i},\sigma_{i}^{2}),\qquad 0\leq\mu_{i}<\sigma_{i}. (425)

Writing pi=e−Vip_{i}=e^{-V_{i}}, a direct computation gives

(426)

The target has mean zero, covariance Cov⁡(x1)=diag⁡(σi2+μi2)\operatorname{Cov}(x_{1})=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\mu_{i}^{2}), and second moment 𝔼​‖x1‖2=∑i(σi2+μi2)\mathbb{E}\|x_{1}\|^{2}=\sum_{i}(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\mu_{i}^{2}).

Curvature.

The Hessian ∇2V​(y)=diag⁡(V1′′​(y1),…,Vd′′​(yd))\nabla^{2}V(y)=\operatorname{diag}\big(V_{1}^{\prime\prime}(y_{1}),\dots,V_{d}^{\prime\prime}(y_{d})\big) is diagonal at every point: its eigenbasis is fixed and its eigenvalues vary with position. With ρi=μi/σi\rho_{i}=\mu_{i}/\sigma_{i},

Vi′′​(y)\displaystyle V_{i}^{\prime\prime}(y) ∈[λmin,i,λmax,i),\displaystyle\in\Big[\lambda_{\min,i},\,\lambda_{\max,i}\Big), (427)
λmin,i\displaystyle\lambda_{\min,i} OPEN=1−ρi2σi2​(attained at ​y=0),\displaystyle=\frac{1-\rho_{i}^{2}}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\ \text{(attained at }y=0),
λmax,i\displaystyle\lambda_{\max,i} OPEN=1σi2​(approached as ​|y|→∞),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma_{i}^{2}}\ \text{(approached as }|y|\to\infty),

so p1p_{1} is λmin\lambda_{\min}-strongly log-concave and λmax\lambda_{\max}-smooth with λmin=mini⁡λmin,i\lambda_{\min}=\min_{i}\lambda_{\min,i}, λmax=maxi⁡λmax,i\lambda_{\max}=\max_{i}\lambda_{\max,i}. Strong log-concavity requires ρi<1\rho_{i}<1 strictly; at ρi=1\rho_{i}=1 the mixture is exactly at the threshold where it would become bimodal and λmin,i=0\lambda_{\min,i}=0. To prescribe a per-coordinate curvature range [λmin,i,λmax,i][\lambda_{\min,i},\lambda_{\max,i}] we invert (427):

σi2=1λmax,i,μi2=λmax,i−λmin,iλmax,i2,so that ​κi≜λmax,iλmin,i=11−ρi2.\sigma_{i}^{2}=\frac{1}{\lambda_{\max,i}},\qquad\mu_{i}^{2}=\frac{\lambda_{\max,i}-\lambda_{\min,i}}{\lambda_{\max,i}^{2}},\qquad\text{so that }\ \kappa_{i}\triangleq\frac{\lambda_{\max,i}}{\lambda_{\min,i}}=\frac{1}{1-\rho_{i}^{2}}. (428)

The choice λmin,i=λmax,i\lambda_{\min,i}=\lambda_{\max,i} (i.e. μi=0\mu_{i}=0) makes coordinate ii Gaussian with precision λmax,i\lambda_{\max,i}. Equivalently, a coordinate with variance viv_{i} and ρi2∈[0,1)\rho_{i}^{2}\in[0,1) has σi2=vi/(1+ρi2)\sigma_{i}^{2}=v_{i}/(1+\rho_{i}^{2}), μi2=vi​ρi2/(1+ρi2)\mu_{i}^{2}=v_{i}\rho_{i}^{2}/(1+\rho_{i}^{2}) and curvature range [(1−ρi4)/vi,(1+ρi2)/vi][(1-\rho_{i}^{4})/v_{i},\,(1+\rho_{i}^{2})/v_{i}].
