Targets.

Table 4 lists the targets. A and B have scales that differ across directions; E1 has Σ=I\Sigma=I, so its curvature varies only within a direction; G is Gaussian. In d=32d=32, H1 spreads its variances over two decades with mild flattening, and H2 is dominated by flattening.

Closed-form interpolated law.

Because the interpolant noise is isotropic, xt=αt​z+βt​x1x_{t}=\alpha_{t}z+\beta_{t}x_{1} remains a product, and each factor is again a two-component mixture:

xt,i∼12​𝒩​(βt​μi,vt,i)+12​𝒩​(−βt​μi,vt,i),vt,i=αt2+βt2​σi2.x_{t,i}\sim\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(\beta_{t}\mu_{i},\,v_{t,i})+\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathcal{N}(-\beta_{t}\mu_{i},\,v_{t,i}),\qquad v_{t,i}=\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}\sigma_{i}^{2}. (429)

Hence the score is available exactly for every tt,

st,i​(x)=∂xlog⁡pt,i​(x)=−xvt,i+βt​μivt,i​tanh⁡(βt​μi​xvt,i),s_{t,i}(x)=\partial_{x}\log p_{t,i}(x)=-\frac{x}{v_{t,i}}+\frac{\beta_{t}\mu_{i}}{v_{t,i}}\tanh\!\Big(\frac{\beta_{t}\mu_{i}\,x}{v_{t,i}}\Big), (430)

and Var⁡(xt,i)=αt2+βt2​(σi2+μi2)\operatorname{Var}(x_{t,i})=\alpha_{t}^{2}+\beta_{t}^{2}(\sigma_{i}^{2}+\mu_{i}^{2}). Every solver is therefore run with the exact score, so the measured error is discretization error alone and is not confounded with score estimation.

N.2.5  Metrics

Let F:ℝd→ℝdF:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the map z↦xrz\mapsto x_{r} implemented by a solver with rr score queries, and let γ=𝒩⁡(0,Id)\gamma=\mathcal{N}(0,I_{d}). The sampler’s output law is the pushforward F#​γF_{\#}\gamma.

KL divergence by change of variables.

If FF is a C1C^{1} bijection, then (F#​γ)​(F⁡(z))=γ⁡(z)/|det∇F​(z)|(F_{\#}\gamma)(F(z))=\gamma(z)/|\det\nabla F(z)|, and substituting x=F⁡(z)x=F(z) in the definition of KL gives

KL(F#γ∥p1)=𝔼z∼γ[logγ(z)−log|det∇F(z)|−logp1(F(z))].\mathrm{KL}\big(F_{\#}\gamma\,\big\|\,p_{1}\big)=\mathbb{E}_{z\sim\gamma}\Big[\log\gamma(z)-\log|\det\nabla F(z)|-\log p_{1}\big(F(z)\big)\Big]. (431)

Every term is available exactly at every zz: log⁡p1\log p_{1} is the closed-form mixture density, and ∇F\nabla F follows from the chain rule through the solver. For a one-query step x↦aj​x+bj​wtj​(x)x\mapsto a_{j}x+b_{j}\,w_{t_{j}}(x) the derivative is aj+bj​∂xwtj​(x)a_{j}+b_{j}\,\partial_{x}w_{t_{j}}(x), with ∂xw=1+∂xs\partial_{x}w=1+\partial_{x}s closed form from (430); multistage and multistep solvers propagate the running Jacobian through their stages. In the product setting FF is coordinatewise, F⁡(z)=(F1​(z1),…,Fd​(zd))F(z)=(F_{1}(z_{1}),\dots,F_{d}(z_{d})), so (431) splits into one-dimensional integrals against the standard normal,

KL=∑i=1dKLi,KLi=𝔼ζ∼𝒩⁡(0,1)​[log⁡φ⁡(ζ)−log⁡Fi′​(ζ)−log⁡pi​(Fi​(ζ))],\mathrm{KL}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mathrm{KL}_{i},\qquad\mathrm{KL}_{i}=\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)}\Big[\log\varphi(\zeta)-\log F_{i}^{\prime}(\zeta)-\log p_{i}\big(F_{i}(\zeta)\big)\Big], (432)

with 𝔼​log⁡φ=−12​(1+log⁡2​π)\mathbb{E}\log\varphi=-\tfrac{1}{2}(1+\log 2\pi) known exactly. The remaining expectation is computed by 256256-point Gauss–Hermite quadrature per coordinate, so no quantity involves Monte Carlo sampling; re-evaluating with 512512 nodes changes the reported values by less than max⁡(1%,10−14)\max(1\%,10^{-14}) in all but 22 of about 1,5001{,}500 cases.

Validity.

Formula (431) requires FiF_{i} to be strictly increasing. We check Fi′​(ζ)>0F_{i}^{\prime}(\zeta)>0 at every quadrature node and coordinate; if the check fails the map has folded and KL is undefined (marked `×′`\times^{\prime} in the figures). On the two-dimensional targets folding occurs only for Euler and Heun at r=4r=4 with κ≥100\kappa\geq 100; DDIM and DPM-Solver++(2M) never fold.

Sanity check against the Gaussian theory.

On a Gaussian coordinate with precision λ\lambda every solver’s map is linear, Fi​(ζ)=q​ζF_{i}(\zeta)=q\,\zeta, and (432) evaluates to 12​(λ​q2−1−log⁡λ​q2)\tfrac{1}{2}\big(\lambda q^{2}-1-\log\lambda q^{2}\big), which is the per-mode identity (102) with 1+e=λ​q1+e=\sqrt{\lambda}\,q. For the elliptic finite-difference rule on Gaussian targets the pipeline reproduces the normalized Zolotarev multiplier q^κ,r​(λ)\hat{q}_{\kappa,r}(\lambda) to relative accuracy 10−1410^{-14}.

N.3  2D Toy Experiments

Setup.

Each target is a two-dimensional Gaussian mixture that traces a line drawing: the word “ZOLO”, a double helix, an ECG trace, a fern frond, and a radial fractal tree. Each plot is made via a mixture of Gaussian spikes. The interpolated law ptp_{t} of a Gaussian mixture has a closed-form score, so every run uses the exact score and all error comes from the discretization. We sample with DPM-Solver++(2M) (Appendix E) using r=8r=8 score evaluations on the grid (46), and draw N=105N=10^{5} samples from the same initial noise zz for every schedule on a given target. The frond ablation below varies center and width separately. The additional-target comparisons (Figures 20, 21, 22 and 23) use four schedules with covariance-based settings, realized by target rescaling (Section I.1):

  • •

    Trigonometric: (λ¯,κ)=(1,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(1,1), the Trigonometric schedule;

  • •

    Rescaled trig: (λ¯,κ)=(λ¯,1)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=(\bar{\lambda},1) with the same center λ¯\bar{\lambda} as Elliptic (ours) below, so the two differ only in the width κ\kappa;

  • •

    Lipschitz-guided: the schedule of Chen et al. (2025, Proposition 3.9), which minimizes the averaged squared Lipschitz constant of the drift for Gaussian targets; in our notation it is (160) (Section K.4), used with the same heuristic (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) as Elliptic;

  • •

    Elliptic (ours): (λ¯,κ)=(1/λmin​(Σ)​λmax​(Σ),λmax​(Σ)/λmin​(Σ))(\bar{\lambda},\kappa)=\bigl(1/\sqrt{\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)},\,\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma)/\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma)\bigr), the covariance heuristic of Appendix J.

Here Σ\Sigma is the exact covariance of the target mixture, so Lipschitz-guided and Elliptic use the same spectral information and differ only in the shape of the schedule. The tree has eight-fold rotational symmetry, so its covariance is a multiple of I2I_{2}: at these covariance settings, Elliptic coincides with rescaled trig and Lipschitz-guided reduces to the square-root schedule. It serves as a control for the covariance rule. In these additional-target figures, the panel titles give the schedule, its center and width (λ¯,κ)(\bar{\lambda},\kappa) and NLL. An alternative center for rescaled trig, c=d/𝔼​‖x1‖2=2/tr⁡Σc=d/\mathbb{E}\|x_{1}\|^{2}=2/\operatorname{tr}\Sigma, is the closed-form schedule of Align Your Steps for isotropic Gaussian data (Sabour et al., 2024, Theorem 3.1); across the four anisotropic targets, including the frond, this alternative gives 1.41.4 to 2.82.8 times the NLL of covariance-centered trig, so we report the covariance center. The practical Align Your Steps schedules optimized from data are not compared here.

Frond centering and width ablation.

For the frond, the covariance heuristic gives center λ¯≈2.56368\bar{\lambda}\approx 2.56368 and width κΣ≈36.1091\kappa_{\Sigma}\approx 36.1091. Figure 18 compares trig and linear at the default center λ¯=1\bar{\lambda}=1 and at the covariance center. The linear schedule is (αt,βt)=(1−t,t)(\alpha_{t},\beta_{t})=(1-t,t); its implementation uses the equivalent variance-preserving form obtained by dividing both coefficients by (1−t)2+t2\sqrt{(1-t)^{2}+t^{2}}. The trig and linear centers are fixed by this rule, not independently optimized. We then hold the covariance center fixed and evaluate elliptic widths {1,10,30,κΣ,100,300,1000,3000,104}\{1,10,30,\kappa_{\Sigma},100,300,1000,3000,10^{4}\}, reusing the centered-trig run at κ=1\kappa=1. The lowest NLL among the tested widths occurs at κ=104\kappa=10^{4}, the upper end of the sweep (Figure 19). The covariance-width elliptic run has NLL 26.3926.39, compared with 21.4321.43 for centered linear and 7.067.06 for elliptic at the best tested width. This comparison assesses the benefit of varying width at a shared center.

Matched-width Lipschitz-guided comparison.

We also evaluate Lipschitz-guided at the same covariance center and κ=104\kappa=10^{4} (Figure 18). This width is matched to the selected elliptic setting, not independently optimized for Lipschitz-guided. Its NLL is 20.0620.06, slightly below centered linear’s 21.4321.43, while its histogram TV is 0.4430.443, compared with 0.3990.399 for centered linear and 0.2650.265 for the selected elliptic run. Thus its NLL advantage over centered linear does not extend to histogram TV.

Metric.

NLL is the average negative log-density of the samples under the exact target mixture, NLL=−1N∑i=1Nlogp1(xi)\mathrm{NLL}=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_{1}(x_{i}), the metric used by Sabour et al. (2024). It is a cross-entropy, so it rewards over-concentrated samples and can fall below the target’s own value; the ground-truth panels in this subsection report the NLL of 10510^{5} exact samples for reference. The histogram TV reported above is half the ℓ1\ell_{1} distance between sampler and target histograms on a shared 100×100100\times 100 grid with an additional outside bin, with the target histogram estimated from 10610^{6} exact draws.

N.4  Image Experiments

N.4.1  Sampling procedure

Oracle calls.

One oracle call is one evaluation of the transferred velocity field bt​(x)b_{t}(x). With classifier-free guidance, this is a single forward pass of the network (SiT-XL/2 or SD 3.5M) on a batch that stacks the conditional and unconditional inputs, and we count it as one call.

Noise and prompts.

For each model, every schedule, solver, and oracle budget is evaluated on identical noise and prompts. The prompts of SiT-XL/2 are drawn uniformly from the 10001000 ImageNet classes (Deng et al., 2009; Russakovsky et al., 2015). For SD 3.5M, the prompts used to compute FID are captions sampled at random from the MS-COCO 2014 validation split (Lin et al., 2014; Chen et al., 2015). Some of the prompts in Figures 1, 29 and 30 were written by the authors.

Encoding and decoding.

Both models were trained in the latent space of a variational autoencoder (VAE). SiT-XL/2 uses sd-vae-ft-ema (Rombach et al., 2022), and SD 3.5M uses its own VAE, which follows the autoencoder design of Stable Diffusion 3 (Esser et al., 2024).88 8 SD 3.5M VAE configuration and weights: https://huggingface.co/stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium/tree/main/vae. To generate images, we sampled standard Gaussian noise in the latent space, solved the ODE using a given schedule and solver, and then decoded the result with the model’s VAE.

Metrics.

We measure sample quality with the Fréchet Inception distance (FID) (Heusel et al., 2017) and Inception Score (IS) (Salimans et al., 2016). We write FID-NNK for an FID score that is computed using N×103N\times 10^{3} generated images. The hyperparameter sweeps calculate a cheaper FID-NNK score because they serve only to find the relative performances of different configurations. Once the best hyperparameters are identified, we calculated FID over more samples to compare different schedules with less noise. A list of which FID scores we calculated can be found in Table 5.
